title: Exercise, lifestyle & environment
summary: Lifestyle and environment drive more of the body's oxidative load than any supplement. Not smoking, losing excess visceral fat, staying fit, keeping blood sugar in range and limiting alcohol produce the largest, best-documented drops in validated markers such as urinary F2-isoprostanes. Exercise works by hormesis: each session briefly raises ROS, which trains the body's own antioxidant systems, and megadose vitamin C/E can blunt that signal. Sleep, air quality, sun protection and gum health matter at a smaller scale, while hydrogen water, grounding, ozone therapy and IV glutathione lack credible evidence.

factors.name: Regular moderate aerobic exercise
factors.headline: Moving from no activity to 150-300 min/week is associated with 30-37% lower mortality in cohorts, but twin, genetic and trial data suggest much of that gap reflects genes and pre-existing illness; the benefits on fitness, blood pressure and glucose are proven in trials.

dose.effective: 150-300 min/week of moderate activity (brisk walking, easy cycling, swimming at a pace where you can talk but not sing), e.g. 30-45 min on 5 days, or roughly 7,000-10,000 steps/day. Splitting it into 1-2 longer sessions ('weekend warrior') appears about as good as spreading it out.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 0 to 10+ times the 7.5 MET-h/week minimum (Arem 2015); 2,000-16,000 steps/day (step meta-analyses). Oxidative-stress RCTs: 45 min/day, 5 days/week at 60-75% HRmax for 12 months (Campbell 2010).
dose.too_much: No excess mortality even at 10 or more times the minimum (HR 0.69 vs inactive); the mortality curve plateaus at 3-5 times the minimum (about 450-750 min/week moderate). Very high lifelong endurance volumes raise questions about coronary calcium and atrial fibrillation (see [overtraining-ultraendurance]).
dose.timeframe: Insulin sensitivity and antioxidant enzymes shift within weeks; resting F2-isoprostane reductions were seen at 12 months and only in women whose VO2max rose more than 15%. For sperm, allow one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days) plus maturation, about 3 months.
dose.notes: Fitness gain, not minutes logged, tracked the fall in oxidative markers. For older adults, mortality benefit levelled off around 6,000-8,000 steps/day; for younger adults around 8,000-10,000. Step speed added little once total steps were counted. Avoid gram-level vitamin C/E during training blocks ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]).

factors.mechanism: Each session raises superoxide and H2O2 in working muscle, mainly from NADPH oxidase 2 at the cell membrane and to a lesser extent mitochondria. (Older views blamed mitochondrial leak; newer biosensor work identifies NOX2 as the main cytosolic source during moderate exercise, with xanthine oxidase also implicated.) These pulses oxidize KEAP1 and release Nrf2 (glutathione synthesis, SOD, catalase, HO-1), activate PGC-1alpha-driven mitochondrial biogenesis and AMPK/p38 signalling, and acutely boost GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake. Repeated pulses raise resting antioxidant capacity (mitohormesis), while reduced visceral fat, better glucose control and lower inflammation remove chronic ROS sources.
factors.interactions: Adds to [weight-loss] (diet-induced weight loss lowered F2-isoprostanes more than exercise alone). Improves [glycemic-control]. High-dose vitamin C/E, resveratrol or NAC around training can blunt molecular adaptations ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). Builds [cardiorespiratory-fitness]. Pairs with [resistance-training] for the largest mortality association. In men, very high cycling volumes are a separate issue ([cycling]); in lean women, heavy vigorous volumes can suppress ovulation ([vigorous-exercise-low-energy]).
factors.caveats: Mortality data are observational: healthier people exercise more, and sick people stop. Effects on resting oxidative markers in already-fit healthy people are small and inconsistent, and many trials use crude markers (MDA/TBARS, 'total antioxidant capacity'). A rise in oxidative markers right after a session is the signal, not damage. Sperm evidence: active men often have better counts, but a large Spanish study and a large preconception cohort found no consistent link; the strongest semen RCT comes from a group with other retracted papers.
factors.debate: How much of the observational 30-50% mortality reduction is causal is contested. Twin data show the association persists within twin pairs [exr-kujala1998], and modelling cumulative activity with lag time preserved a robust inverse dose-response [exr-lee2021]; but a newer twin analysis found that after accounting for familial factors and prevalent disease the benefit shrank to near zero, pointing to genetic confounding and reverse causation [exr-kankaanpaa2025]. The largest long-term RCT in older adults (Generation 100) found no mortality difference versus guideline advice, although controls were themselves active [exr-stensvold2020], and a critical review of ~50,000 RCT participants found no proven reduction in mortality or CVD [exr-ballin2021]. Supporters note that RCTs compare active with slightly-less-active people over short periods. For semen, positive cross-sectional data [exr-gaskins2015, exr-zou2018, exr-vaamonde2012] contrast with null findings [exr-minguezalarcon2014, exr-wise2011, exr-wise2025]; the main RCT [exr-hajizadehmaleki2017] comes from a group whose related trials were retracted.

factors.name: Vigorous exercise and high-intensity interval training (HIIT)
factors.headline: Minute for minute, intervals raise VO2max and muscle mitochondria more than steady moderate exercise (about +1-3 mL/kg/min extra VO2max; 1.7-3.9x more mitochondrial gain per hour), and vigorous training improved redox markers where gentle training did not; total mitochondrial gains converge when volume is matched.

dose.effective: 75-150 min/week of vigorous activity, or 2-3 interval sessions/week, e.g. 4 x 4 min at 85-95% HRmax with 3 min easy between (similar to the ~90%-of-peak-heart-rate intervals used in Generation 100), or 4-6 x 4-6 min at >90% HRmax (Paulsen 2014). Sprint intervals (3 x 20 s all-out) work too.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 2-4 sessions/week for 2-16 weeks; Generation 100 used 2 sessions/week for 5 years in 70-77-year-olds.
dose.too_much: Oxidative load rises with intensity x volume. Ramping HIIT to daily hard sessions over 4 weeks cut mitochondrial respiration and worsened glucose tolerance. Keep hard sessions to about 2-3 per week with easy days between.
dose.timeframe: VO2max and mitochondrial gains within 2-6 weeks; antioxidant-enzyme changes in 6-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Intensity is one of the surest ways to abolish fitness 'non-response'. People with heart disease should get medical clearance first.

factors.mechanism: Higher intensity recruits more fibres and produces larger calcium, AMP/AMPK and ROS signals per minute (NOX2-derived ROS were required for full HIIT adaptation in mice), driving PGC-1alpha, Nrf2 and mitochondrial protein synthesis. Volume is a separate driver of mitochondrial content, while relative intensity matters more for mitochondrial respiratory function. Excess intensity x volume leads to sustained ROS, glutathione depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction.
factors.interactions: Same caution about [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training] (resveratrol blunted HIIT gains in two trials). Combines with [resistance-training]. The most efficient route to [cardiorespiratory-fitness]. Excess volume leads to [overtraining-ultraendurance]. In men, the one large semen RCT found moderate continuous training beat HIIT for sperm markers.
factors.caveats: Hard mortality data for HIIT specifically are thin: Generation 100's HIIT advantage was not statistically significant. Many HIIT-vs-moderate comparisons are small, short and not matched for energy. 'Zone 2 is special' and 'only intensity matters' are both overstatements.
factors.debate: Intensity versus volume is a live argument. MacInnis, Skelly and Gibala argue intensity matters more for mitochondrial content [exr-macinnis2019, exr-macinnis2017a], while Bishop's group argues volume matters more [exr-bishop2019, exr-granata2018]. A 353-study meta-regression found similar total mitochondrial gains for continuous (23%), HIIT (27%) and sprint training (27%) after adjustment, with intervals far more time-efficient [exr-molmen2025]. A 2025 review rejects the popular claim that 'Zone 2' is uniquely good for mitochondria in the general public [exr-storoschuk2025]. HIIT beats moderate training for VO2max by a small margin in healthy adults [exr-milanovic2015] and a larger one in cardiometabolic patients [exr-weston2014], but gives similar fat loss [exr-wewege2017]. For redox markers, vigorous protocols looked better [exr-torresrojo2025], but the meta-analysis held only 7 RCTs, and HIIT and moderate exercise carried the lowest risk of large oxidative damage when volume was moderate [exr-zhou2022].

factors.name: Resistance (strength) training
factors.headline: Muscle-strengthening is associated with 10-27% lower mortality, with the biggest drop at about 30-60 min/week and the best results when combined with aerobic exercise (41% lower vs neither); it reliably builds strength (about 25-30% in older adults) and fights sarcopenia, while its 'antioxidant' effects are small.

dose.effective: 2-3 sessions/week (about 30-60 min/week total) on non-consecutive days, covering major muscle groups; 1-3 sets of 8-12 reps at a load you could lift a couple more times. Older adults benefit most from progressively heavier loads.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 0 to 150+ min/week; RCTs in older adults: 2-3 sessions/week for 8-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Some cohorts show the mortality benefit fading above about 60 min/week (J-shape), but the largest cohort found no upturn. Rapid jumps in volume caused a 7-fold rise in urinary isoprostanes and a performance drop in an overreaching study.
dose.timeframe: Strength gains within 4-8 weeks; muscle mass in 8-12 weeks; antioxidant enzyme changes (glutathione peroxidase) in 8-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Do it in addition to aerobic activity: in NIH-AARP weight training was not associated with lower mortality in people doing no aerobic exercise. Avoid high-dose vitamin C/E and post-workout cold plunges if muscle gain is the goal.

factors.mechanism: Mechanical tension and metabolic stress activate mTOR and satellite cells; local ROS and NOX-derived signals contribute to hypertrophy signalling (p38, ERK, p70S6K, which vitamin C/E blunted). Added muscle increases glucose disposal, lowering glycemic oxidative stress, and repeated sessions modestly up-regulate glutathione peroxidase.
factors.interactions: High-dose vitamin C/E blunted lean-mass and bone-density gains in older men and hypertrophy signalling in younger adults ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]); post-workout [cold-water-immersion] blunted strength gains. Strength appears to feed fitness: genetic analyses suggest grip strength raises [cardiorespiratory-fitness], not the reverse. Combines with [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
factors.caveats: Mortality data are self-reported and observational; people who lift weights differ in many ways. In older adults, muscle and function benefits are well proven by RCTs, but mortality benefit is not. Meta-analysis found a small decrease in SOD and no change in catalase, so 'strength training is an antioxidant' is an overstatement.
factors.debate: Whether 'more is worse' is disputed. Two meta-analyses found J-shaped curves with maximal benefit at about 30-60 min/week [exr-momma2022, exr-shailendra2022], echoed in older women [exr-kamada2017]; but the largest single cohort (216,339 older adults) found any weight training lowered mortality with no clear upturn, just diminishing returns [exr-shailendra2024], and the J-shape rests on few people at high volumes with wide confidence intervals. An umbrella review rated the resistance-training mortality evidence only 'suggestive' [exr-rahmati2025]. On causality, Mendelian randomization supports grip strength protecting against coronary disease and AF [exr-tikkanen2018], while grip strength's mortality association comes from observational data [exr-leong2015]. For oxidative stress, only glutathione peroxidase rose reliably [exr-cordeiro2025]; a 2026 meta-analysis in older adults found redox data from just 6 trials with moderate-to-high bias [exr-chenhuichen2026].

factors.name: Overtraining, ultra-endurance and lifelong very high exercise volumes
factors.headline: Very long or excessive exercise spikes oxidative damage markers (F2-isoprostanes up ~75% after a 50 km race; up to 7-fold in overreaching), and decades of high-volume endurance training are linked to more coronary calcium and about 2.5x the odds of atrial fibrillation, yet very fit and very active people still have the lowest mortality.

dose.effective: Train within a load you recover from: performance, sleep, mood and (for women) menstrual cycles should not decline over weeks. Build volume gradually and include easy weeks.
dose.studied_range: 50 km ultramarathon (~6.5 h); 12-week resistance block peaking at 14 t/week; 4-week progressive HIIT overload; lifelong volumes above 2000-3000 MET-min/week (roughly 3.5-5+ h/week of running) in coronary studies; 5+ Vasaloppet 90 km ski races.
dose.too_much: Oxidative/metabolic: daily very hard sessions for weeks impaired mitochondria and glucose tolerance. Cardiac: lifelong >2000 MET-min/week linked to more coronary plaque (OR 3.2); 5+ long-distance ski races to higher AF risk (HR 1.29). Male reproductive: chronic high mileage (~100+ km/week) linked to lower testosterone and semen quality ([endurance-hypogonadism-sperm]).
dose.timeframe: Acute marker spikes resolve within about 24 h after an ultramarathon; overreaching markers stayed high 96 h after sessions; cardiac remodelling and calcification reflect years to decades.
dose.notes: Occasional long events are not a health problem for trained people; chronic under-recovery is. Athletes with palpitations or a high calcium score should see a cardiologist rather than stop exercising.

factors.mechanism: Prolonged high oxygen flux plus muscle damage and immune activation (neutrophil NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase) overwhelm glutathione and vitamin E; ROS shift from signal to damage, and mitochondrial respiration falls. Repeated atrial stretch, high vagal tone and inflammation may remodel the atria (AF substrate); repeated haemodynamic and inflammatory stress may promote calcified plaque. Low energy availability suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
factors.interactions: Adequate sleep ([short-sleep]) and energy intake matter for recovery; in women see [vigorous-exercise-low-energy], in men [endurance-hypogonadism-sperm] and [cycling]. High-dose antioxidants do not solve this and may hinder adaptation ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]).
factors.caveats: Most oxidative data come from small samples of athletes. Coronary studies are cross-sectional, mostly in men, and measure plaque, not events. Spikes after an event do not prove long-term harm.
factors.debate: The 'extreme exercise J-curve' is contested. Hypothesis papers argue chronic extreme endurance training may cause atrial fibrosis, coronary calcification and arterial stiffening [exr-okeefe2012], and a Copenhagen cohort reported strenuous joggers' mortality was no better than sedentary people's (HR 1.97) [exr-schnohr2015], but that estimate was extremely imprecise (95% CI 0.48-8.14), and much larger cohorts found no excess mortality at 10x the guideline [exr-arem2015], benefit across all running doses [exr-lee2014] and no upper limit for fitness [exr-mandsager2018, exr-kokkinos2022]. Lifelong athletes do have more coronary plaque [exr-aengevaeren2017, exr-merghani2017, exr-mohlenkamp2008]; whether it is more benign (more calcified) [exr-aengevaeren2017, exr-merghani2017] or not [exr-debosscher2023] is disputed. Outcome data so far are reassuring: high-volume men with high CAC did not die more (HR 0.77, NS) [exr-defina2019], and high volume carried similar coronary-event risk but the lowest mortality [exr-berry2025]; Tour de France riders outlived the general population [exr-marijon2013]. For AF, athletes have higher odds (OR 2.46) [exr-newman2021, exr-andersen2013], and population data suggest a J-shape [exr-morseth2016, exr-morseth2018] with higher risk in very active men but lower in women [exr-kunutsor2021, exr-elliott2020], while moderate activity lowers AF [exr-mozaffarian2008, exr-mishima2021].

factors.name: High-dose antioxidant supplements during training (vitamin C/E, resveratrol, NAC)
factors.headline: Gram-level vitamin C plus vitamin E, and 150-250 mg/day resveratrol, blunted molecular and some functional training adaptations in several RCTs (e.g. 45% smaller VO2max gain with resveratrol; lean-mass gain 1.4% vs 3.9% with C+E in older men), although meta-analyses find no significant loss of VO2max, endurance or strength overall.

dose.effective: Avoid routine supplementation at about 500-1000 mg/day vitamin C plus 235-400 IU vitamin E, or 150-250+ mg/day resveratrol, during training blocks. Get antioxidants from food. Correct true deficiencies (e.g. low vitamin C or low glutathione status) under guidance.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin C 500-1000 mg/day plus vitamin E 117.5-400 IU (4-12 weeks); resveratrol 150-250 mg/day (4-8 weeks); NAC 1200-2400 mg/day orally or IV infusion; quercetin ~1000 mg/day.
dose.too_much: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E/day removed the insulin-sensitivity gain of 4 weeks' training in one trial; 1000 mg C plus 235 mg E blocked mitochondrial-protein gains and blunted bone-density gains in older men.
dose.timeframe: Effects appeared within 4-12 weeks of combined training and supplementation.
dose.notes: Timing has not been directly tested: blunting occurred both with daily dosing and when doses were taken just before and after sessions, so moving the pill a few hours away from workouts is not proven to help. Food-level intakes (fruit, vegetables, tea, cocoa) have not shown this effect. Acute NAC or other antioxidants before a single competition is a different question from chronic use during training.

factors.mechanism: Exercise ROS (largely NOX2-derived H2O2) act as second messengers that activate Nrf2, PGC-1alpha, MAPKs (p38, JNK, ERK) and insulin-signalling adaptations. Flooding cells with reducing agents can blunt this signal, reducing induction of SOD2, GPx, COX4 and mitochondrial biogenesis and hypertrophy signalling. Redundant pathways mean the blunting is partial and inconsistent.
factors.interactions: Directly undermines [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [resistance-training]. See the general supplement entries [vitamin-c-supplement], [vitamin-e-supplement], [isolated-polyphenol-supplements], [n-acetylcysteine] and [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
factors.caveats: Trials are small (11-54 people), use different doses and outcomes, and many find molecular blunting without performance loss. Isoflavones may even help lean-mass gains. NAC may help people with low glutathione.
factors.debate: Pro-blunting: vitamin C/E abolished insulin-sensitivity gains [exr-ristow2009], blocked mitochondrial-protein increases [exr-paulsen2014a, exr-gomezcabrera2008], blunted hypertrophy signalling [exr-paulsen2014b], lean-mass gains [exr-bjornsen2016] and bone gains in older men [exr-stunes2017]; resveratrol blunted VO2max, blood pressure and lipid improvements [exr-gliemann2013] and HIIT power gains [exr-scribbans2014], and impaired training effects on muscle oxidative and inflammatory markers [exr-olesen2014]; NAC infusion blunted adaptive signalling [exr-petersen2012]. Against: other RCTs found no effect on endurance adaptation or insulin sensitivity [exr-yfanti2010, exr-yfanti2011] or only partial cellular effects [exr-morrison2015]; a meta-analysis of 18 RCTs found no significant effect on VO2max (SMD -0.14), endurance, lean mass or strength [exr-clifford2020], and a strength-specific review found no effect on strength [exr-dutra2020]. Critics argued the resveratrol data do not show 'mainly negative' effects [exr-smoliga2013], and a polyphenol meta-analysis found resveratrol's harm non-significant (SMD -0.54) and isoflavones possibly helpful [exr-martineznegrin2022]. Underneath sits the question of whether exercise ROS are necessary at all: without any supplement, men with the smallest exercise-induced oxidative stress adapted least [exr-margaritelis2018], while reviews still weigh how essential the ROS signal is versus redundant pathways [exr-powers2024, exr-merry2016b]. A 'personalised' camp argues antioxidants help only deficient people: NAC improved performance only in men with low glutathione [exr-paschalis2018, exr-margaritelis2018b]. Narrative reviews converge on 'no benefit, possible harm' for chronic megadoses [exr-merry2016b, exr-mason2020, exr-higgins2020, exr-nikolaidis2012].

factors.name: Prolonged sitting and physical inactivity
factors.headline: The most sedentary quarter of adults had about 2.6x the mortality of the least sedentary in accelerometer studies, and walking breaks in sitting cut post-meal glucose and insulin by a moderate amount (SMD about -0.5); direct evidence that sitting itself raises oxidative stress is weak.

dose.effective: Break up sitting every 20-30 min with 2-5 min of light walking (better than just standing); aim to replace sitting with any movement. About 60-75 min/day of moderate activity offset the extra mortality of sitting 8+ h/day.
dose.studied_range: Acute crossover trials: 2-min light or moderate walking every 20-30 min over 5-9 h; cohorts: under 4 to over 8 h/day sitting.
dose.too_much: More than 8 h/day sitting combined with low activity; more than 20 h/week TV was linked to 44% lower sperm concentration in young men.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and insulin effects within a single day; insulin resistance appears within days of bed rest or step reduction.
dose.notes: Even high activity only attenuated, not eliminated, the risk tied to heavy TV viewing, perhaps because TV time travels with snacking and other habits.

factors.mechanism: Inactive muscle takes up little glucose (less GLUT4 translocation, lower lipoprotein lipase activity); repeated post-meal glucose and triglyceride spikes drive mitochondrial superoxide and NADPH oxidase activity. Over time, lost fitness, fat gain and inflammation add chronic ROS sources. Short-term disuse lowers mitochondrial content without raising muscle H2O2.
factors.interactions: Countered by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [post-meal-walking] and [exercise-snacks]; worsens [glycemic-control] and [excess-adiposity]. In men, prolonged sitting may add scrotal heat ([everyday-scrotal-heat]).
factors.caveats: Bed rest cut insulin sensitivity 42% but did not raise mitochondrial H2O2 or oxidative markers, so 'sitting causes oxidative stress' is not established directly; the one oxidative crossover study used a crude marker (d-ROMs) and only showed trends. Sedentary-time associations with mortality are rated weak in umbrella reviews and are hard to separate from low activity and poor health.
factors.debate: Whether sitting is an independent risk or mainly a marker of low activity is debated. A harmonised meta-analysis of 1 million adults found 60-75 min/day of moderate activity eliminated the excess mortality of high sitting time (but not of high TV time) [exr-ekelund2016]; accelerometer data still show a steep gradient for sedentary time [exr-ekelund2019], while an umbrella review graded the sedentary-mortality evidence as weak [exr-rahmati2025]. For metabolism, activity breaks lower glucose and insulin versus continuous sitting [exr-loh2020, exr-dunstan2012, exr-buffey2022], but when energy expenditure was matched the advantage of breaks over a single continuous bout was small for glucose and absent for insulin and triglycerides [exr-loh2020]. Direct oxidative effects are unproven: disuse lowered mitochondrial capacity without increasing muscle H2O2 [exr-dirks2020, exr-edwards2021], and the only sitting/oxidative crossover trial was small with borderline results [exr-takahashi2015].

factors.name: Short or insufficient sleep
factors.headline: Cutting sleep raises oxidative stress in human studies (endothelial oxidative stress after 6 weeks of 1.5 h less sleep; lower glutathione after one sleepless night), but the dramatic 'sleep loss kills via gut ROS' finding is from flies and mice.

dose.effective: 7-9 h per night on a regular schedule (adults; AASM/SRS: 7 h or more).
dose.studied_range: Human studies: one night of total deprivation; 6 weeks of 1.5 h/night restriction; observational comparison of <=6 h vs >8 h.
dose.too_much: Regularly <=6 h was associated with ~12% higher urinary 8-isoprostane; chronic restriction increased endothelial oxidative stress.
dose.timeframe: Glutathione drop after a single night; endothelial changes within 6 weeks.
dose.notes: Consistency matters as well as duration. Treat sleep apnea if present (see [sleep-apnea]).

factors.mechanism: Wakefulness raises metabolic rate and sympathetic tone, consumes glutathione and cysteine, and reduces melatonin (itself a radical scavenger and regulator of DNA repair). In animals, ROS accumulate in the gut with severe deprivation. Short sleep also worsens insulin resistance and appetite regulation.
factors.interactions: Interacts with [shift-work-circadian]. Poor sleep worsens [glycemic-control] and weight gain ([weight-loss-excess-adiposity]) and impairs recovery from [overtraining-ultraendurance].
factors.caveats: Vaccaro 2020 (Cell) was done in flies and mice with extreme deprivation; antioxidants rescued survival there, which does not mean antioxidant pills replace sleep in humans. Human data are small or observational.

factors.name: Night-shift work and circadian misalignment
factors.headline: Shift work is linked to about 17% more cardiovascular events and roughly 10% more type 2 diabetes, and lab studies that flip sleep and meals by 12 hours raise glucose, blood pressure and inflammatory markers within days; night workers show more oxidative damage and lower antioxidant defences, though these data are cross-sectional.

dose.effective: Where possible limit consecutive nights and years of rotating nights; keep the day-sleep room dark and quiet; avoid large meals during the biological night (roughly midnight to 6 am); get bright light during the shift and wear dark glasses on the way home; keep a regular schedule on days off.
dose.studied_range: Lab misalignment for 3-10 days or 3 weeks of 28-hour days; cohorts with up to decades of rotating nights (≥3 night shifts/month).
dose.too_much: CVD risk rose ~7% per additional 5 years of shift work after the first 5 years; CHD risk rose with years of rotating nights and waned after stopping.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and blood-pressure effects within 3 days of misalignment; cardiometabolic disease over years.
dose.notes: Melatonin before day sleep is being tested for DNA repair (borderline result); see [melatonin]. Short or poor sleep often coexists ([short-sleep]).

factors.mechanism: Light at night suppresses melatonin and desynchronises the central clock from peripheral clocks in liver, muscle and fat. Misalignment lowers insulin sensitivity, raises blood pressure and inflammatory cytokines and disturbs clock-controlled antioxidant and DNA-repair genes (including Nrf2 targets and OGG1). Reduced night-time melatonin is proposed to impair repair of 8-oxoguanine.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [short-sleep], [evening-light-exposure] and [late-eating]; worsens [glycemic-control] and weight gain ([excess-adiposity]).
factors.caveats: Shift workers differ from day workers in income, smoking and health (healthy-worker and selection effects). Lower urinary 8-OH-dG during night work is interpreted as reduced repair rather than less damage, which is an assumption. Sperm and egg data are observational: rotating-shift men had ~11% lower sperm concentration and lower fecundity, and women on non-day shifts had 2.3 fewer mature oocytes at IVF, but a large nurse cohort found no effect of shift work on time to pregnancy.
factors.debate: IARC classifies night shift work as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A) [kcc-iarc2019], yet a meta-analysis of 10 prospective studies found no association with breast cancer even after 30 years [kcc-travis2016]. Cardiometabolic associations are consistent [kcc-torquati2018, kcc-gan2015, kcc-gao2020, kcc-vetter2016] and supported by lab misalignment studies [kcc-scheer2009, kcc-morris2015, kcc-morris2016, kcc-buxton2012]. For oxidative stress, a cross-sectional study found worse markers in night workers but no link with social jetlag [kcc-teixeira2019]; the reduced-repair reading of 8-OH-dG [kcc-bhatti2016, kcc-bhatti2017] rests on an untested assumption and the melatonin trial was borderline [kcc-zanif2025]. Fertility: a meta-analysis linked shift work to menstrual disruption and infertility (with very high heterogeneity) [kcc-stocker2014], while nurses showed no effect on time to pregnancy [kcc-gaskins2015].

factors.name: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea
factors.headline: Repeated night-time oxygen drops and re-oxygenation act like ischemia-reperfusion; CPAP treatment raised total antioxidant capacity in a meta-analysis.

dose.effective: Get tested if you snore loudly, stop breathing during sleep, or have daytime sleepiness; use CPAP or other prescribed therapy nightly.
dose.studied_range: CPAP studies of weeks to months.
dose.timeframe: Changes within weeks to months of consistent CPAP use.
dose.notes: Weight loss often reduces apnea severity.

factors.mechanism: Cycles of hypoxia and re-oxygenation activate NADPH oxidase and xanthine oxidase and cause mitochondrial ROS bursts, much like ischemia-reperfusion injury.
factors.interactions: Strongly linked to [weight-loss-excess-adiposity]; worsened by [alcohol] at night.
factors.caveats: Total antioxidant capacity is a crude marker; studies are heterogeneous.

factors.name: Smoking tobacco (and quitting)
factors.headline: Smoking roughly doubles circulating F2-isoprostanes in a dose-dependent way; quitting lowers them within 2 weeks and to a new steady state by about 4 weeks, making it the single largest lifestyle lever.

dose.effective: Quit completely. In an RCT, cutting down from ~27 to ~18 cigarettes/day did not lower F2-isoprostanes or any other harm marker except carbon monoxide.
dose.studied_range: Studies compared heavy, moderate and non-smokers; cessation studies followed people from 2 weeks to 1 year.
dose.too_much: No safe level: urinary 8-epi-PGF2a was ~1.7x the nonsmoker level in moderate and ~3.3x in heavy smokers.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostanes fall within days, are ~20-40% lower at 2-3 weeks, and plateau about 4 weeks after quitting; cardiovascular risk falls ~39% within 5 years but takes 10-15+ years to approach never-smoker levels.
dose.notes: Nicotine replacement did not prevent the fall in isoprostanes, suggesting combustion products, not nicotine, drive most of it.

factors.mechanism: Each puff delivers large amounts of free radicals in the gas and tar phases (semiquinone radicals, NO, peroxynitrite, H2O2), plus metals and aldehydes. Smoke also activates neutrophils and vascular NADPH oxidase, depletes vitamin C and E, and uncouples eNOS.
factors.interactions: Effects add to [alcohol], [secondhand-smoke] and [outdoor-air-pollution]. Weight gain after quitting does not cancel the drop in oxidative markers. Smoking is also the main source of cadmium ([heavy-metals]) and worsens [periodontal-disease].
factors.caveats: Five days of 2 g/day vitamin C lowered smokers' isoprostanes in Reilly 1996 (vitamin E alone did not), but that is not a substitute for quitting. Smoking harms sperm parameters (meta-analysis) and is relevant to egg health (cross-link to fertility areas).

key_numbers.label: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a, heavy smokers
Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a, moderate smokers
Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a, nonsmokers

factors.name: Secondhand (passive) smoke
factors.headline: Secondhand smoke raises heart disease risk by roughly 20-30% with a dose-response, and even 30 minutes impairs coronary blood flow in healthy non-smokers.

dose.effective: Keep home and car completely smoke-free; avoid indoor smoky venues.
dose.studied_range: Experimental exposures of 30 min to a few hours; cohort exposure from household smoking.
dose.too_much: No safe level identified for cardiovascular effects; 30 min of exposure impaired coronary flow reserve in healthy nonsmokers.
dose.timeframe: Acute vascular effects within minutes to hours.
dose.notes: Ventilation and smoking in another room do not remove the exposure.

factors.mechanism: Sidestream smoke contains the same radical-generating tar and oxidant gases as mainstream smoke; tar from secondhand smoke generates H2O2 and breaks DNA in cells.
factors.interactions: Adds to [outdoor-air-pollution] and [indoor-combustion-smoke].
factors.caveats: One cross-sectional study of women with modest exposure (>=15 min, 2 days/week) found no difference in 8-isoprostane, so low-level exposure may not show up on systemic markers even though vascular effects are documented.

factors.name: E-cigarettes (vaping)
factors.headline: Vaping causes less oxidative stress than smoking but more than not using anything: a single e-cigarette acutely raised 8-iso-PGF2a, and dual use is worse than smoking alone.

dose.effective: Best: use neither. For a smoker who cannot otherwise quit, a complete switch lowers toxicant exposure; dual use should be avoided.
dose.studied_range: Acute single-session crossover; large cross-sectional cohort (PATH); 24-week switching RCT.
dose.too_much: Dual use (vaping plus smoking) had 9% higher F2-isoprostanes than smoking only.
dose.timeframe: Acute effects within minutes; switching changes over weeks.
dose.notes: Long-term data are still limited.

factors.mechanism: Heated propylene glycol/glycerol forms carbonyls (formaldehyde, acrolein), and coils release metals; nicotine activates NOX2. Exposure to radicals is far lower than from combustion.
factors.interactions: Only reduces harm versus [tobacco-smoking] if it fully replaces cigarettes.
factors.caveats: Long-term independent data are limited; the acute study tested one session in healthy adults, and the cohort data are cross-sectional.

factors.name: Alcohol
factors.headline: Alcohol raises lipid-peroxidation markers even at moderate intake (4 drinks/day of red wine raised urinary 8-iso-PGF2a versus the same wine without alcohol); there is no antioxidant benefit from drinking.

dose.effective: Less is better. If drinking, stay at or below ~100 g alcohol/week (about 7 US standard drinks or 12 UK units), spread out, with alcohol-free days; avoid binges.
dose.studied_range: Experimental: 41 g/day (4 drinks) red wine for 4 weeks; acute dosing in volunteers; cohorts across 0 to >350 g/week.
dose.too_much: Mortality rose above ~100 g/week; heavy and binge drinking drive CYP2E1 induction and liver injury.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostane rise within 4 weeks of daily moderate drinking; acute rise after single doses.
dose.notes: The polyphenols in red wine did not offset the alcohol; dealcoholized wine performed better.

factors.mechanism: Ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and, with chronic use, by induced CYP2E1, which leaks superoxide and H2O2. Acetaldehyde forms protein/DNA adducts and depletes glutathione; a high NADH/NAD+ ratio, iron mobilization and gut-derived endotoxin activating Kupffer-cell NADPH oxidase add to the load.
factors.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking]. Can worsen [short-sleep] quality, [sleep-apnea] and [weight-loss-excess-adiposity] (alcohol is calorie-dense).
factors.caveats: The 'red wine is an antioxidant' story is not supported by biomarker data. Observational 'J-curves' for heart disease are confounded.

key_numbers.label: Urinary 8-iso-PGF2a after 4 wk red wine
Urinary 8-iso-PGF2a after 4 wk dealcoholized wine

factors.name: Losing excess body fat (if overweight or obese)
factors.headline: Excess (especially visceral) fat is one of the strongest population drivers of oxidative stress; a 12-month diet-based weight-loss trial cut F2-isoprostanes by about 23%, and bariatric surgery lowers them further.

dose.effective: If BMI >=25 or waist is high, aim for 5-10% weight loss over 6-12 months via a sustained calorie deficit (e.g., ~500 kcal/day), ideally combined with exercise.
dose.studied_range: Duggan 2016: 12 months of reduced-calorie diet with or without exercise in women with BMI >25; CALERIE 2: prescribed 25% calorie restriction for 2 years in non-obese adults; sleeve gastrectomy in BMI >40.
dose.too_much: Very-low-calorie diets and rapid loss carry their own risks (gallstones, muscle loss) and need supervision.
dose.timeframe: Reductions visible by 6-12 months and scale with amount of weight lost.
dose.notes: Visceral fat matters more than subcutaneous fat. Calorie restriction lowered isoprostanes even in non-obese people.

factors.mechanism: Enlarged adipocytes and infiltrating macrophages produce ROS via NADPH oxidase, release free fatty acids that overload mitochondria, and secrete inflammatory cytokines. Obesity also causes insulin resistance and hyperglycemia. Weight loss reverses these sources.
factors.interactions: Works with [aerobic-exercise-moderate] (exercise adds fitness-related benefits); improves [glycemic-control] and [sleep-apnea].
factors.caveats: F2-isoprostanes vary with metabolic rate; one cohort found higher isoprostanes predicted less later weight gain, so interpret single measurements cautiously. Obesity is consistently linked to poorer sperm parameters (cross-link to fertility areas).

key_numbers.label: F2-isoprostane change, diet arm (12 mo)
F2-isoprostane change, diet + exercise (12 mo)
F2-isoprostane change, exercise only (12 mo)
F2-isoprostane change, controls (12 mo)

factors.name: Outdoor air pollution (PM2.5, ozone, traffic)
factors.headline: Fine particles raise oxidative and inflammatory markers within days; each 10 µg/m³ of short-term PM2.5 was linked to ~1.6% higher malondialdehyde. Individually modest, but it affects everyone in polluted areas.

dose.effective: Aim to live and exercise where annual PM2.5 is near the WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³; on high-pollution days (AQI 'unhealthy') move hard exercise indoors or away from traffic, and use HEPA filtration indoors (see [hepa-air-purifier]).
dose.studied_range: Epidemiology across typical urban levels (roughly 10-100 µg/m³ PM2.5).
dose.too_much: WHO 2021: annual PM2.5 above 5 µg/m³ and peak-season 8-h ozone above 60 µg/m³ are associated with harm; no clear safe threshold.
dose.timeframe: Marker changes within hours to days of exposure.
dose.notes: Distance from heavy traffic and indoor filtration are the practical levers for individuals.

factors.mechanism: Particles carry transition metals and quinones that redox-cycle (Fenton chemistry), activate NADPH oxidase in airway and immune cells, and trigger systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Ozone directly oxidizes lung-lining lipids and proteins.
factors.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking] and [secondhand-smoke]. Reduced by [hepa-air-purifier].
factors.caveats: Effect sizes on systemic markers are small per unit exposure; most evidence is observational. Air pollution is also linked to poorer semen quality (cross-link to sperm area).

factors.name: Indoor HEPA air purification
factors.headline: HEPA purifiers cut indoor PM2.5 by roughly half to two-thirds and lower blood pressure by about 2-4 mmHg and some inflammatory markers within days, but longer trials in children with asthma, pregnant women and older adults have mostly found no clinical benefit.

dose.effective: Run a HEPA purifier sized for the room (check its clean-air delivery rate) continuously in the bedroom and main living space when outdoor or indoor PM2.5 is elevated, with windows closed.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 48 h to 1 week of real vs sham purification in dormitories with outdoor PM2.5 roughly 40-100 µg/m³.
dose.timeframe: Effects within 48 h to 1 week; they disappear when purification stops.
dose.notes: Benefits are largest where indoor air is polluted; in clean-air regions the gain is small.

factors.mechanism: Removes redox-active particles before they reach the lungs, reducing airway NADPH-oxidase activation, inflammatory cell activation and systemic lipid peroxidation.
factors.interactions: Counters [outdoor-air-pollution] and [indoor-combustion-smoke]; does not remove gases like NO2 unless the unit has activated carbon.
factors.caveats: Trials were short, in young healthy Chinese students exposed to high pollution; long-term clinical outcomes are not yet shown.

key_numbers.label: Indoor PM2.5, sham purifier
Indoor PM2.5, real purifier

factors.name: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking
factors.headline: Wood smoke at smoky-home levels raised airway oxidative stress in one chamber study but had no systemic effect in another; gas cooking is linked to childhood asthma, though the quality of that evidence is debated.

dose.effective: Use range hoods vented outdoors when cooking (especially on gas), keep wood stoves well-sealed and burning cleanly, avoid open fireplaces as daily heat, and ventilate.
dose.studied_range: Chamber studies: 3-4 h at 220-354 µg/m³ wood-smoke particles.
dose.too_much: Exposure in poorly vented homes with daily solid-fuel burning (much higher in low-income countries using biomass).
dose.timeframe: Airway markers changed within hours.
dose.notes: Electric or induction cooking removes the NO2 source.

factors.mechanism: Combustion particles and gases (NO2, aldehydes, PAHs) generate airway ROS and inflammation; NO2 is itself an oxidant.
factors.interactions: Similar pathways to [outdoor-air-pollution]; mitigated by [hepa-air-purifier] for particles.
factors.caveats: Controlled wood-smoke studies are small and inconsistent. The gas-stove literature is mostly cross-sectional; a 2013 meta-analysis found OR 1.32 for asthma while a 2023 review judged the evidence too low-quality for causal conclusions.

factors.name: Sun/UV exposure (photoaging and skin DNA damage)
factors.headline: Chronic unprotected UV is the main driver of visible skin aging and of skin cancer: a single exposure switched on collagen-degrading MMPs and raised collagen breakdown 58% in human skin, and identical twins with more sun exposure looked older.

dose.effective: Avoid sunburn. Around midday and whenever the UV index is high, use shade, clothing and a hat, plus daily broad-spectrum sunscreen on exposed skin (see [sunscreen]).
dose.studied_range: Experimental studies used single or repeated (every 2 days) erythemal UV doses on buttock skin; twin and cohort data reflect lifetime exposure.
dose.too_much: Any sunburn, tanning beds, and long cumulative outdoor exposure without protection.
dose.timeframe: MMP induction within hours of one exposure, sustained about 7 days with repeated exposure; visible photoaging accrues over years to decades.
dose.notes: Vitamin D: a consensus panel concluded that sunscreen used to prevent sunburn is unlikely to compromise vitamin D status; people with low levels or strict photoprotection needs should test and supplement rather than tan.

factors.mechanism: UVB (290-320 nm) is absorbed directly by DNA, forming cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and 6-4 photoproducts. UVA (320-400 nm) penetrates deeper into the dermis and is absorbed by cellular chromophores that generate singlet oxygen and superoxide, producing 8-oxo-dG, lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial DNA deletions; in whole human skin UVA also forms CPDs, which outnumber 8-oxo-dG and are repaired more slowly. ROS-activated MAP kinase signalling drives AP-1, which induces MMP-1 (collagenase), MMP-3 and MMP-9 and suppresses new procollagen, while NF-kB drives inflammation. Repeated sub-burning exposures leave behind fragmented collagen: photoaging.
factors.interactions: [tobacco-smoking] and traffic-related [outdoor-air-pollution] add to extrinsic skin aging. Oral antioxidants do not replace UV protection: 30 mg/day beta-carotene ([beta-carotene-supplement]) had no effect on photoaging or skin cancer in Nambour, and the SU.VI.MAX antioxidant capsule raised skin cancer in women. Protection and repair options: [sunscreen], [topical-retinoids], and in high-risk people [nicotinamide].
factors.caveats: Whole-body oxidative-marker effects of ordinary sun exposure are not well documented; the evidence concerns skin. Visible light and near-infrared also generate ROS in skin in lab and biopsy studies, but whether everyday doses cause visible aging is unproven (visible light does matter for melasma and darker skin types). Twin and survey studies are observational and partly self-reported.
factors.debate: Mechanism weighting: the textbook picture of UVA as an 'oxidative' waveband is complicated by evidence that CPDs, not 8-oxo-dG, are the predominant UVA lesion in whole human skin [skb-mouret2006]. Beyond UV: visible light induced ROS and MMP-1 in skin equivalents [skb-liebel2012] and IR-A induced MMP-1 in human skin in vivo [skb-schroeder2008], but Diffey and Cadars argue solar IR doses equal those of furnace workers who show little chronic damage, so IR-protection claims are premature [skb-diffey2016]. Vitamin D: concern that sun avoidance causes deficiency is countered by a consensus review concluding normal sunscreen use does not compromise status [skb-passeron2019], though that panel included cosmetics-industry scientists.

MMP induction blocked by tretinoin pretreatment

factors.name: Chronic psychological stress and depression
factors.headline: Chronic stress and depression are associated with higher oxidative damage markers (depression: F2-isoprostanes effect size ~0.5), but causality and the size of any modifiable effect are uncertain.

dose.effective: Treat depression and anxiety with proven methods (therapy, medication when indicated, exercise, sleep); reduce chronic stressors where possible.
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional comparisons of high vs low perceived stress and depressed vs non-depressed groups.
dose.timeframe: Unknown for oxidative markers.
dose.notes: Exercise and sleep improvements are the best-evidenced stress interventions that also affect oxidative stress.

factors.mechanism: Chronic stress raises cortisol and catecholamines, increases metabolic rate and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), and is associated with lower telomerase activity; catecholamine auto-oxidation produces ROS.
factors.interactions: Stress worsens [short-sleep], drinking ([alcohol]), smoking and eating, which are likely bigger oxidative contributors than stress itself.
factors.caveats: The famous Epel 2004 study was cross-sectional in 58 women; it shows association, not cause. Confounding by health behaviours is likely in most studies.

factors.name: Meditation, mindfulness and yoga
factors.headline: Mind-body practices reliably lower cortisol and blood pressure modestly, but evidence that they reduce oxidative damage comes from small, weakly controlled trials.

dose.effective: If you enjoy it: ~20-45 min sessions, most days (yoga trials typically 2-5 sessions/week for 8-12 weeks).
dose.studied_range: Yoga/MBSR trials of 6-16 weeks.
dose.timeframe: 8-12 weeks in most trials.
dose.notes: Physical yoga also counts as light exercise.

factors.mechanism: Lower sympathetic and HPA-axis activity reduces cortisol and catecholamines; gene-expression studies show down-regulation of NF-kB inflammatory pathways.
factors.interactions: Addresses [psychological-stress]; can improve [short-sleep].
factors.caveats: Oxidative-marker trials are small (e.g., 29 people), often lack active controls, and use crude markers like malondialdehyde. Grade honestly as limited.

factors.name: Sauna bathing (Finnish sauna) and passive heat
factors.headline: Frequent sauna use is linked to lower cardiovascular death and inflammation in Finnish cohorts, and heat therapy improves vascular function in trials, but direct oxidative-stress benefits are unproven; sauna clearly impairs sperm (reversibly).

dose.effective: Cohort 'high' group: 4-7 sessions/week, sessions longer than 19 min, in a traditional Finnish sauna (hot and dry, ~80-90 C as in the sperm study); trial: 40.5 C hot-water immersion for 60 min, 4-5x/week for 8 weeks.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 1 to 4-7 sessions/week, <11 to >19 min; sperm study: 2 x 15 min/week at 80-90 C for 3 months.
dose.too_much: Men trying to conceive should avoid sauna: 2 sessions/week at 80-90 C for 3 months reduced sperm count and motility and damaged chromatin; avoid alcohol in the sauna; caution with unstable heart disease, pregnancy and low blood pressure.
dose.timeframe: Vascular changes in 8 weeks; sperm recovered ~6 months after stopping.
dose.notes: Cohort men who used saunas more often were also fitter and healthier; benefits may partly reflect that.

factors.mechanism: Heat stress induces heat-shock proteins, increases shear stress and nitric oxide production (like exercise), and may trigger mild hormetic ROS signalling. For testes, heat disrupts spermatogenesis and increases sperm oxidative/chromatin damage.
factors.interactions: Partially mimics [aerobic-exercise-moderate] vascular effects but is not a substitute for exercise. Cross-link to sperm area: heat is a strong, reversible harm to sperm.
factors.caveats: The KIHD cohort found no association between sauna frequency and GGT (the oxidative-stress proxy studied) despite lower CRP. Oxidative claims for sauna are mostly extrapolation.

factors.name: Cold-water immersion and winter swimming
factors.headline: Regular winter swimmers show higher baseline antioxidant enzymes (a hormesis signal), but human evidence for health benefits is small and inconsistent, and cold plunges right after strength training blunt muscle gains.

dose.effective: If you do it: brief immersions (seconds to a few minutes) in cold water, with acclimatization and never alone; keep it away from (at least several hours after) strength sessions.
dose.studied_range: Winter-swimming studies over a season; post-exercise CWI 10 min after each strength session for 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: Cold shock and arrhythmia risk on sudden immersion, especially with heart disease; hypothermia.
dose.timeframe: Antioxidant adaptations seen after a winter season.
dose.notes: Each plunge itself causes acute oxidative stress; adaptation follows repetition.

factors.mechanism: Cold triggers a catecholamine surge and increased metabolic rate (brown-fat thermogenesis), generating a transient ROS pulse that may up-regulate glutathione, SOD and catalase. Post-exercise cooling reduces blood flow and anabolic signalling.
factors.interactions: Blunts adaptations to [resistance-training] if done immediately after.
factors.caveats: Winter swimmers are a self-selected healthy group; most studies are small, single-sex and uncontrolled. Reviews rate many claimed benefits as resting on weak or anecdotal data.

factors.name: Heavy metals: lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury
factors.headline: Toxic metals deplete glutathione and drive oxidative damage; even at normal background levels, urinary cadmium tracked oxidative DNA damage in non-smokers.

dose.effective: Do not smoke (the main cadmium source); test well water for arsenic; check old homes for lead paint and pipes; choose low-mercury fish (salmon, sardines) over high-mercury species (swordfish, king mackerel, shark).
dose.studied_range: Observational studies at background and occupational exposure levels.
dose.too_much: Occupational exposures and contaminated water are the main high-dose risks.
dose.timeframe: Body burdens of cadmium and lead decline slowly (years).
dose.notes: Chelation 'detox' for people without documented poisoning is not supported.

factors.mechanism: Cadmium, lead and arsenic bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inhibit antioxidant enzymes; redox-active metals (iron, copper) generate hydroxyl radical via Fenton chemistry; arsenic can generate H2O2.
factors.interactions: Cadmium exposure is largely from [tobacco-smoking].
factors.caveats: Spot-urine biomarker studies are prone to confounding: in one study the strongest metal associations were for essential selenium and copper.

factors.name: Blood-sugar control and diabetes
factors.headline: Type 2 diabetes was associated with ~75% higher urinary 8-iso-PGF2a, which tracked day-to-day glucose swings (r = 0.86) more than HbA1c; reducing glucose spikes is a meaningful lever.

dose.effective: Keep fasting glucose and HbA1c in the normal range (individualized targets with diabetes); limit post-meal spikes with fibre-rich whole foods, fewer refined carbohydrates, and a short walk after meals.
dose.studied_range: Case-control comparison using continuous glucose monitoring.
dose.too_much: Large post-meal excursions and sustained hyperglycemia.
dose.timeframe: Glucose swings respond within days; HbA1c over ~3 months.
dose.notes: Exercise and weight loss are the main non-drug tools.

factors.mechanism: High glucose overloads mitochondria, causing superoxide overproduction that activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways; AGE-RAGE binding further activates NADPH oxidase and NF-kB.
factors.interactions: Improved by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [resistance-training], [weight-loss-excess-adiposity] and [short-sleep] correction.
factors.caveats: Monnier 2006 was small (21 patients); the 'swings matter more than average glucose' idea is supported mechanistically but outcome trials targeting variability are limited.

factors.name: Gum disease (periodontitis)
factors.headline: Chronic periodontitis is associated with lower systemic antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde, and periodontal treatment lowers oxidative markers.

dose.effective: Brush twice daily, clean between teeth daily, and get professional cleaning and periodontal treatment if gums bleed or recede.
dose.studied_range: Non-surgical periodontal therapy studies with >=6 weeks follow-up.
dose.timeframe: Markers improved within 6 weeks to months after treatment.
dose.notes: Smoking and diabetes strongly worsen periodontitis.

factors.mechanism: Chronic bacterial infection recruits neutrophils that release superoxide, hypochlorous acid and other oxidants locally, with spill-over systemic inflammation.
factors.interactions: Worsened by [tobacco-smoking] and poor [glycemic-control].
factors.caveats: Most data are from saliva and gum fluid; systemic effects are less consistent and few trials are randomized.

factors.name: Hydration
factors.headline: Being dehydrated increased muscle H2O2 after resistance exercise in one small study; there is no evidence that drinking extra water beyond thirst lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Drink to thirst; aim for pale-yellow urine; replace fluids lost in heavy sweating.
dose.studied_range: One crossover study with 24 h fluid restriction.
dose.too_much: Overdrinking (hyponatremia) is a risk in endurance events.
dose.notes: 'Alkaline' or 'structured' water claims have no support.

factors.mechanism: Dehydration raises cell stress and may increase ROS production in exercising muscle.
factors.interactions: Relevant to [overtraining-ultraendurance] and [sauna].
factors.caveats: Evidence is a single small study; 'flushing out toxins' with water is not a real antioxidant mechanism.

factors.name: Hydrogen-rich water / molecular hydrogen
factors.headline: Molecular hydrogen scavenges hydroxyl radicals in lab and animal studies, but human trials are small and show at most modest effects on lipids, not established oxidative-stress benefits.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Trials used ~0.5-1.5 L/day of hydrogen-rich water.
dose.studied_range: Pilot RCTs of weeks to 6 months.
dose.too_much: Appears safe.
dose.notes: Hydrogen escapes quickly from water once opened.

factors.mechanism: H2 reacts selectively with hydroxyl radical and peroxynitrite; may also signal via Nrf2. Doses from drinking water are tiny and transient.
factors.interactions: No known interactions.
factors.caveats: Most trials are small and come from a few research groups; the telomere result came from a 40-person pilot with many outcomes, and the lipid meta-analysis pooled only 7 small studies.

factors.name: Grounding / earthing
factors.headline: Claims that touching the ground supplies 'antioxidant electrons' have no credible mechanism and rest on small, mostly unblinded studies by proponents.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Walking barefoot outdoors is harmless and pleasant if you enjoy it.
dose.studied_range: Small studies of grounding mats/patches over nights to weeks.
dose.notes: No validated oxidative biomarker improvement in rigorous trials.

factors.mechanism: Proposed mechanism (free electrons neutralizing radicals) is not physiologically plausible: radical chemistry occurs inside cells and is buffered by enzymes and glutathione.
factors.interactions: None.
factors.caveats: The main review is by advocates; independent replication is lacking.

factors.name: Ozone therapy (autohemotherapy, ozone saunas)
factors.headline: Ozone is a strong oxidant and a regulated air pollutant; 'ozone therapy' is marketed as hormetic, but a Cochrane review could draw no firm conclusions even for its best-studied use (diabetic foot ulcers).

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress.
dose.studied_range: Clinical trials of ozone for wounds and other conditions; small and high risk of bias.
dose.too_much: Inhaled ozone is toxic to the lungs; WHO's peak-season 8-h outdoor guideline is 60 µg/m³.
dose.notes: Intravenous and blood-handling procedures carry their own procedural risks.

factors.mechanism: Ozone reacts with lipids to form ozonides, aldehydes and H2O2; proponents claim this triggers Nrf2-mediated hormesis.
factors.interactions: Opposite of [outdoor-air-pollution] advice: ozone exposure is a recognized harm.
factors.caveats: Hormesis claims are mechanistic; human outcome evidence is poor.

factors.name: Intravenous (IV) or oral glutathione
factors.headline: IV glutathione is cleared from blood with a half-life of ~14 minutes; oral glutathione raised blood stores 17-35% in one 6-month RCT, but no trial shows clinical benefit for oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Not recommended. Oral trial used 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months; levels returned to baseline within a month of stopping.
dose.studied_range: IV: single 2 g/m² infusion pharmacokinetics; oral: 6-month RCT.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown; usual infusion risks apply to IV use.
dose.timeframe: IV effect gone within about an hour; oral effect builds over months and reverses within a month.
dose.notes: Cells make their own glutathione from cysteine, glycine and glutamate; exercise, sleep and not smoking support it.

factors.mechanism: Exogenous glutathione is broken down in plasma and by gamma-glutamyl transferase into amino acids; cells resynthesize glutathione internally.
factors.interactions: Lifestyle factors that preserve glutathione: avoiding [tobacco-smoking] and [alcohol], [short-sleep] correction.
factors.caveats: Biomarker increases do not equal health benefit; no outcome trials.

factors.name: Improving cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max)
factors.headline: Fitness is one of the strongest predictors of survival: each 1-MET higher VO2max (about 3.5 mL/kg/min) is associated with 11-17% lower mortality, and the least fit have about 4x the risk of the most fit, with no upper limit; but genetic analyses question how much of this is caused by fitness itself.

dose.effective: Aim to move out of the bottom fifth for your age and sex, then keep improving: each +1 MET counts. Combine 150+ min/week of aerobic activity with 1-2 weekly interval sessions (e.g. 4 x 4 min at 85-95% HRmax); add sessions or intensity if fitness does not budge.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: fitness from under 5 to over 14 METs on treadmill tests; training studies: 60-300 min/week for 6-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: No upper limit of benefit was seen for measured fitness, even at the 98th percentile (elite).
dose.timeframe: VO2max rises measurably within 4-8 weeks of training; fitness change over years tracks mortality.
dose.notes: The lowest mortality in 750,302 veterans was at about 14 METs (roughly 49 mL/kg/min). In older adults (70-77 years), being moderately fit gave most of the benefit. 'Non-responders' to standard programs responded when weekly time or intensity was raised.

factors.mechanism: Training raises stroke volume, blood and haemoglobin volume, capillary density and muscle mitochondrial content (PGC-1alpha), via the same redox-signalling and hormesis pathways as [aerobic-exercise-moderate]. High fitness travels with lower blood pressure, visceral fat, insulin resistance and inflammation, all chronic ROS sources.
factors.interactions: Built by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and even [exercise-snacks]; strength gains appear to feed fitness ([resistance-training]). Lower body fat raises VO2max per kg ([weight-loss]).
factors.caveats: Baseline fitness and trainability partly reflect genes, body composition and health status, so people with undiagnosed disease test as 'unfit'. Most data come from people referred for treadmill tests. VO2max in mL/kg/min also falls with fat mass, so part of the signal is adiposity.
factors.debate: Proponents point to large, consistent cohorts with graded associations and no upper limit [exr-mandsager2018, exr-kokkinos2022, exr-kodama2009, exr-han2022, exr-lang2024], an AHA call to treat fitness as a vital sign [exr-ross2016], and evidence that improving fitness over time tracks lower mortality [exr-imboden2019]. Skeptics note that a two-sample Mendelian randomization found genetically predicted VO2max was not causally associated with longevity, while activity, lean mass and lower fat did raise VO2max [exr-kjaergaard2025], that genetic analyses point from strength to fitness rather than the reverse [exr-norris2024], that the certainty of the meta-analytic evidence is very low to moderate [exr-lang2024], and that the only long-term exercise RCT in older adults did not reduce mortality significantly [exr-stensvold2020]. In older adults, benefit may plateau above moderate fitness [exr-tari2025]. Trainability is also debated: non-response to standard doses disappears at higher doses [exr-montero2017] or intensities [exr-ross2015].

factors.name: Walking after meals
factors.headline: A 10-15 minute walk after each main meal lowered post-meal glucose 12% more than one daily 30-minute walk in type 2 diabetes (22% after dinner), and post-meal exercise reliably blunts glucose spikes (effect size about -0.3); oxidative-stress benefits are inferred, not measured directly.

dose.effective: 10-15 min of easy-to-brisk walking after each main meal, especially the largest (often evening) meal; longer bouts (over 30 min) did more in meta-analysis.
dose.studied_range: Crossover trials: 2-min walks every 20-30 min, 10 min after each meal, 3 x 15 min post-meal, up to 60 min.
dose.too_much: None known at walking intensity.
dose.timeframe: Acute: lowers the glucose curve of that meal and 24-h mean glucose; long-term HbA1c effects are not well established.
dose.notes: Effects are biggest in people with type 2 diabetes, prediabetes or obesity and after carbohydrate-heavy meals. Light walking beat standing breaks. Evidence on the ideal start time is inconsistent.

factors.mechanism: Contracting muscle takes up glucose independently of insulin (AMPK, NOX2-ROS and calcium-mediated GLUT4 translocation), flattening the post-meal glucose and triglyceride peaks that drive mitochondrial superoxide, NADPH oxidase activation and AGE formation.
factors.interactions: Directly supports [glycemic-control] and blunts spikes from [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] meals. A practical way to break [sedentary-time]. Complements, but does not replace, [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
factors.caveats: Most trials are short crossover studies with continuous glucose monitors in small groups; long-term outcome trials are lacking. Oxidative-marker evidence is limited to small studies with crude markers.
factors.debate: That post-meal activity lowers glucose is well replicated [exr-reynolds2016, exr-dipietro2013, exr-kang2023, exr-buffey2022, exr-dunstan2012]. Debated: whether timing or just total movement matters. Breaks beat continuous exercise only modestly once energy expenditure is matched [exr-loh2020], and one meta-analysis found longer bouts mattered more than early start times [exr-kang2023]. Whether lower glucose spikes translate into less oxidative stress in people is mostly inferred; a small crossover found only trends in a crude oxidative marker [exr-takahashi2015].

factors.name: Exercise snacks and vigorous intermittent lifestyle activity (VILPA)
factors.headline: In non-exercisers, three 1-2 minute bursts of vigorous everyday activity a day (stairs, fast uphill walking, carrying loads) were associated with 38-40% lower mortality and 48-49% lower cardiovascular death, and small RCTs show stair or sprint 'snacks' raise VO2peak modestly (about 4% for sprint snacks); the cohort data may overstate the benefit.

dose.effective: 3-5 bouts a day of about 1 minute of vigorous effort (fast stair climbing, e.g. 60 steps; brisk uphill walking; 20-second sprints), totalling about 3-5 min/day; or 6 x 1-min hard intervals before meals.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 0 to ~10 VILPA bouts/day (median 3-5); RCTs: 3 x 60-step stair climbs or 3 x 20-s sprints, 3 days/week for 6 weeks.
dose.too_much: None known; the mortality curve flattened beyond about 8 bouts/day.
dose.timeframe: VO2peak gains in 6 weeks; glucose effects the same day.
dose.notes: A practical entry point for people who do not exercise. Benefit for cardiovascular events was clearer in women than men in UK Biobank.

factors.mechanism: Brief vigorous efforts produce the same metabolic, calcium and ROS signals as interval training (AMPK, PGC-1alpha), raise heart rate near maximum, and improve post-meal glucose uptake.
factors.interactions: A stepping stone to [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [cardiorespiratory-fitness]; breaks up [sedentary-time]; pre-meal snacks complement [post-meal-walking].
factors.caveats: VILPA data come from wrist accelerometers in UK Biobank volunteers (healthier than average) and one smaller US sample; people able to climb stairs fast may simply be healthier. RCTs are small (9-28 people) and short.
factors.debate: The UK Biobank analyses report large, near-linear benefits for mortality, cancer and cardiovascular events [exr-stamatakis2022, exr-stamatakis2023, exr-stamatakis2025, exr-ahmadi2023]. A US national replication found a similar 44% lower mortality, but when people with prevalent heart disease or cancer were excluded the confidence intervals mostly crossed 1, consistent with reverse causation [exr-koemel2026]. Training studies confirm fitness gains but they are modest and small [exr-jenkins2019, exr-little2019], and pre-meal snacks improved glucose in only 9 people [exr-francois2014]. Proponents frame snacks as proof-of-concept rather than a replacement for guidelines [exr-islam2022]. The related 'weekend warrior' pattern is better supported: concentrating activity into 1-2 days gave similar mortality and cardiovascular associations to spreading it out [exr-odonovan2017, exr-dossantos2022, exr-khurshid2023, exr-kim2025].

factors.name: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen
factors.headline: The best-proven way to prevent oxidative skin aging: in the Nambour RCT, daily sunscreen stopped measurable photoaging (24% less aging than discretionary use over 4.5 years), cut squamous-cell tumours by 39%, and was followed by half as many melanomas over the next 10 years.

dose.effective: Broad-spectrum SPF 15 or higher applied every morning to the face, neck, arms and hands, as in the Nambour trial; reapply after swimming, heavy sweating or long periods outdoors.
dose.studied_range: SPF 15+ broad-spectrum, daily for 4.5 years, adults 25-75 (photoaging analysis in those under 55); melanoma follow-up 10 years after the trial ended.
dose.too_much: No harm was seen in the trial. All six common organic filters are absorbed into blood above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after one application; the clinical significance is unknown.
dose.timeframe: Photoaging differences after 4.5 years; melanoma differences emerged over the following decade.
dose.notes: Sunscreen filters block photons before they generate ROS; they are not antioxidants. Iron-oxide (tinted) sunscreens also block visible light, which improved melasma in one RCT. Sunscreen is one part of sun protection alongside shade, clothing and timing.

factors.mechanism: Organic and mineral UV filters absorb or scatter UVB and UVA, preventing direct DNA photoproducts and the UVA-driven singlet oxygen and superoxide that lead to 8-oxo-dG, lipid peroxidation and AP-1/MMP-mediated collagen breakdown. Standard filters do little against visible light and near-infrared; adding antioxidants to sunscreen reduced IR-A-induced MMP-1 in one small trial.
factors.interactions: Works on the cause of [uv-sun-exposure]. [topical-vitamin-c] and other topical antioxidants are add-ons, not substitutes. Oral [beta-carotene-supplement] added nothing in the same trial. Sunscreen does not meaningfully lower vitamin D status at normal use ([vitamin-d]).
factors.caveats: The only long-term RCT is Nambour (one Australian community, high UV). The melanoma result rests on 11 versus 22 cases and was borderline (P=0.051). Sunscreen did not reduce basal-cell carcinoma.
factors.debate: Observational meta-analyses of mostly case-control studies found no association between sunscreen use and melanoma (OR 1.10) [skb-silva2018], feeding claims that sunscreen does not prevent skin cancer. Rueegg and colleagues showed that adjusting for sun exposure, sunburn and skin type consistently shifts estimates toward protection, and that the only RCT showed HR 0.49 [skb-rueegg2019, skb-green2011]: sun-seeking, fair-skinned people use more sunscreen, which confounds the observational data. Safety: systemic absorption of organic filters [skb-matta2020] prompted calls for more toxicology, but no harm has been shown. Vitamin D concerns are addressed by [skb-passeron2019].

factors.name: Topical vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid serum), alone or with vitamin E and ferulic acid
factors.headline: Vitamin C only gets into skin as L-ascorbic acid at pH below 3.5 (best at about 20%); small vehicle-controlled trials (7 RCTs, 139 people in total) show modest smoothing of wrinkles and lighter pigment, and a 15% C + 1% E + ferulic acid mix doubled UV protection in pig skin, an add-on to sunscreen rather than a replacement.

dose.effective: 10-20% L-ascorbic acid at pH below 3.5, applied once daily in the morning under sunscreen; the best-studied combination is 15% L-ascorbic acid + 1% alpha-tocopherol + ferulic acid.
dose.studied_range: 5-20% L-ascorbic acid for 3-6 months in clinical trials; 4 days of pretreatment in photoprotection studies.
dose.too_much: Concentrations above 20% did not increase skin uptake; the low pH can sting or irritate.
dose.timeframe: Skin levels saturate after about 3 daily applications and fall with a half-life of about 4 days; visible change needs 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Common derivatives (magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, ascorbyl palmitate) did not raise skin vitamin C in pig skin. L-ascorbic acid is unstable in solution; ferulic acid improved the stability of the C+E formula. Eating or swallowing vitamin C does not deliver comparable skin levels ([vitamin-c-supplement]).

factors.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble antioxidant in skin, scavenging UV-generated radicals and regenerating alpha-tocopherol from the tocopheroxyl radical. It is also the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases needed to make stable collagen, and it inhibits tyrosinase, which explains the pigment-lightening effect.
factors.interactions: Synergy with vitamin E and ferulic acid in the same formula. Complements [sunscreen] (blocks photons) by mopping up ROS from the photons that get through, including visible and IR-A light. [topical-retinoids] have stronger evidence for wrinkles.
factors.caveats: The trials are small, short, split-face or split-arm, and often run or funded by the product developers. There are no long-term trials of visible aging and none on skin cancer. 'Doubled photoprotection' means a protection factor of about 8, measured in pig skin, well below a typical sunscreen.
factors.debate: Supporters point to vehicle-controlled improvements in wrinkles and pigmentation [skb-humbert2003, skb-correia2023] and to a 31-study Bayesian pooling showing dose-dependent prevention of UV pigmentation [skb-dedormael2019]. Sceptics note the pooled studies were all run in-house by L'Oreal, the key formulation papers come from the group that developed the C+E+ferulic serum [skb-lin2003, skb-lin2005, skb-pinnell2001], and the only independent systematic review found just 139 participants across 7 trials [skb-correia2023]. No independent large RCT exists.

factors.name: Topical retinoids (tretinoin, retinol)
factors.headline: The best-proven topical treatment for photoaging: tretinoin improved 14 of 15 treated faces versus none on vehicle in 16 weeks, retinol 0.4% smoothed fine wrinkles even at age 87, and tretinoin blocked 70-80% of UV-induced collagenase; it does not prevent skin cancer.

dose.effective: Prescription tretinoin cream at night (0.1% in the classic trials; lower strengths if irritated), or over-the-counter retinol (0.4% lotion up to 3 times a week in the elderly-skin trial); build up from every second or third night.
dose.studied_range: Tretinoin 0.1% daily for 16 weeks to 5.5 years; retinol 0.4% up to 3 times weekly for 24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Irritation, redness and peeling (retinoid dermatitis) are common and dose-related. Avoid during pregnancy as a precaution, although first-trimester topical tretinoin exposure showed no excess birth defects in a 106-pregnancy cohort.
dose.timeframe: Visible improvement from about 16-24 weeks, with continued use needed to maintain it.
dose.notes: Retinoids are not antioxidants: they work downstream of UV-generated ROS by blocking AP-1-driven MMPs and rebuilding matrix. Use with daily [sunscreen].

factors.mechanism: Retinoic acid binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors, which antagonize AP-1 (c-Jun/c-Fos). This blocks the UV- and ROS-triggered induction of MMP-1, MMP-3 and MMP-9, while increasing procollagen I and glycosaminoglycan synthesis and normalizing epidermal turnover.
factors.interactions: Complements [sunscreen] (prevention) and [uv-sun-exposure] avoidance; stronger evidence than [topical-vitamin-c] for wrinkles. Oral retinoid-like compounds such as high-dose [beta-carotene-supplement] are a different story and are not a substitute.
factors.caveats: Most photoaging trials are small and vehicle-controlled over months, with clinician-graded outcomes. In the large VATTC trial, high-dose tretinoin did not prevent basal- or squamous-cell carcinoma, and the trial stopped early because of excess deaths in the tretinoin arm.
factors.debate: Efficacy for photoaging is not seriously disputed [skb-weiss1988, skb-kafi2007, skb-fisher1997]. The disputes concern cancer and safety: VATTC showed no prevention of keratinocyte carcinoma [skb-weinstock2012] and an unexpected mortality excess [skb-weinstock2009]; the investigators judged it unlikely to be causal given minor baseline imbalances and no plausible mechanism for a topical cream, but the signal has never been explained. Pregnancy: systemic retinoids are teratogens, yet a prospective cohort found no excess malformations after topical tretinoin [skb-loureiro2005], so advice to avoid it is precautionary.

factors.name: Micro- and nanoplastics
factors.headline: Plastic particles have been reported in blood, placenta, testis and brain, and one NEJM cohort linked plastic in carotid plaque to 4.5x more heart attacks, strokes and deaths, but the tissue numbers rest on a method that can mistake fat for polyethylene, and nothing yet shows that cutting exposure lowers body burden or risk.

dose.effective: No proven dose or intervention. Low-cost steps that cut measured particle release: don't microwave food, drinks or infant formula in plastic (up to 2 billion nanoparticles per cm2 in 3 min), prefer tap over bottled water where tap is safe (~240,000 particles/L in bottled water by single-particle imaging), use loose tea or non-plastic teabags (one plastic teabag at 95 C: ~15 billion particles), and vacuum regularly.
dose.studied_range: Estimated intake 39,000-52,000 particles/year from food (74,000-121,000 with inhalation); tissue concentrations reported from ~1.6 ug/mL (blood) to ~4,900 ug/g (brain) by pyrolysis GC/MS.
dose.timeframe: Unknown: uptake, clearance and half-lives of plastic particles in people have not been measured.
dose.notes: Exposure studies count particles released into water or food simulants in the lab; whether those particles are absorbed is unknown. No human study has tested whether any change lowers tissue levels.

factors.mechanism: In cells and animals, polystyrene and other particles trigger oxidative stress (mitochondrial ROS, NADPH oxidase), NLRP3/NF-kB inflammation, barrier disruption and immune changes; additives and adsorbed chemicals may contribute. Most experiments use pristine spheres at doses above estimated human exposure.
factors.interactions: Heated plastic food contact also leaches [plastics-chemicals]; household dust also carries flame retardants. No study has tested whether air purifiers or vacuuming lower microplastic body burden.
factors.caveats: Pyrolysis GC/MS cannot cleanly separate polyethylene and PVC signals from fats and other tissue components; microscopy-based methods in the same tissues find only a handful of particles. No study has met all basic quality-control criteria. Cross-sectional autopsy data cannot show cause (dementia brains may simply clear less).
factors.debate: Tissue burden: Py-GC/MS studies report milligram-per-gram plastic in brain [env-nihart2025], hundreds of ug/g in testis [env-hu2024] and placenta [env-garcia2024]. Against this, a validation study concluded Py-GC/MS is currently unsuitable for polyethylene and PVC in biological samples because of matrix interference [env-rauert2025]; lipid interference forces much higher polyethylene detection limits [env-almeida2026]; a QA/QC screen of 101 human studies found none met all essential criteria [env-lane2026]; analytical chemists published correspondence on the brain study [env-amonikh2025]; the brain paper required a correction for duplicated images and methods [env-nihart2025b]; and a comment on the testis study listed missing blanks and validation, to which the authors replied by trimming their reliable polymer list from 12 to 6 [env-uppu2025, env-hu2025]. Microscopy finds far fewer particles: 16 particles in 15 olfactory bulbs [env-amatolourenco2024]. Cardiovascular: plaque polyethylene predicted events (HR 4.53) [env-marfella2024], but this was one observational cohort measuring exactly the polymers (PE, PVC) that Py-GC/MS struggles with [env-rauert2025], and several letters were published with an author reply [env-glazier2024, env-wang2024, env-kalkman2024, env-holda2024, env-marfella2024b]. Mechanism: animal reproductive studies mostly report harm, but most lacked particle characterization or dose-response [env-due2026]. Exposure counts are also disputed: the teabag study drew a published comment [env-busse2020].
