factors.name: PFAS ('forever chemicals')
factors.headline: PFAS stay in blood for years (half-lives 2.7-5.3 years) and are linked to weaker vaccine responses, higher cholesterol, lower birth weight and some cancers; NASEM advises testing likely-exposed people with extra screening above 2 and 20 ng/mL, and regular plasma or blood donation measurably lowered serum PFOS in an RCT.

dose.effective: If likely exposed (contaminated water, firefighting foam, PFAS work), ask for a serum test: NASEM sum of 7 PFAS <2 ng/mL = usual care; 2-20 ng/mL = cut exposure plus lipid screening; >20 ng/mL = also thyroid testing and kidney/testicular cancer and ulcerative colitis checks. Cut intake by treating contaminated tap water ([water-filtration]). To speed elimination: plasma donation every 6 weeks for 12 months lowered PFOS by 2.9 ng/mL (blood every 12 weeks: 1.1 ng/mL); prescription cholestyramine 4 g three times daily for 12 weeks lowered PFOS by 60% in highly exposed adults.
dose.studied_range: Donation RCT in firefighters with PFOS >=5 ng/mL; cholestyramine trials in residents with PFOS ~50-190 ng/mL.
dose.too_much: EFSA tolerable weekly intake: 4.4 ng/kg body weight per week for PFOA+PFNA+PFHxS+PFOS; NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased risk.
dose.timeframe: Years: after clean water was supplied, serum PFHxS, PFOS and PFOA fell only 13%, 20% and 26% per year.
dose.notes: Donate blood or plasma only if eligible and for its own sake; PFAS reduction is a side benefit. Bile-acid sequestrants have GI side effects and interfere with absorption of other drugs; trials are small and only in highly exposed people. Women eliminate some PFAS faster (menstruation, pregnancy, breastfeeding).

factors.mechanism: PFAS bind serum albumin and liver fatty-acid proteins, activate PPAR-alpha and other nuclear receptors, alter lipid and bile-acid handling, and in cells and animals raise ROS and modulate NF-kB and immune cell signalling. Human oxidative-stress marker data are mixed.
factors.interactions: Blood or plasma donation also lowers iron stores (relevant to [iron-excess]). Bile-acid sequestrants block enterohepatic recycling of PFAS. Shares food-contact and water routes with [plastics-chemicals].
factors.caveats: Most health links are observational; kidney function, menstruation, pregnancy and breastfeeding all change serum PFAS and can create reverse-causation artefacts. Elimination studies measure blood levels, not health outcomes.
factors.debate: Clinical relevance: NASEM concluded PFAS are linked to cancers, thyroid dysfunction, cholesterol changes and lower birth weight and set serum action levels [env-nasem2022]; EFSA based its intake limit on reduced vaccine antibodies in children [env-efsa2020, env-grandjean2012]. On cholesterol, a 2025 bias-focused meta-analysis found positive pooled links driven by cross-sectional studies, with longitudinal estimates near null [env-hussey2025]. Oxidative stress: PFOS tracked higher 8-isoprostane in pregnancy [env-siwakoti2024] and 8-OHdG in adults [env-lin2020], but a meta-analysis found PFAS-oxidative stress associations mostly inconsistent [env-chen2023]. Elimination: donation lowers PFOS [env-gasiorowski2022] and sequestrants lower it more [env-moller2024, env-andersson2025], but no study shows a health benefit, and the firefighter treatment-program data are uncontrolled [env-delaere2025]. A fibre trial hinted at falling long-chain PFAS but only in a secondary analysis [env-schlezinger2025].

factors.name: Home water filtration (reverse osmosis, activated carbon)
factors.headline: Where tap water carries PFAS, reverse-osmosis and well-maintained carbon filters remove much of it and home-filter users in a contaminated county had lower serum PFAS, but real-world filter testing is thin, short-chain PFAS slip through more easily, and there is no human evidence that filtering changes microplastic body burden.

dose.effective: Most worthwhile when local water reports show PFAS, especially in the ~10-100 ng/L range or above (where water clearly raises blood levels, most consistently PFHxS). Options: under-sink reverse osmosis, or a carbon-block filter certified for PFOA/PFOS reduction; change cartridges on schedule.
dose.studied_range: Lab and certification tests of point-of-use devices; only five real-life tap studies; observational serum comparisons.
dose.timeframe: Serum PFAS falls slowly after exposure stops (roughly 13-26% per year for PFHxS, PFOS, PFOA).
dose.notes: Neglected activated-carbon cartridges can release captured PFAS back into water. Below ~10 ng/L the benefit for blood levels is uncertain. Filtering does not affect PFAS from food or consumer products.

factors.mechanism: Reduces intake rather than acting on oxidative stress directly: activated carbon adsorbs long-chain PFAS, ion-exchange resins bind anionic PFAS, and reverse osmosis membranes reject most PFAS molecules.
factors.interactions: Pairs with [pfas] serum testing; the elimination side (donation, sequestrants) is covered there. For bottled water vs tap and plastics see [microplastics].
factors.caveats: Serum benefit is shown only by observational comparisons in a heavily contaminated area. Device performance varies by product, PFAS chain length and maintenance.
factors.debate: Benefit size depends on water levels: a 2026 evidence summary found clear water-to-blood links at 10-100 ng/L but inconsistent ones below ~10 ng/L [env-tefera2026], whereas a California study found detectable PFAS in general public supplies raised serum PFHxS ~80% [env-fillman2026]. Filters: home-filter users had lower serum PFAS [env-cuffney2023], and stopping contaminated water lowers serum over years [env-li2018], but a review warns real-world performance is poorly characterized and short-chain PFAS are harder to remove [env-mackeown2024].

factors.name: Metformin
factors.headline: Metformin lowers glucose partly by mildly inhibiting mitochondrial complex I; in exercise trials it blunted some training gains (about half the VO2max gain in one study, less muscle growth in the MASTERS trial), it lowers vitamin B12 by about 19% over years, and in PCOS it helps ovulation but less than letrozole or clomiphene.

dose.effective: Usual prescribed range 500-2000 mg/day (e.g. 850 mg twice daily in the DPP). The exercise-blunting trials used 1700-2000 mg/day.
dose.studied_range: 500-3000 mg/day in exercise studies; 1700 mg/day (MASTERS); 2550 mg/day for 4.3 years (de Jager B12 trial); 1700 mg/day for up to 13 years (DPP/DPPOS).
dose.too_much: B12 deficiency risk rises about 13% per year of use; check B12 periodically on long-term use (deficiency roughly <150 pmol/L or <=203 pg/mL; borderline up to ~220 pmol/L or 298 pg/mL).
dose.timeframe: Training interactions appear within 12-16 weeks; B12 falls within 6 weeks to 3 months and deficiency accumulates over years; ovulation effects within a few cycles.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. People with diabetes, prediabetes or PCOS who take metformin should keep exercising: exercise still improves fitness and glucose on metformin, the blunting is partial and inconsistent, and the disease benefits of each are established. Ask about B12 testing on long-term use.

factors.mechanism: Metformin accumulates in mitochondria and inhibits respiratory-chain complex I, lowering the cell's energy charge and activating AMPK; it also acts through AMPK-independent, gut and lysosomal routes [med-owen2000, med-rena2017]. It suppresses NF-kB-linked inflammatory signalling independent of diabetes status [med-cameron2016]. Exercise adaptations depend partly on mitochondrial redox and energy-stress signals, and metformin abolished the exercise-induced rise in muscle mitochondrial respiration in older adults [med-konopka2019], a plausible way it can dampen a hormetic signal. B12 loss reflects reduced ileal absorption, raising homocysteine [med-dejager2010].
factors.interactions: May partially blunt adaptations to [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [resistance-training] (a parallel to [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). Improves [glycemic-control]. Main fertility use is in [pcos]. Long-term B12 depletion adds to that from [ppi-acid-suppressants]. [statins] have a similar exercise-interaction debate; [glp1-agonists] are the newer weight-and-glucose alternative.
factors.caveats: The blunting trials were mostly in healthy older adults or people with prediabetes taking metformin for research, not in people who need it for diabetes. Metformin is not an anti-aging supplement: TAME has not reported, and the survival advantage seen in one UK cohort was not reproduced in Danish twin data. Sperm data are tiny and uncontrolled.
factors.debate: Exercise blunting: RCTs found metformin reduced lean-mass and thigh-muscle gains [med-walton2019], VO2max and mitochondrial gains [med-konopka2019], and insulin-sensitivity gains [med-malin2012], and a 2026 meta-analysis of 9 trials found a modest VO2peak penalty (-1.19 mL/kg/min) and smaller blood-pressure falls [med-etayourtasun2026]; but other trials found no attenuation of glycaemic or fitness benefits [med-boule2013, med-pilmark2021, med-terada2019], and transcriptomic work suggests some aging-related muscle pathways may even be favourably shifted [med-kulkarni2020]. Longevity: TAME advocates cite metformin users outliving non-diabetic controls [med-barzilai2016, med-bannister2014]; a Danish twin and registry reanalysis found the opposite (IRR 1.32-1.64) [med-keys2022], and critics argue healthy-person benefit is unproven [med-konopka2019tame, med-miller2020]. Fathers: a Danish cohort linked paternal metformin during sperm development to birth defects (aOR 1.40) [med-wensink2022], but a larger Norway-Taiwan study controlling for diabetes severity found no association (pooled RR 0.89) [med-meng2024].

factors.name: GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide, tirzepatide)
factors.headline: Semaglutide and tirzepatide cut body weight by about 15-21% in 68-72-week trials, semaglutide cut major cardiovascular events by 20% in people with heart disease and overweight (SELECT), and they lower CRP, but roughly a quarter to a third of weight lost is lean mass unless resistance training is added.

dose.effective: Semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly (obesity dose); tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg once weekly, reached by gradual dose escalation.
dose.studied_range: Semaglutide 2.4 mg/week for 68 weeks (STEP 1); tirzepatide 5-15 mg/week for 72 weeks (SURMOUNT-1); liraglutide 1.2-3 mg/day in older and fertility studies.
dose.too_much: Lean mass made up about 35% of weight lost on semaglutide and 25% on tirzepatide; older or frail people risk sarcopenia. GI side effects are the main reason for stopping (4.5% vs 0.8% on placebo for semaglutide).
dose.timeframe: Weight and inflammatory markers fall over months, with weight plateauing around 1-1.5 years; in STEP 4, switching to placebo after 20 weeks regained 6.9% of body weight by week 68.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. To protect muscle, pair the drug with resistance training (lean-mass share fell to ~17.5% with lifestyle plus resistance training) and adequate protein. Women: see the egg entry for contraception and the label's 2-month semaglutide washout before trying to conceive.

factors.mechanism: Most of the redox benefit likely comes from losing visceral fat, which lowers adipose NADPH oxidase activity, inflammatory cytokines and insulin resistance; GLP-1 receptor signalling may also have direct anti-inflammatory effects. In a 40-RCT meta-analysis the CRP fall tracked blood-pressure and insulin-resistance improvement rather than HbA1c [med-bray2021]. The drugs slow gastric emptying, which is why they can change absorption of oral medicines [med-fda-zepbound2023].
factors.interactions: Delivers the benefits of [weight-loss] in people with [excess-adiposity]; improves [glycemic-control]. Combine with [resistance-training] and adequate protein to limit lean-mass loss. Alternative or add-on to [metformin] in [pcos]. In obese men with low testosterone it raised testosterone and preserved sperm, unlike [testosterone-anabolic-steroids]. Very-low-calorie intake on these drugs overlaps with [calorie-restriction].
factors.caveats: The MDA (lipid peroxidation) result rests on only 3 trials in the 2026 meta-analysis; IL-6 and TNF-alpha effects were not significant. Weight is regained after stopping (STEP 4). Long-term data on muscle function and bone in younger people are limited. Supply via compounded or unregulated products is outside the evidence base.
factors.debate: Inflammation/oxidative stress: one meta-analysis calls the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant evidence strong [med-bray2021], while a 2026 update finds consistent CRP and adiponectin effects but variable IL-6/TNF-alpha and a thin MDA evidence base [med-kanbay2026]. Lean mass: reviewers argue the loss is proportional and adaptive, with better muscle quality [med-neeland2024], and a 2026 meta-analysis found the lean-mass share similar to diet-based weight loss [med-eisa2026]; another 2026 systematic review found muscle-related losses exceeded prespecified benchmarks in about two thirds of incretin trials [med-batsis2026]. Sperm: a small RCT found GLP-1 treatment maintained diet-induced sperm-count gains [med-andersen2022] and semaglutide improved morphology in hypogonadal diabetic men [med-gregoric2025], but systematic reviews note no change in healthy men and too few trials to judge [med-deameh2026, med-peel2026].

factors.name: Statins
factors.headline: Statins lower LDL and, in proportion, oxidized LDL (-39% on atorvastatin 80 mg) and F2-isoprostanes, and cut CRP by 37% in JUPITER; only about 1 in 15 muscle complaints on statins is caused by the drug, and CoQ10 for statin muscle pain has conflicting trial evidence.

dose.effective: Prescribed by cardiovascular risk: moderate intensity (e.g. atorvastatin 10-20 mg, rosuvastatin 5-10 mg) or high intensity (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg).
dose.studied_range: Rosuvastatin 20 mg (JUPITER, 1.9 years median); atorvastatin 10 vs 80 mg (12 weeks, oxidative markers); simvastatin 20-40 mg (exercise and CoQ10 trials).
dose.too_much: High-intensity regimens give a slightly larger muscle-symptom excess (RR 1.08 vs 1.03); JUPITER saw more physician-reported diabetes.
dose.timeframe: LDL and oxidized LDL fall within weeks; event reduction accrues over 1-5 years; excess muscle symptoms occur mainly in year 1.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. If muscle symptoms appear, ask about a supervised re-challenge or dose change rather than quitting; most symptoms are not drug-caused. CoQ10 (100-600 mg/day in trials) is harmless but not reliably helpful. Most women should stop statins once pregnancy is recognized, but very high-risk patients may continue with their doctor (FDA 2021).

factors.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition lowers cholesterol and also isoprenoid intermediates, reducing prenylation of Rho and Rac and hence NADPH oxidase activation and ROS production in cell and animal studies [med-oesterle2017]. In humans the fall in F2-isoprostanes tracked the fall in LDL, implying much of the 'antioxidant' effect follows from removing oxidizable lipoprotein [med-decaterina2002]. The same mevalonate pathway makes coenzyme Q10, which statins lower in blood [med-taylor2015].
factors.interactions: Lower oxidized LDL more than [vitamin-e-supplement] (adding vitamin E to simvastatin added nothing). [coq10] is often taken for statin myalgia with mixed evidence. May blunt gains from [aerobic-exercise-moderate] in one RCT, yet fitness plus statins carried the lowest mortality in a cohort. Similar exercise debate to [metformin]. Complements [mediterranean-diet] and [glycemic-control] for cardiovascular risk.
factors.caveats: Pleiotropic claims come mostly from cells and animals and are hard to separate from LDL lowering. The exercise-blunting finding rests on one small 12-week trial. Statin effects on sperm are probably negligible, though one 17-man pilot found a 31% fall in sperm count on atorvastatin.
factors.debate: CoQ10 for statin myopathy: a 6-trial meta-analysis found no significant effect [med-banach2015] and a well-run RCT in confirmed myalgia found none [med-taylor2015], whereas a 12-trial meta-analysis found reduced pain, weakness and cramps [med-qu2018]; individual-patient data show most muscle complaints on statins are not drug-caused [med-ctt2022]. Exercise: simvastatin abolished fitness and mitochondrial gains in one RCT [med-mikus2013], but statin users who were fit had the lowest mortality [med-kokkinos2013] and atorvastatin did not reduce habitual activity vs placebo [med-panza2016]; reviewers call for trials in healthy users [med-miller2020]. Pleiotropy beyond LDL remains disputed [med-oesterle2017, med-decaterina2002]. Pregnancy: no excess malformations [med-bateman2015, med-vahedianazimi2021, med-dutta2026], but a Taiwan cohort linked use to low birth weight and preterm birth [med-chang2021]. Sperm: a small pilot reported harm [med-ponsrejraji2014]; a systematic review and a large clinic study found no clinically relevant effect [med-anagnostis2021, med-keihani2018a].

factors.name: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin)
factors.headline: Lower oxidative stress is one of many proposed reasons for these drugs' heart and kidney benefits, but that part is mostly mechanistic; the practical redox-diet point is safety: combined with a ketogenic diet they can cause euglycemic ketoacidosis, sometimes within a week.

dose.effective: As prescribed (e.g. empagliflozin 10-25 mg/day, dapagliflozin 10 mg/day).
dose.studied_range: Case reports involve standard doses; euDKA occurred after one dose in one case and after one week of a ketogenic diet in another.
dose.too_much: Ketogenic or very-low-carbohydrate diets, prolonged fasting, acute illness, surgery and dehydration raise euDKA risk; blood glucose may look normal.
dose.timeframe: Ketoacidosis can develop within days of starting a ketogenic diet on the drug.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Tell the prescriber before starting a ketogenic diet, extended fasting or a very-low-carb plan; seek urgent care for nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or malaise even if glucose is normal.

factors.mechanism: SGLT2 inhibitors make the kidney excrete glucose, causing natriuresis, a shift toward ketone fuel, lower uric acid and less AGE signalling; reduced oxidative stress and inflammation are proposed contributors from mechanistic studies [med-cowie2020]. Insulin-independent glucose loss, high glucagon and volume depletion promote ketogenesis, which a carbohydrate-free diet amplifies [med-peters2015, med-mistry2021].
factors.interactions: Dangerous with [ketogenic-diet], [low-carb-diet] and prolonged [intermittent-fasting]. Part of [glycemic-control] therapy alongside [metformin] and [glp1-agonists].
factors.caveats: No human outcome data show that their oxidative-stress effects matter clinically; the heart-failure and kidney benefits are established on clinical outcomes and are not the subject here.
factors.debate: Which mechanisms explain the cardiorenal benefits is debated, with haemodynamic, natriuretic and metabolic explanations competing with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant ones [med-cowie2020]. On euDKA itself no substantive published disagreement was found: case series agree on the risk and on avoiding ketogenic diets [med-peters2015, med-mistry2021].

factors.name: Acetaminophen (paracetamol)
factors.headline: Every dose is detoxified with glutathione: even 600-1200 mg speeds glutathione turnover, 4 g/day raised liver enzymes (ALT >3x normal) in 31-44% of healthy adults within two weeks, and overdose exhausts glutathione; the prenatal autism/ADHD association shrinks to nothing in sibling comparisons.

dose.effective: Occasional use at labelled doses (e.g. 500-1000 mg per dose) for pain or fever.
dose.studied_range: 50-1200 mg single doses (glutathione turnover); 4 g/day for 14 days (liver enzymes); 4 g/day for 12 weeks (resistance-training trial).
dose.too_much: Label maximum for healthy adults is 4 g/day; at that dose ALT rose in a third of healthy volunteers. Overdose is a medical emergency. People with low glutathione reserves (fasting, malnutrition, heavy alcohol use, liver disease) have less margin.
dose.timeframe: Glutathione drain is per dose; ALT rises appeared within days at 4 g/day and resolved after stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. In pregnancy, follow the 2021 consensus advice: use it when medically indicated (fever needs treating), at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and check with a clinician before long-term use. Do not combine products that both contain acetaminophen.

factors.mechanism: A small fraction of each dose is oxidized by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which is neutralized by conjugation with glutathione; therapeutic doses measurably accelerate cysteine and glutathione turnover [med-lauterburg1987]. When glutathione runs out (overdose), NAPQI binds liver proteins and causes oxidative hepatocyte death, which is why the glutathione precursor N-acetylcysteine is the antidote. Acetaminophen also weakly inhibits COX and has anti-androgenic effects in rodent fetal testis [med-kristensen2011].
factors.interactions: Shares the glutathione pool with other detox demands; [n-acetylcysteine] replenishes cysteine for glutathione. [alcohol] and [calorie-restriction]/fasting reduce the safety margin. In older adults it did not blunt (and may have enhanced) gains from [resistance-training]. Often chosen instead of [nsaids] around conception and in pregnancy.
factors.caveats: Therapeutic-dose glutathione depletion in healthy people is transient and not shown to cause harm; ALT rises at 4 g/day resolved. Male-fertility signals (longer time to pregnancy) come from one cohort and were not seen when exposure was modelled continuously.
factors.debate: Pregnancy: a consensus statement of 91 scientists [med-bauer2021] and a 2025 Navigation Guide review (27 of 46 studies positive) [med-prada2025] urge precaution over neurodevelopmental risk; teratology experts warned against causal inference [med-alwan2022], and a 2.5-million-child Swedish sibling analysis found no association with autism, ADHD or intellectual disability (HR 0.98) [med-ahlqvist2024]. Male reproduction: Danish cohort and rat data link prenatal mild analgesics to cryptorchidism but the Finnish cohort did not [med-kristensen2011]; adult male urinary paracetamol was linked to longer time to pregnancy in the top quartile only [med-smarr2016]. Exercise: OTC acetaminophen enhanced muscle gains in older adults [med-trappe2011], while reviews warn COX inhibitors may impair adaptation in the young [med-lundberg2018].

factors.name: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, COX-2 inhibitors)
factors.headline: Daily maximal OTC ibuprofen (1200 mg) halved muscle growth from 8 weeks of strength training in young adults, yet similar doses did not hurt (and seemed to help) older adults; in young men daily ibuprofen produced compensated hypogonadism, and around ovulation NSAIDs can stop the follicle from rupturing.

dose.effective: Occasional use at labelled doses (e.g. ibuprofen 200-400 mg per dose) for pain or inflammation.
dose.studied_range: Ibuprofen 1200 mg/day for 8 weeks (young adults) or 12 weeks (older adults); ibuprofen 1600 mg/day and etoricoxib in women with arthritis.
dose.too_much: Chronic daily high doses are where training and testicular effects appear; GI bleeding, kidney and cardiovascular risks rise with dose and duration.
dose.timeframe: Training effects over 8-12 weeks; hormonal changes in men within weeks; ovulatory effects in the same cycle.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. If you take NSAIDs for a chronic condition and are trying to conceive or training for muscle, discuss timing (avoiding continuous use around ovulation) and alternatives with the prescriber.

factors.mechanism: NSAIDs block COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin synthesis. Prostaglandins help drive satellite-cell activity and muscle protein turnover after exercise [med-schoenfeld2012, med-lundberg2018], are needed for follicle rupture at ovulation [med-stone2002], and influence Leydig-cell steroidogenesis; ibuprofen transcriptionally repressed testosterone production in human testis explants [med-kristensen2018].
factors.interactions: May blunt hypertrophy from [resistance-training] in young people (compare [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). [acetaminophen] is the usual alternative around conception. Fish oil ([omega3-fish]) is sometimes used for inflammatory pain without the ovulation issue.
factors.caveats: Occasional use is unlikely to matter for muscle. The testicular study is short-term with a hormonal (not semen) outcome. Ovulation data come mainly from women with inflammatory arthritis on continuous NSAIDs.
factors.debate: Muscle: maximal OTC ibuprofen blunted hypertrophy and strength in young adults [med-lilja2018], while ibuprofen or acetaminophen enhanced gains in older adults [med-trappe2011]; reviewers suggest age and growth potential explain the split and that occasional use is harmless [med-schoenfeld2012, med-lundberg2018]. Men: ibuprofen induced compensated hypogonadism [med-kristensen2018], but reviews note human semen data on NSAIDs are scarce and effects look smaller than for opioids [med-drobnis2017]. Women: see the egg entry for ovulation and miscarriage debates [med-micu2011, med-li2018, med-chen2024].

factors.name: Proton-pump inhibitors & acid suppressants
factors.headline: Two or more years of PPIs is linked to B12 deficiency (OR 1.65), iron deficiency (OR 2.49) and low magnesium (RR 1.43) in observational studies, but the 17,598-person COMPASS RCT found no excess harm over 3 years except slightly more gut infections.

dose.effective: As prescribed (e.g. omeprazole 20-40 mg/day, pantoprazole 40 mg/day), ideally at the lowest effective dose and for a defined duration.
dose.studied_range: Pantoprazole 40 mg/day for ~3 years (COMPASS); >=2 years' supply in case-control studies.
dose.too_much: Associations strengthen above ~1.5 pills/day and with longer use (iron deficiency OR 4.27 at >1.5 pills/day for >=10 years).
dose.timeframe: Nutrient effects appear over years; iron-deficiency association weakens after stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Ask the prescriber how to step down rather than stopping on your own. On long-term use, ask whether B12, iron (ferritin) and magnesium checks make sense.

factors.mechanism: Gastric acid frees food-bound B12 and keeps non-heme iron soluble, so chronic acid suppression reduces their absorption; magnesium loss reflects impaired intestinal uptake. Higher gastric pH also lets oral bacteria colonize the gut and reduces microbial diversity [med-imhann2016].
factors.interactions: Adds to the B12 drain of [metformin]. Iron deficiency interacts with [iron-excess] advice (supplementing iron when deficient is different from excess). Microbiome shifts overlap [antibiotics-microbiome] and may affect polyphenol metabolism ([dietary-fiber-microbiome]).
factors.caveats: Observational associations are prone to confounding by indication and illness; the RCT used pantoprazole in older adults with cardiovascular disease and did not measure nutrient levels.
factors.debate: Harms: large case-control studies link long-term PPIs to B12 and iron deficiency [med-lam2013, med-lam2017] and a meta-analysis to hypomagnesemia [med-cheungpasitporn2015]; a B12 meta-analysis found only a modest, heterogeneous association with no difference in serum B12 in most studies [med-choudhury2023], and the COMPASS RCT found no excess harms besides enteric infection [med-moayyedi2019]. Sperm: a Dutch registry linked PPI use 6-12 months earlier to threefold odds of low motile sperm count [med-huijgen2016], while a US clinic study of 248 users found no effect [med-keihani2018b].

factors.name: Antibiotics and the gut microbiome
factors.headline: A 4-day broad-spectrum antibiotic course wiped out much of the gut microbiota in healthy men; most of it recovered within 6 weeks, but 9 common species were still missing in most men at 6 months.

dose.effective: Not applicable: take antibiotics when clinically indicated, for the prescribed course.
dose.studied_range: Meropenem, gentamicin and vancomycin for 4 days in 12 healthy men.
dose.too_much: Repeated or unnecessary courses; effects on polyphenol-converting bacteria are not quantified.
dose.timeframe: Near-baseline recovery in about 1.5 months; some species absent at 180 days.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Never stop a prescribed antibiotic course early on the basis of microbiome concerns. A fibre- and plant-rich diet supports recovery generally, but no specific post-antibiotic protocol is proven.

factors.mechanism: Gut bacteria convert many dietary polyphenols into the metabolites that are actually absorbed, so a depleted microbiome may temporarily change what people get from polyphenol-rich foods; after antibiotics, enterobacteria and pathobionts bloom and butyrate producers and bifidobacteria fall [med-palleja2018].
factors.interactions: Relevant to the benefits of [dietary-fiber-microbiome] and polyphenol foods; [ppi-acid-suppressants] shift the microbiome more than antibiotics at population level [med-imhann2016]. Treating [genital-tract-infection] with antibiotics can lower seminal ROS.
factors.caveats: Evidence is from a small study in young men; health consequences of the residual changes are unknown.
factors.debate: The same data support both resilience (near-full recovery in 6 weeks) and a lasting imprint (species still missing at 6 months) [med-palleja2018]; at population level, PPI effects on the microbiome exceeded those of antibiotics [med-imhann2016]. No direct human outcome data link these changes to oxidative stress.

factors.name: Antioxidant supplements during chemotherapy or radiotherapy
factors.headline: In a radiotherapy RCT, vitamin E (with beta-carotene initially) nearly tripled second primary cancers during supplementation (HR 2.88), and antioxidant use during breast-cancer chemotherapy was linked to more recurrence (HR 1.41); older reviews found no loss of efficacy, so the default is: do not take high-dose antioxidants during treatment without the oncology team.

dose.effective: None recommended during active treatment without oncologist approval; food sources are not the concern.
dose.studied_range: Alpha-tocopherol 400 IU/day with or without beta-carotene 30 mg/day (head and neck radiotherapy); self-reported vitamins A, C, E, carotenoids, CoQ10 (breast chemotherapy).
dose.too_much: Any high-dose antioxidant supplement concurrent with radiation or ROS-generating chemotherapy; smokers having radiotherapy are the clearest risk group.
dose.timeframe: Risk concentrated during the supplementation/treatment period.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Tell the oncology team about every supplement, including 'fertility' antioxidant blends used during fertility preservation.

factors.mechanism: Radiotherapy and many chemotherapy drugs kill tumour cells partly through ROS; antioxidants could protect tumour cells as well as normal tissue, though some trials suggest selective protection of normal tissue [med-lawenda2008].
factors.interactions: A special case of [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail], [vitamin-e-supplement] and [beta-carotene-supplement] risks; relevant to [chemo-radiation] and fertility preservation; [n-acetylcysteine] and [coq10] are commonly self-prescribed in this setting.
factors.caveats: The breast-cancer data are observational and the result for antioxidants was borderline (CI 0.98-2.04). Some specific agents are used under oncology supervision to reduce toxicity; this is not covered here.
factors.debate: Caution camp: an RCT showed more second cancers with vitamin E during radiotherapy [med-bairati2005], a JNCI review concluded antioxidants should be discouraged [med-lawenda2008], and SWOG S0221 linked antioxidant use to recurrence [med-ambrosone2020]. Reassurance camp: a systematic review of 19 RCTs found no decrease in chemotherapy efficacy and often fewer toxicities, though trials were underpowered [med-block2007], and a 49-RCT review judged harm unclear except for smokers on radiotherapy [med-yasueda2016].

Recurrence HR, antioxidant use during chemo

factors.name: Supplement-drug interactions (anticoagulants, nitrates, St John's wort)
factors.headline: Vitamin E raised haemorrhagic stroke 22% in trials, NAC with nitroglycerin caused symptomatic hypotension and intolerable headache in a third of patients, and St John's wort sped up oral-contraceptive breakdown (breakthrough bleeding in 7 of 12 women); fish oil, by contrast, did not raise bleeding overall in 120,643 trial patients.

dose.effective: Not applicable: this is about avoiding harmful combinations.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin E 50-800 IU/day (stroke trials) and 100-400 IU/day with warfarin; NAC 10 g/day IV or oral with nitroglycerin; high-hyperforin St John's wort (>10 mg hyperforin/day); omega-3 up to 4 g/day purified EPA.
dose.too_much: Vitamin E above ~400 IU/day with anticoagulants; any NAC with nitrate therapy without supervision; any St John's wort with hormonal contraceptives, transplant drugs or other CYP3A substrates; high-dose purified EPA (bleeding RR ~1.5, absolute +0.6%).
dose.timeframe: Interactions act within days of starting the combination.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Bring a list of all supplements to every prescriber and pharmacist; ask before combining supplements with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, nitrates, hormonal contraception or immunosuppressants.

factors.mechanism: Vitamin E may antagonize vitamin K-dependent clotting factors at high doses [med-corrigan1981]; omega-3s alter platelet function without clearly raising bleeding [med-wachira2014]; NAC supplies thiols that potentiate nitroglycerin's vasodilation [med-horowitz1988]; St John's wort's hyperforin induces CYP3A, accelerating breakdown of ethinyl estradiol and progestins [med-hall2003, med-whitten2006].
factors.interactions: Applies to [vitamin-e-supplement], [omega3-fish], [n-acetylcysteine], [turmeric-curcumin] and [curcumin-supplements]. Contraceptive failure from St John's wort parallels the oral-contraceptive interaction of tirzepatide ([glp1-agonists]).
factors.caveats: Curcumin is often listed as a warfarin potentiator, but the evidence is case-level; it was not among the higher-risk items named in a 2021 systematic review of warfarin interactions [med-tan2021]. Vitamin E 400 IU/day did not change prothrombin time in a small warfarin study.
factors.debate: Fish oil: reviews and a 2024 meta-analysis found no increase in clinically significant bleeding even with antithrombotic drugs [med-wachira2014, med-javaid2024], though high-dose purified EPA showed a small dose-related signal [med-javaid2024]. Vitamin E: no prothrombin-time change at <=400 IU/day with warfarin [med-corrigan1981], but a 9-trial meta-analysis found more haemorrhagic strokes [med-schurks2010]. NAC with nitrates: the combination reduced cardiac events in angina trials yet was limited by hypotension and headache [med-horowitz1988, med-ardissino1997]. Warfarin and herbs: most supplements are safe in moderation but dozens potentiate warfarin [med-tan2021].

Bleeding RR, omega-3 (all trials)

factors.name: HFE hemochromatosis (C282Y homozygosity) and iron overload
factors.headline: About 1 in 156 people of northern European descent are C282Y homozygotes; untreated iron loading caused documented organ disease in about 28% of homozygous men (about 1% of women in one cohort, more in UK Biobank), and regular blood removal to a ferritin below 50-100 ug/L prevents it.

dose.effective: Test transferrin saturation and ferritin; if TSAT >45% (women) or >50% (men) with ferritin >200/300 ug/L, genotype HFE. In C282Y homozygotes, phlebotomy (typically 400-500 mL blood) to ferritin <50 ug/L during induction, then maintenance at <100 ug/L.
dose.studied_range: Diagnostic thresholds and phlebotomy targets from EASL 2022 and ACG 2019 guidelines; outcomes from cohorts of 31,192 (Melbourne) and 451,243 (UK Biobank) people.
dose.too_much: Over-phlebotomy to iron deficiency causes fatigue and anemia; ferritin targets exist for that reason. Avoid iron supplements and iron-fortified 'antioxidant' blends, and avoid high-dose vitamin C supplements, which increase non-heme iron absorption.
dose.timeframe: Iron accumulates over decades (disease usually after 40 in men, after menopause in women); induction phlebotomy takes months, then lifelong maintenance.
dose.notes: Ferritin above 1,000 ng/mL at diagnosis marks higher risk of advanced liver fibrosis. C282Y/H63D compound heterozygotes rarely develop disease without fatty liver, diabetes or excess alcohol. High ferritin with normal TSAT is usually fatty liver, alcohol or inflammation, not hemochromatosis.

factors.mechanism: Loss of HFE function lowers hepcidin, so the gut absorbs and macrophages release too much iron; transferrin saturates and non-transferrin-bound iron enters liver, pancreas, heart and joints. Labile iron catalyzes Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 -> hydroxyl radical), driving lipid peroxidation, fibrosis and cell death.
factors.interactions: Alcohol and fatty liver multiply liver damage, see [alcohol] and [excess-adiposity]. Iron supplements and multivitamins with iron are contraindicated (see [iron-excess], [multivitamin-mineral]); megadose [vitamin-c-supplement] raises iron absorption. Diabetes in homozygotes interacts with [glycemic-control].
factors.caveats: Genotype alone is not disease: penetrance is incomplete and much lower in women, who lose iron through menstruation and pregnancy. Heterozygotes (single C282Y) do not need treatment. Consumer genotyping that reports HFE should be confirmed clinically with iron studies before any action.
factors.debate: UK Biobank found C282Y homozygosity caused substantial incident morbidity in both men (15.7% vs 5.0%) and women (10.1% vs 3.4%) and argued for expanded early case-finding [tst-pilling2019], whereas an earlier cohort found documented disease in only 1.2% of homozygous women [tst-allen2008] and USPSTF judged evidence insufficient to estimate benefit from population genetic screening [tst-whitlock2006]. Ferritin's accuracy for detecting overload is rated very low certainty [tst-garciacasal2021].

factors.name: G6PD deficiency (oxidant drug and fava bean sensitivity)
factors.headline: An X-linked enzyme defect carried by roughly 400-500 million people; carriers are usually well but can hemolyze after fava beans, high-risk drugs (dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, methylene blue) or very high IV vitamin C, so knowing your status changes what you must avoid.

dose.effective: One G6PD activity test (or genotype) before high-risk drugs or IV vitamin C infusions, especially with African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern or Asian ancestry. If deficient: avoid fava beans and CPIC high-risk drugs.
dose.studied_range: CPIC 2022 classification of drugs by systematic review: high risk (dapsone, methylene blue, pegloticase, primaquine, rasburicase, tafenoquine, toluidine blue), medium (nitrofurantoin), low-to-no risk (vitamin C at standard doses, vitamin K, many sulfonamides).
dose.too_much: Very high-dose IV vitamin C (gram-level infusions) can trigger hemolysis in deficient people; methylene blue, sometimes sold as a 'mitochondrial' or nootropic supplement, is classed high risk.
dose.timeframe: Hemolysis typically starts within 1-3 days of the trigger and resolves after it is removed.
dose.notes: Activity tests can read falsely normal during or right after a hemolytic episode; heterozygous women may have intermediate activity and still hemolyze.

factors.mechanism: G6PD makes NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway; NADPH keeps glutathione reduced. Red cells have no other NADPH source, so oxidant drugs, fava-bean glycosides (vicine, convicine) or infection-related oxidants overwhelm glutathione, oxidize hemoglobin into Heinz bodies and destroy the cells.
factors.interactions: Pro-oxidant effects of megadose vitamin C (see [vitamin-c-supplement]) and of high-dose antioxidant stacks ([high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]) matter here because ascorbate can act as an oxidant in the presence of iron and oxygen. Infections ([febrile-illness]) are themselves triggers.
factors.caveats: Most carriers are lifelong asymptomatic; this is about avoiding specific triggers, not about general oxidative stress. Ordinary dietary antioxidants and standard-dose vitamin C are not a concern.
factors.debate: Regulatory warnings conflict and evidence for many listed drugs is sparse; CPIC authors disagreed about the strength of the nitrofurantoin evidence [tst-gammal2023], while older reviews list a broader range of triggers [tst-cappellini2008]. CPIC classes standard-dose vitamin C as low-to-no risk [tst-gammal2023], but a systematic review of IV vitamin C flags hemolysis at very high doses and supports pre-infusion G6PD testing [tst-alangari2026].

key_numbers.label: People affected worldwide

factors.name: GSTM1 / GSTT1 null genotype and isothiocyanate handling
factors.headline: Roughly half of people lack both GSTM1 copies; null carriers handle broccoli's sulforaphane differently and in one cohort gained the most lung-cancer protection from isothiocyanates, but results conflict and the advice (eat crucifers) is the same whatever the genotype.

dose.effective: No test needed. Whatever the genotype, regular cruciferous vegetables (for example 1/2 cup broccoli sprouts or a serving of crucifers most days) are the lever.
dose.studied_range: Crossover feeding with standard and high-glucosinolate broccoli; urinary isothiocyanate cohort of 18,244 men; case-control meta-analysis of 6,934 men for infertility.
dose.timeframe: Sulforaphane pharmacokinetics differ within hours; any cancer association reflects years of intake.
dose.notes: Consumer 'detox' panels often report GSTM1 status; it should not drive supplement purchases.

factors.mechanism: GSTM1 and GSTT1 conjugate isothiocyanates and electrophilic toxins to glutathione for excretion. Null carriers may keep sulforaphane in circulation longer (more Nrf2 activation) or form less of the conjugated metabolites, depending on the study.
factors.interactions: Relevant to [broccoli-sprouts], [cruciferous-other] and [sulforaphane-supplements]; may modify the effect of [tobacco-smoking] carcinogens.
factors.caveats: Associations with male infertility and endometriosis come from case-control studies with population heterogeneity and possible publication bias; no intervention study uses genotype to change outcomes.
factors.debate: In Shanghai men, isothiocyanate protection was concentrated in GSTM1-null and double-null carriers [tst-london2000], whereas a crossover study suggested GSTM1-positive people retain different sulforaphane metabolites that might give them more benefit [tst-gasper2005], and a 114-person feeding study found genotype made little difference to excretion [tst-steck2007]. GSTM1 null was associated with male infertility in a meta-analysis [tst-wu2013], but a broad meta-analysis of endometriosis polymorphisms found GSTT1, not GSTM1, among the more robust signals [tst-mear2020].

factors.name: High iron stores (high-normal ferritin)
factors.headline: Higher ferritin consistently predicts type 2 diabetes (about +22% per 100 ug/L) and Mendelian randomization supports a causal diabetes link, but the heart-disease side of the 'iron hypothesis' failed: genetic data even suggest slightly less coronary disease with higher iron, and the one phlebotomy RCT (FeAST) was null on its primary outcome.

dose.effective: No target has been validated by trials. Practical reading: ferritin roughly 30-200 ug/L (women) or 30-300 ug/L (men) with normal transferrin saturation is unremarkable; persistently high ferritin together with high transferrin saturation warrants medical evaluation for haemochromatosis rather than self-treatment.
dose.studied_range: FeAST lowered mean ferritin from ~123 to ~80 ng/mL by phlebotomy over ~4.5 years.
dose.too_much: Pathological overload (haemochromatosis, transfusion) damages liver, pancreas, heart, joints and gonads.
dose.timeframe: Ferritin falls over months with phlebotomy or donation; disease associations accrue over years.
dose.notes: Ferritin is also an acute-phase protein: inflammation, obesity, fatty liver, alcohol and infection all raise it, so a single high value often reflects inflammation rather than iron. Check CRP and transferrin saturation alongside.

factors.mechanism: Iron stored in ferritin is safe; danger comes from the small labile iron pool that catalyses Fenton chemistry and drives ferroptosis (iron-dependent lipid peroxidation when GPX4/glutathione defences fail). Hepatic and pancreatic iron may impair insulin secretion and action. Serum ferritin itself partly leaks from damaged cells, which ties it to oxidative stress independently of stores.
factors.interactions: Blood donation lowers stores [blood-donation]. Red meat raises heme iron intake [processed-red-meat]. Interpreting ferritin requires accounting for [chronic-inflammation], [excess-adiposity] and alcohol; high ferritin co-travels with [glycemic-control] problems. Avoid iron pills when stores are high [iron-excess].
factors.caveats: Observational ferritin-disease links are heavily confounded because ferritin rises with inflammation and fatty liver. Do not induce iron deficiency in pursuit of 'low ferritin': [iron-deficiency] carries real harms. Haemochromatosis genetics is covered elsewhere.
factors.debate: Supporting a harmful role: Sullivan's hypothesis [nut-sullivan1981], ferritin-diabetes meta-analyses [nut-jiang2019, nut-kunutsor2013, nut-zhao2012], MR showing iron raises diabetes risk [nut-wang2021, nut-liu2024] and shortens lifespan [nut-daghlas2021], and FeAST's secondary cancer reduction [nut-zacharski2008]. Against: prospective studies found no ferritin-CHD association [nut-danesh1999, nut-sempos2000], FeAST was null on its primary endpoints [nut-zacharski2007] with an editorial calling the evidence far from ironclad [nut-hu2007] and another doubting the cancer result [nut-edgren2008], MR suggests higher iron is mildly protective for coronary disease [nut-gill2017, nut-liu2024] and hypercholesterolemia [nut-gill2019], and ferritin may mostly mark cell damage [nut-kell2014, nut-depalma2010]. Reviewers have long called the iron-heart question unresolved [nut-wood2004].

factors.name: Iron deficiency (with or without anaemia)
factors.headline: Iron deficiency is one of the world's leading nutritional harms: even without anaemia it causes fatigue (iron cut fatigue scores 48% vs 29% placebo in women with ferritin <50 ug/L), and in pregnancy anaemia is linked to ~30% more low birthweight and ~60% more preterm birth.

dose.effective: Treat documented deficiency: typical oral regimens give 40-100 mg elemental iron once daily or on alternate days for about 3 months, then recheck ferritin; 80 mg/day for 12 weeks was used in the fatigue RCT. Prevention: RDA 8 mg/day (men, postmenopausal women), 18 mg/day (menstruating women), 27 mg/day (pregnancy); vegetarians need ~1.8x more because non-heme iron is less bioavailable.
dose.studied_range: Oral iron 60-80 mg/day in most adult trials; prenatal 30-60 mg/day.
dose.too_much: Continuing high-dose iron after repletion pushes stores up [iron-excess]; IOM UL 45 mg/day (GI effects) applies to healthy people, not to supervised treatment.
dose.timeframe: Haemoglobin rises within 2-4 weeks; ferritin repletion takes ~3 months; fatigue improved by 12 weeks.
dose.notes: At-risk groups: heavy menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, infants and adolescents, vegans/vegetarians, frequent blood donors, endurance athletes, coeliac disease and other GI disease, bariatric surgery, chronic PPI use. In men and postmenopausal women, unexplained iron deficiency needs investigation for GI blood loss.

factors.mechanism: Iron is needed for haemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial cytochromes and iron-sulfur clusters, catalase and many DNA-synthesis enzymes. Deficiency impairs oxygen delivery and mitochondrial energy production, immunity and brain neurotransmitter synthesis. It is not an 'antioxidant' state: anaemia is itself associated with oxidative stress in red cells.
factors.interactions: Frequent donation can cause it [blood-donation]. Vitamin C-rich foods with meals raise non-heme absorption [vitamin-c-foods]; tea and coffee with meals reduce it [green-tea] [coffee]. For fertility relevance see [iron-egg].
factors.caveats: Ferritin is the best single test but is falsely raised by inflammation; in that setting transferrin saturation <20% helps. Cognitive benefits of iron in non-anaemic people are less certain than fatigue benefits.
factors.debate: That deficiency harms health is not contested [nut-pasricha2021]. Debate centres on thresholds and on non-anaemic deficiency: fatigue benefits appeared in an RCT [nut-vaucher2012] and a 2025 meta-analysis found psychiatric and cognitive gains only in iron-deficient participants [nut-fiani2025], while an earlier review judged cognitive trials small and weak [nut-falkingham2010]. In pregnancy, Cochrane supports routine iron [nut-finkelstein2024] but also notes more haemoglobin above 130 g/L [nut-penarosas2015], and high maternal haemoglobin/ferritin are themselves linked to gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia [nut-young2023, nut-khambalia2016].

factors.name: Regular blood donation
factors.headline: Donating lowers iron stores, and donors live longer, but most of that is the 'healthy donor effect': in 1.2 million donors the 18.6% lower mortality per annual donation shrank to 7.5% after adjustment, a large cohort found no heart benefit, and frequent donation often causes iron deficiency.

dose.effective: Donate for altruism, not as a health intervention. Standard whole-blood intervals (in the UK about 12 weeks for men and 16 for women), with ferritin checks or iron supplementation for frequent donors.
dose.studied_range: One donation removes ~200-250 mg iron. RCT of 550-800 mL phlebotomy in metabolic syndrome; donation intervals of 8-16 weeks (INTERVAL).
dose.too_much: Each week shorter donation interval lowered ferritin ~5-6.5% and raised low-haemoglobin deferrals; frequent donors reported more tiredness and restless legs.
dose.timeframe: Ferritin falls within months of regular donation.
dose.notes: Therapeutic phlebotomy for haemochromatosis is a medical treatment and is clearly beneficial in that condition; this entry is about healthy people.

factors.mechanism: Removes iron (as haemoglobin) and thereby lowers ferritin and, in theory, the labile iron available for Fenton chemistry. Short-term blood-pressure falls after phlebotomy may reflect volume and haemodynamic effects rather than iron.
factors.interactions: Lowers [iron-status-ferritin]; can cause [iron-deficiency], especially in young women and frequent donors.
factors.caveats: Donors are pre-screened for good health and continue donating only while healthy, so observational comparisons overstate benefits. No study has shown that donation reduces oxidative-stress outcomes or disease in healthy people.
factors.debate: For a benefit: the Kuopio cohort found 88% fewer heart attacks in recent donors [nut-salonen1998], a small RCT of phlebotomy in metabolic syndrome lowered systolic BP by 16.6 mmHg [nut-houschyar2012] (commentary noted design drawbacks [nut-manco2012]), and FeAST suggested fewer cancers [nut-zacharski2008]. Against: the 38,244-man Health Professionals cohort found no CHD benefit despite lower ferritin [nut-ascherio2001], FeAST was null for death and CV events [nut-zacharski2007], and Scandinavian and Dutch data show a strong healthy donor effect [nut-ullum2015, nut-atsma2011]. INTERVAL showed the harms side: more symptoms and iron deficiency with frequent donation [nut-diangelantonio2017, nut-kaptoge2019, nut-vandenhurk2018].

factors.name: Morning and daytime bright light
factors.headline: Bright daytime, especially morning, light anchors the body clock earlier (a summer camping weekend gave ~69% of a full week's shift), light therapy modestly improves sleep problems, and among 88,905 UK Biobank sensor-wearers the brightest days were linked to 17-34% lower mortality, but these outcome links are observational.

dose.effective: Daytime light of at least 250 lux melanopic EDI at eye level, which typical indoor lighting often fails to reach but outdoor daylight easily exceeds; in practice, time outdoors in the first hours after waking and working near windows.
dose.studied_range: Camping in natural light for a weekend to a week; office workers with measured circadian light; light-therapy trials with light boxes for sleep problems.
dose.too_much: Never look directly at the sun; balance with skin UV protection ([uv-sun-exposure]).
dose.timeframe: Circadian shifts within days; sleep improvements within weeks.
dose.notes: Late chronotypes shifted the most toward solar time in the camping study.

factors.mechanism: Melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells signal the suprachiasmatic nucleus; light in the early biological day advances the clock, strengthens rhythm amplitude and supports a timely, robust evening melatonin rise, which aligns metabolic, antioxidant and DNA-repair rhythms with behaviour.
factors.interactions: Complements dim evenings ([evening-light-exposure]); helps shift workers re-entrain ([shift-work-circadian]); supports sleep ([short-sleep]).
factors.caveats: Mortality and diabetes associations with light patterns come from a week of wrist-sensor data and could reflect health, mobility and time outdoors (exercise). Light-therapy meta-analysis showed publication bias and smaller effects in RCTs. Some of the leading cohort authors disclose lighting-industry funding.
factors.debate: Camping and office studies show earlier, stronger rhythms with more daylight [kcc-wright2013, kcc-stothard2017, kcc-figueiro2017], and UK Biobank links brighter days to lower mortality [kcc-windred2024b]; an expert consensus sets daytime targets [kcc-brown2022]. Sceptics note the outcome data are observational with possible reverse causation (sick people go outside less), light-therapy effects are small with publication bias [kcc-vanmaanen2016], and some cohort authors disclose lighting-industry funding [kcc-windred2024b]. No trial has tested daylight exposure on oxidative-stress markers.

factors.name: Evening and night-time light (room light, screens, light while sleeping)
factors.headline: Ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99% of people and shortened melatonin by about 90 minutes, half-maximal suppression occurs at only ~25 lux, sleeping with a light or TV on was linked to 17-33% more weight gain and obesity, and one night at 100 lux raised next-morning insulin resistance.

dose.effective: In the 3 hours before bed keep light at the eye below about 10 lux melanopic EDI (dim, warm lamps below eye level); keep the bedroom as dark as possible (≤1 lux melanopic EDI; blackout curtains or an eye mask); reduce screen brightness and use low-melanopic (warm) display settings, or stop screens before bed.
dose.studied_range: Room light <200 lux vs <3 lux for 8 h before bed; 10-2,000 lux for 5 h; ~4 h of e-reader use for 5 nights; 100 lux during one night of sleep; habitual bedroom light ≥3 lux.
dose.too_much: Sleeping with a TV or ceiling light on; bright overhead lighting or full-brightness screens late in the evening.
dose.timeframe: Melatonin suppression within minutes to hours; circadian delay after a few evenings; metabolic effects after one night.
dose.notes: Brightness matters more than screen colour filters: in one trial, iPhone Night Shift did not improve sleep, and blue-blocking glasses have indeterminate effects on sleep. See also [morning-light]. Melatonin supplements are covered under [melatonin].

factors.mechanism: Melanopsin-driven signals from the retina inhibit pineal melatonin synthesis and phase-delay the clock. Melatonin is a direct radical scavenger and induces antioxidant enzymes and DNA repair; suppressing it, plus sympathetic activation during lit sleep, worsens insulin sensitivity. Follicular fluid melatonin protects oocytes from oxidative stress in laboratory studies.
factors.interactions: Delays the melatonin rise that makes [late-eating] worse for glucose; adds to [shift-work-circadian]; contributes to [short-sleep].
factors.caveats: Health-outcome links (obesity, diabetes, mortality) are observational and confounded by urban living, income, sleep and mental health. Sperm data are one small cross-sectional study of men at a fertility clinic and one ecological study of outdoor light at night; we did not create a separate sperm factor. No human study has tied evening light to egg quality, although melatonin protects oocytes in laboratory work.
factors.debate: Laboratory trials consistently show melatonin suppression and circadian delay [kcc-gooley2011, kcc-phillips2019, kcc-chang2015, kcc-schollhorn2023], and one night of lit sleep impaired insulin sensitivity [kcc-mason2022]; cohorts link light at night to obesity, diabetes and mortality [kcc-park2019, kcc-obayashi2013, kcc-windred2024a, kcc-windred2024b]. A letter argued the e-reader findings overstate real-life relevance and the authors defended them [kcc-zeitzer2015, kcc-changczeisler2015]; screen-colour fixes have weak support (Night Shift [kcc-duraccio2021]; blue-blocking glasses indeterminate [kcc-singh2023]); and cohort authors disclose lighting-industry funding [kcc-windred2024a]. Sperm associations [kcc-green2020, kcc-tian2024] are preliminary.

factors.name: Flame retardants (PBDEs and organophosphate replacements)
factors.headline: Old PBDEs are fading from bodies but persist for years, and their organophosphate replacements are in almost every urine sample; PBDEs carry the best human evidence (about 3.7 IQ points per 10-fold higher prenatal exposure), while oxidative-stress and fertility links are small, inconsistent single-cohort findings.

dose.effective: Wash hands before eating and after handling electronics or foam (urinary metabolites fell by up to about half in a week); wet-mop and HEPA-vacuum to cut dust; when replacing pre-2014 sofas or foam, choose TB117-2013 products labelled flame-retardant-free (replacement lowered dust levels of all measured flame retardants). Replacing only the foam works too.
dose.studied_range: Dust TPHP/TDCIPP up to 1.8 mg/g in US homes; urinary OPFR metabolites (BDCIPP, DPHP) detected in 85-95% of people; serum PBDEs fell up to 80% between 2005 and 2016 in a Boston cohort.
dose.too_much: No validated harm threshold. PBDE IQ link is per 10-fold exposure; e-waste and older California homes (TB117 foam) had the highest exposures.
dose.timeframe: OPFR metabolites clear within days (urine reflects the last day or so); PBDE serum half-lives are about 1-4 years depending on congener.
dose.notes: Urinary OPFR metabolites vary by season (BDCIPP about 2-fold higher in summer) and between days; hand-wipe levels predict urine better than dust levels do.

factors.mechanism: PBDEs resemble thyroid hormones and lower thyroxine; in cells and animals both PBDEs and organophosphate esters raise mitochondrial ROS and lipid peroxidation. In humans, PBDE mixtures tracked higher urinary 8-isoprostane in pregnancy [eia-sehgaln2025] and OPE metabolites tracked 8-OHdG, 8-isoprostane and MDA in small panels [eia-ingle2020ox, eia-li2026ope], but NHANES found no link between serum PBDEs and blood oxidative markers [eia-yuan2017].
factors.interactions: Shares the dust exposure route with [plastics-chemicals] and [pfas]; the same hand-washing and wet-cleaning steps cut several at once (see [house-dust]). Thyroid effects overlap with iodine status.
factors.caveats: Most human studies are small and cross-sectional, use a single urine sample for chemicals with hours-long half-lives, and test many metabolites against many outcomes. Phasing out commercial penta- and octa-BDE (2004 in the US) [eia-sjodin2020] replaced one problem with another class (organophosphate esters such as TDCIPP, TPHP, TCIPP) that has far less toxicity data: a textbook regrettable substitution. California's 2014 switch to a fabric smolder standard (TB117-2013) made flame-retardant-free furniture possible [eia-rodgers2021], but older furniture keeps emitting for years.
factors.debate: Fertility associations point in opposite directions: PBDEs predicted longer time to pregnancy in a low-income Californian cohort [eia-harley2010], a finding disputed in a published letter [eia-goodman2010]; follicular BDE-153 predicted failed implantation in 65 IVF patients [eia-johnson2012], yet in 215 EARTH patients serum BDE-153 predicted higher implantation and live birth [eia-ingle2020]. For organophosphate replacements, the large EARTH IVF signal [eia-carignan2017] has not been replicated in an independent IVF cohort, and semen findings range from weak and inconsistent [eia-ingle2018] to positive in Chinese clinic men [eia-li2023ope]. Oxidative-stress links are positive in small panels [eia-ingle2020ox, eia-li2026ope, eia-sehgaln2025] but null in NHANES [eia-yuan2017]. The neurodevelopment evidence is the most settled [eia-lam2017].

factors.name: Gas and propane stoves (NO2, benzene)
factors.headline: Gas burners raise indoor NO2 and emit benzene (2.8-6.5 ug per minute, 10-25 times electric); gas cooking is linked to about 30% higher odds of childhood asthma, and removing indoor gas combustion cut asthma symptoms in randomized heater trials, but the size of the stove effect is fiercely contested.

dose.effective: Switching to induction or electric removes the source (kitchen NO2 -51% at 3 months in a randomized trial; 21 to 6 ppb in an asthma before-after study). Otherwise: use a range hood that vents outdoors on high, cook on back burners, open a window, and use a HEPA-plus-activated-carbon purifier (NO2 -27%). Never use a gas oven or burners to heat the home.
dose.studied_range: NO2 emissions about 7.8 ng/J; US stoves add about 4 ppb to long-term NO2 on average; benzene from burners 2.8-6.5 ug/min; leaking idle stoves also release benzene.
dose.too_much: WHO 2021 annual NO2 guideline is 10 ug/m3 (about 5.3 ppb); gas stoves alone add about 75% of that on average and can exceed the 1-h US standard (100 ppb) within minutes in small, unventilated kitchens.
dose.timeframe: Indoor NO2 falls within a week of swapping the stove; asthma control improved within 2-3 months in an uncontrolled study.
dose.notes: Exposure is four times higher in homes under 800 ft2 than over 3000 ft2. A hood that recirculates rather than vents outside does little for NO2.

factors.mechanism: NO2 is a free-radical gas that oxidizes airway-lining lipids and antioxidants and drives airway inflammation; benzene is a haematotoxic carcinogen metabolized to quinones that redox-cycle. In 144 COPD patients, low indoor NO2 (median 6.8 ppb) did not track urinary 8-OHdG or MDA [eia-mchugh2023], so systemic oxidative-stress effects at typical levels are unproven.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [indoor-combustion-smoke] (which also covers wood); a carbon-filter purifier ([hepa-air-purifier]) helps, a plain HEPA unit does not remove NO2. Ventilation ([ventilation-co2]) is the cheap partial fix.
factors.caveats: Most stove-asthma studies are cross-sectional with self-reported exposure, and gas-stove homes differ in income, housing size, crowding and damp. The 12.7% attributable-fraction figure assumes causality. The 2026 stove-swap study had no control group, so regression to the mean and seasonal change could explain part of the improvement. Industry-funded reviews reach conclusions opposite to the independent emission and epidemiology studies (see debate).
factors.debate: One side: a meta-analysis of 41 studies found OR 1.32 for gas cooking and childhood asthma with no publication bias [eia-lin2013], used to estimate that 12.7% of US childhood asthma is attributable to gas stoves [eia-gruenwald2022], and emissions work shows NO2 and benzene at levels above health benchmarks [eia-lebel2022, eia-kashtan2023, eia-kashtan2024]. The other side: a systematic review by a consultancy that has worked for gas-industry clients judged the literature too weak and biased for causal conclusions [eia-li2023gas], an American Gas Association-funded commentary rejected the attributable fraction [eia-li2024gas], an independent commentary called it an example of questionable research practices [eia-cox2023], and the 47-country ISAAC analysis did not find a clear gas-cooking association [eia-wong2013]. The most causal evidence comes from removing unflued gas heaters, not stoves [eia-pilotto2004, eia-howdenchapman2008].

Kitchen NO2 reduction after electric stove swap

factors.name: VOCs and formaldehyde (new furniture, paint, air fresheners, candles, incense)
factors.headline: Formaldehyde and other VOCs from new materials, fragranced products and burning are linked to childhood asthma (OR about 1.1-1.2 per 10 ug/m3 formaldehyde) and urinary oxidative-DNA markers, but the evidence is mostly cross-sectional; heavy long-term incense use is linked to respiratory squamous-cell cancers.

dose.effective: Air out new furniture, flooring and freshly painted rooms (VOCs are highest at first occupancy and fall over months); choose low-VOC paint and solid wood or certified low-formaldehyde composite wood; skip plug-in air fresheners and fragranced sprays; burn candles and incense rarely, away from draughts, with a window open; do not rely on potted plants.
dose.studied_range: Asthma meta-analyses spanned roughly 10-60 ug/m3 indoor formaldehyde (median of studies about 22.5 ug/m3).
dose.too_much: WHO indoor guideline for formaldehyde: 0.1 mg/m3 (0.08 ppm), set to prevent sensory irritation and considered protective against nasal cancer. Formaldehyde is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen at occupational levels.
dose.timeframe: Concentrations fall within hours of ventilating; emissions from new materials decline over months to about a year.
dose.notes: Terpenes from essential oils and "natural" air fresheners react with ozone indoors to make formaldehyde and fine particles. Plants would need 10-1000 per m2 of floor to matter.

factors.mechanism: Formaldehyde and acrolein are reactive aldehydes that form DNA and protein adducts and deplete glutathione; aromatic VOCs (benzene, toluene) are metabolized by CYP2E1 with ROS release. In 128 Chinese adults, 16 urinary VOC metabolites tracked urinary 8-OHdG and 8-OHG after false-discovery correction [eia-qian2021].
factors.interactions: Ventilation ([ventilation-co2]) lowers every indoor-sourced VOC; activated-carbon filters adsorb some VOCs, HEPA alone does not ([hepa-air-purifier]). Candles and incense also emit particles like [indoor-combustion-smoke]. Occupational formaldehyde and solvents: see [occupational-solvents].
factors.caveats: Home formaldehyde correlates with new construction, renovation, damp, smoking and income; the asthma meta-analyses pool mostly cross-sectional studies with large heterogeneity. Fragranced-product harm is mostly inferred from emission chemistry, not health outcomes. The reproductive data for formaldehyde come from occupational settings (see [occupational-solvents-egg] and [occupational-solvents-sperm]).
factors.debate: Three meta-analyses agree on a modest asthma association (OR 1.17, 1.10 and 1.20 per 10 ug/m3) [eia-mcgwin2010, eia-yu2020, eia-lam2021], but all note that most studies are cross-sectional, so the direction of causation and confounding by housing cannot be excluded [eia-mcgwin2010]. Whether the WHO 0.1 mg/m3 guideline protects against cancer is argued from non-linear animal dose-response [eia-nielsen2010]; linear unit-risk approaches give lower acceptable levels. For incense, a 61,320-person cohort found more respiratory squamous carcinomas but no overall lung cancer excess [eia-friborg2008]. The claim that houseplants clean indoor air is contradicted by a quantitative re-analysis of the chamber studies [eia-cummings2020].

factors.name: Household cleaning products (sprays, bleach, quaternary ammonium disinfectants)
factors.headline: Weekly use of cleaning sprays was linked to about 50% more new adult asthma, and women who cleaned at home lost lung function about 3.6 mL/yr faster over 20 years; quaternary ammonium disinfectants cut fertility in mice, but human fertility data are thin and conflicting.

dose.effective: Use liquids on a cloth instead of sprays; use soap or detergent and water for routine cleaning and keep disinfectants (bleach, quats) for genuine need (illness, raw meat); never mix bleach with acids or ammonia; ventilate while cleaning; microfibre cloths and wet-mopping remove dust without chemicals.
dose.studied_range: ECRHS: cleaning sprays at least weekly (42% of participants) up to 4+ days a week.
dose.too_much: Asthma risk was dose-dependent: RR 1.49 for weekly sprays and 2.11 for physician-diagnosed asthma with sprays on 4+ days a week.
dose.timeframe: Lung function differences accumulated over 20 years; asthma incidence over the multi-year ECRHS follow-up and over 2 years in NutriNet-Sante.
dose.notes: "Green" products were also associated with asthma symptoms in a 30,000-person cohort, so the label is not a guarantee; fragranced green products still emit terpenes.

factors.mechanism: Hypochlorite, chloramines and quats are airway irritants that oxidize lung-lining fluid and trigger neutrophilic inflammation; repeated low-level injury is the proposed route to asthma and lung-function decline. Quats inhibit mitochondrial function and raise inflammatory cytokines in cells; in 43 people, blood QACs tracked higher cytokines and lower mitochondrial function [eia-hrubec2021].
factors.interactions: Terpene-based cleaners add to [vocs-formaldehyde]. Wet cleaning is still worth doing for [house-dust]; the issue is sprays and disinfectant overuse, not cleaning.
factors.caveats: Exposure is self-reported in all large cohorts. People with early asthma may avoid sprays (reverse causation would bias toward null) or clean more because of allergies. Professional cleaners have lower income and more smoking. QAC fertility harm is shown only in mice; in humans the only reproductive data are on nurses, where a retrospective study found 2-fold late miscarriage with disinfectants [eia-lawson2012] but a prospective one did not [eia-ding2021].
factors.debate: Respiratory harm is consistently found in independent cohorts [eia-zock2007, eia-svanes2018, eia-dumas2019, eia-pachecodasilva2026], although healthcare-worker studies are all at high risk of bias [eia-romerostarke2021]. For quats and fertility, academic mouse studies found subfertility in both sexes [eia-melin2014, eia-melin2016, eia-kirkpatrick2025], while industry steering committees disputed the first study [eia-hostetler2015] and a review relying on unpublished guideline studies rated those mouse studies unreliable and found no reproductive toxicity at expected exposures [eia-desesso2021]. A multi-institution review calls QACs a class of emerging concern [eia-arnold2023]. Bleach use was linked to more childhood infections in a cross-sectional study [eia-casas2015], which cannot exclude that families with sick children clean more.

factors.name: House dust control (wet cleaning, HEPA vacuuming, hand-washing)
factors.headline: Dust is a reservoir for phthalates, flame retardants, PFAS and lead that young children swallow at about 60-70 mg a day; one week of wet cleaning or hand-washing roughly halved some flame-retardant metabolites, but dust control alone has not lowered children's blood lead or improved mite-allergic asthma in trials.

dose.effective: Wet-mop hard floors and damp-dust weekly; vacuum with a sealed HEPA vacuum; shoes off at the door; wash children's hands before eating and after floor play; replace crumbling foam; tailor allergen and smoke control to the specific sensitivities of a child with asthma.
dose.studied_range: Gibson 2019: one week of instructed cleaning, hand-washing, or both. Dust ingestion: 36-72 mg/day in infants and young children, 12-32 mg/day in adults.
dose.timeframe: Hand and urine levels of short-lived chemicals drop within a week; persistent chemicals (PBDEs, PFAS, lead) change over months to years.
dose.notes: Dust control is an exposure-reduction measure; no trial shows a health or fertility benefit from dust control on its own.

factors.mechanism: Not an oxidative intervention in itself: it lowers intake of dust-borne chemicals (see [flame-retardants], [plastics-chemicals], [pfas], [heavy-metals]) and allergens that drive airway inflammation.
factors.interactions: The cheapest shared lever for [flame-retardants], [plastics-chemicals], [microplastics] and lead. Avoid adding spray cleaners ([cleaning-products]) while doing it.
factors.caveats: Intervention studies are small, short and measure exposure markers, not health. Education-only lead programmes fail; removing the source (lead paint, contaminated soil) matters more than cleaning. Dust levels of short-lived chemicals vary day to day.
factors.debate: Cochrane found that household education and dust-control interventions did not lower children's blood lead [eia-nussbaumerstreit2020] and that mite-control measures did not help mite-allergic asthma [eia-gotzsche2008] (a review Cochrane now flags as outdated). Against that, a multifaceted, individually tailored home programme in 937 inner-city children cut allergen levels and symptom days for two years [eia-morgan2004], and a small cleaning/hand-washing trial lowered flame-retardant biomarkers [eia-gibson2019]. The difference is likely between single generic measures and targeted, multi-component ones.
