factors.name: Occupational solvents and chemical fumes (glycol ethers, dry-cleaning solvents, paints, formaldehyde)
factors.headline: Workers exposed to solvents show higher lipid-peroxidation markers, and glycol ether exposure roughly doubled the odds of low motile sperm count; women exposed at work had more miscarriage in older, mostly retrospective studies. The risk is concentrated in specific jobs, not in ordinary home use.

dose.effective: If you work with solvents, paints, adhesives, dry-cleaning fluid, formaldehyde or disinfectants: use local exhaust ventilation and closed systems, wear the correct respirator and chemical gloves, ask your employer for safety data sheets, and when trying to conceive (either partner) or pregnant, ask for reassignment from high-exposure tasks.
dose.studied_range: Shipyard painters at 2-ethoxyethanol TWA 0-80.5 mg/m3; dry-cleaning operators; laboratory and pharmaceutical workers; formaldehyde-exposed workers.
dose.too_much: Occupational exposure limits do not account for reproductive effects; painters below biological exposure limits still showed oxidative changes.
dose.timeframe: Sperm effects reflect exposure in the roughly 3 months before the sample.
dose.notes: The most toxic glycol ethers (2-methoxy- and 2-ethoxyethanol) are now restricted in many countries, so older studies may overstate current risk in regulated workplaces.

factors.mechanism: Glycol ethers are metabolized to alkoxyacetic acids that are toxic to spermatocytes; toluene, perchloroethylene and formaldehyde raise lipid peroxidation and antioxidant enzyme activity in exposed workers [eia-moro2010, eia-li2024pce].
factors.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking] and [alcohol] in men with marginal semen; household VOCs at much lower levels are covered in [vocs-formaldehyde].
factors.caveats: Exposure is usually assigned by job title or expert rating, not measured. Manual work correlates with heat, smoking and lower income. Healthy-worker and recall bias affect miscarriage studies.
factors.debate: See [occupational-solvents-sperm] and [occupational-solvents-egg]. A systematic review of 49 time-to-pregnancy studies found the evidence for solvents equivocal, unlike lead and pesticides [eia-snijder2012].

key_numbers.label: Low motile sperm count, high glycol ether exposure

factors.name: Damp and mould at home
factors.headline: Damp and visible mould are linked to 30-50% more respiratory and asthma outcomes and about 30% more new asthma; repairing damp homes reduced adult wheeze (OR 0.64) in Cochrane-reviewed studies. Claims that indoor mould causes systemic "mycotoxin illness" diagnosed by urine tests are unproven.

dose.effective: Fix leaks and rising damp; keep indoor humidity down; use bathroom and kitchen extract fans; dry laundry outside or vented; clean small mould patches with detergent and water and dry the area; get professional remediation for large or hidden mould; insulate and heat cold walls.
dose.studied_range: Visible mould, damp spots, water damage or mould odour in homes, schools and offices.
dose.too_much: No dose threshold; mould odour carried the highest new-asthma estimate (1.73).
dose.timeframe: Symptoms improved within months of remediation in controlled before-after studies.
dose.notes: Do not rely on direct-to-consumer urine mycotoxin tests: CDC called them unvalidated.

factors.mechanism: Fungal spores, fragments and microbial products act through allergic (IgE) and innate immune pathways; damp also feeds dust mites and bacteria. Oxidative stress is shown for some mycotoxins in cell and animal studies only (mechanistic).
factors.interactions: Damp homes are often cold, poorly ventilated and low-income, and often have gas heaters ([gas-stoves]); insulation and better heating improved health in New Zealand trials [eia-howdenchapman2007, eia-howdenchapman2008]. Ventilation ([ventilation-co2]) lowers humidity.
factors.caveats: Damp and mould are reported by occupants, and symptomatic people may notice and report mould more. Poverty, crowding and cold confound. Remediation trials cannot be blinded. No fertility data.
factors.debate: The respiratory association is consistent across meta-analyses [eia-fisk2007, eia-quansah2012] and supported by remediation studies [eia-sauni2015] and WHO guidance [eia-who2009mould]. The contested ground is systemic illness: an allergy society position paper finds many hypothesized mould illnesses unproven [eia-bush2006], CDC warned against unvalidated urine mycotoxin tests [eia-kawamoto2015], while critics argue that an earlier occupational-medicine statement minimizing mould effects was shaped by litigation-related conflicts of interest [eia-craner2008].

key_numbers.label: Increase in respiratory/asthma outcomes with damp and mould
Adult wheeze after repairing mould damage

factors.name: Indoor radon
factors.headline: Radon raises lung cancer risk about 16% per 100 Bq/m3 of long-term exposure with no safe threshold; for a lifelong non-smoker that is roughly 0.4% to 0.7% lifetime risk at 0 vs 400 Bq/m3, but for smokers it is 10% to 16%, so testing and fixing high homes matters most for smokers and ex-smokers.

dose.effective: Test your home with a passive detector for at least 3 months (lowest lived-in floor); if above 100 Bq/m3 (WHO reference level; US EPA action level 148 Bq/m3 = 4 pCi/L) install sub-slab depressurisation (more than 80% reduction in most remediated homes) or improve under-floor ventilation; quit smoking, which removes most of the radon-related risk.
dose.studied_range: European controls averaged 97 Bq/m3; 11% of homes were above 200 and 4% above 400 Bq/m3.
dose.too_much: WHO: national reference level 100 Bq/m3, not above 300 Bq/m3.
dose.timeframe: Risk reflects exposure 5-34 years before diagnosis; the excess risk from past exposure fades over decades rather than months.
dose.notes: Radon is unrelated to how clean or modern a home looks; levels vary by geology and by house, so only measurement tells.

factors.mechanism: Radon decay products deposit in airways and emit alpha particles that produce dense ionization tracks, double-strand DNA breaks and reactive oxygen species, including in neighbouring (bystander) cells; ROS generation is one proposed basis of the synergy with tobacco smoke [eia-sethi2012]. Antioxidants have not been shown to modify the risk.
factors.interactions: Multiplicative with [tobacco-smoking] (about 25 times higher absolute risk in smokers at the same radon level). Ventilation ([ventilation-co2]) lowers radon modestly; sub-slab systems work better.
factors.caveats: Lung cancer is the only established outcome. No fertility or pregnancy effects are established at residential levels. Single short-term tests misclassify annual exposure.
factors.debate: Pooled case-control studies with measured home radon in Europe and North America found a linear, no-threshold increase consistent with miner data [eia-darby2005, eia-krewski2005]. A county-level ecological analysis found the opposite (more radon, less lung cancer) and was used to argue for a threshold or protective hormesis [eia-cohen1995]; re-analysis showed the same negative correlation for all smoking-related cancers but not others, i.e. confounding by smoking [eia-puskin2003]. For smokers, modelling shows quitting reduces radon-related risk more than mitigation does [eia-mendez1998].

factors.name: Home ventilation and indoor CO2
factors.headline: Better ventilation dilutes every indoor-sourced pollutant and improved sleep quality in small bedroom trials; whether CO2 itself (at 1,000-3,000 ppm) impairs thinking is contested, with blinded studies split, so treat a CO2 monitor as a ventilation gauge, not a toxin meter.

dose.effective: As a rule of thumb, keep bedroom and living-room CO2 mostly below about 1,000 ppm (a cheap NDIR CO2 monitor shows this): open a window or trickle vent at night, run kitchen and bathroom extract fans that vent outdoors, and keep mechanical ventilation (MVHR) filters clean. On high outdoor-pollution days, close windows and rely on filtration instead.
dose.studied_range: Bedrooms at about 660-835 vs 2,400-2,600 ppm CO2; offices at 12 vs 24 L/s per person; chamber CO2 600-5,000 ppm.
dose.timeframe: Air changes within hours; sleep and next-day effects within days.
dose.notes: Outdoor air also brings in traffic and wildfire pollution, so in polluted cities ventilation and filtration have to be balanced.

factors.mechanism: Not directly antioxidant: ventilation lowers indoor NO2, formaldehyde, VOCs, radon, humidity and airborne infection, reducing airway oxidant and inflammatory load. CO2 at indoor levels is not toxic in the classical sense; bioeffluents and other co-pollutants may explain the symptoms seen in poorly ventilated rooms.
factors.interactions: The shared fix for [gas-stoves], [vocs-formaldehyde], [damp-mould] and partly [radon]; trades off against [outdoor-air-pollution] on bad days, when [hepa-air-purifier] is the better tool.
factors.caveats: Trials are small, short, and often unblinded to the smell of stale air. Office sick-leave data are observational. No fertility data.
factors.debate: Pure-CO2 studies conflict: decision-making fell at 1,000 and 2,500 ppm in one blinded chamber study [eia-satish2012] and cognitive scores rose sharply with better ventilation and fewer VOCs [eia-allen2016], but adding pure CO2 up to 3,000 ppm did nothing when bioeffluents were removed [eia-zhang2017], NASA-style testing up to 5,000 ppm found no dose-response [eia-scully2019], and children sleeping at 2,000-3,000 ppm showed no next-morning cognitive change [eia-klausen2023]. Bedroom ventilation improved sleep in students [eia-stromtejsen2016]. A multidisciplinary review found consistent links between low ventilation and sick-building symptoms, sick leave and allergy [eia-sundell2011, eia-milton2000].

key_numbers.label: Short-term sick leave, lower vs higher office ventilation

factors.name: Parabens in cosmetics and personal-care products
factors.headline: Almost everyone excretes methylparaben (99% of Americans), mainly from leave-on products like lotion, sunscreen and makeup; switching to paraben-free products cuts urine levels by 30-45% within 3-5 days, but harm at everyday exposure is unproven and the oxidative-stress and breast-tumour signals are weak.

dose.effective: Switch leave-on products used on large skin areas (body lotion, sunscreen, foundation) to paraben-free versions; rinse-off products matter less. Three days of products labelled paraben-free cut urinary methyl- and propylparaben by 44-45% in teenage girls; 5 days without usual products cut methylparaben by 30% in young women.
dose.studied_range: Urinary methylparaben medians about 50-130 ug/L in US and European adults; exposure-reduction studies of 2-5 days and a 1-month web-based behavioural RCT.
dose.too_much: No human harm threshold is established. EU limits: methyl- and ethylparaben 0.4% each (0.8% combined), propyl- and butylparaben 0.14%, five other parabens banned since 2014-2015. German 24-h urine data put about 5% of people above acceptable intake for single parabens under deliberately conservative assumptions.
dose.timeframe: Urine levels track use within hours and fall within 1-3 days of stopping (dermal half-life about 9-12 h).
dose.notes: Parabens are also in some foods and medicines. A single spot urine ranks paraben exposure moderately well (intraclass correlation about 0.4-0.5) because product habits are stable, better than for BPA. 'Paraben-free' products use other preservatives, some of which (methylisothiazolinone) caused an allergy epidemic.

factors.mechanism: Parabens are weak estrogen-receptor agonists, with potency rising with alkyl chain length (butyl > propyl > methyl), and are anti-androgenic in vitro. In sperm in vitro they raise mitochondrial and cytosolic ROS and oxidative DNA adducts [epc-samarasinghe2018]. In pregnant women, butyl- and propylparaben tracked 20-27% higher urinary isoprostane per interquartile increase [epc-watkins2015], but in a larger repeated-measures study parabens dropped out once correlated phthalates were modelled [epc-ferguson2019].
factors.interactions: Travels with phthalates and fragrance in the same products ([plastics-chemicals], [fragrance-musks]), which confounds single-chemical studies. Sunscreen is a major paraben source in men [epc-nassan2017], so switching to a paraben-free sunscreen keeps the [sunscreen] benefit. Paraben-preserved lubricants matter for semen samples ([lubricants-sperm]). See [parabens-sperm], [parabens-egg], [clean-beauty-labels].
factors.caveats: Detection is not harm: no human study links everyday paraben levels to disease with consistency. Paraben levels are patterned by sex, ethnicity and product habits [epc-calafat2010, epc-smith2012], so outcome studies are open to socioeconomic and lifestyle confounding. Spot-urine reliability is debated: moderate in clinic cohorts [epc-smith2012, epc-dewalque2015], poor in a small controlled-use study [epc-huang2021]. A study reporting that cutting parabens and phthalates 'reversed' cancer-associated gene expression in breast aspirates [epc-dairkee2023] was uncontrolled and used surrogate markers; it does not show lower cancer risk.
factors.debate: Breast cancer: Darbre et al. found parabens in 20 breast tumours [epc-darbre2004]; the accompanying editorial and a letter stressed there was no normal-tissue comparison and that presence does not show causation [epc-harvey2004, epc-jeffrey2004]. Oxidative stress: positive pregnancy associations [epc-watkins2015] versus a larger analysis attributing them to phthalate co-exposure [epc-ferguson2019]. Risk assessment: German biomonitoring found a cumulative hazard index above 1 at the 95th percentile but called its assumptions most conservative [epc-moos2017]. Substitution: as the preservative methylisothiazolinone spread in cosmetics, contact allergy to it rose to 3.7% of patch-tested patients [epc-lundov2013] and halved again after EU restrictions [epc-uter2020], a reminder that 'free-of' products carry their own trade-offs.

factors.name: Triclosan and triclocarban (antibacterial soaps and products)
factors.headline: Antibacterial soaps with triclosan worked no better than plain soap, so the FDA removed triclosan and triclocarban from consumer washes from 2017 (wastewater loads then fell 80-90%); the remaining exposure has weak, inconsistent links to thyroid, birth weight and fertility, while triclosan toothpaste modestly reduces gingivitis.

dose.effective: Wash hands with plain soap and water (or alcohol sanitizer away from a sink); skip products marketed as 'antibacterial' for everyday home use; check toothpaste, deodorant, cosmetics and imported products for triclosan. Products labelled triclosan-free lowered urinary triclosan by 36% in 3 days.
dose.studied_range: Urinary triclosan geometric means of about 1-100 ng/mL across countries; toothpaste use raised plasma triclosan from under 1 to 26-296 ng/g.
dose.too_much: No human harm threshold established. Top-quartile triclosan (over 72 ng/mL in a post-conception urine) went with 16% lower fecundability in one cohort; EU allows at most 0.3% in specified products.
dose.timeframe: Plasma half-life about 21 h; most of a dose is excreted within 24 h.
dose.notes: The 2016 FDA rule covered consumer washes, not toothpaste or hand sanitizers; it deferred benzalkonium chloride, benzethonium chloride and chloroxylenol, which have become the common replacements.

factors.mechanism: Triclosan disrupts thyroid hormone homeostasis and shows estrogenic/androgenic activity in animals and cells; it is a mitochondrial uncoupler and raises ROS experimentally. In humans, triclosan tracked higher urinary 8-OHdG and isoprostane in pregnancy, but not independently of phthalates [epc-ferguson2019], and went with 31% higher IL-6 [epc-watkins2015]; triclocarban correlated non-significantly with 8-OHdG [epc-iyer2018].
factors.interactions: Co-occurs with parabens and BP-3 in personal-care products ([parabens], [uv-filters]). Relevant to [periodontal-disease] because triclosan toothpaste reduces gingivitis. See [triclosan-sperm], [triclosan-egg].
factors.caveats: Most outcome studies use one spot urine (intraclass correlation about 0.47 [epc-meeker2013]); higher-income groups have higher triclosan [epc-han2016], a confounding risk. A 14-day toothpaste study found no thyroid change despite large plasma rises [epc-allmyr2009], and a systematic review could not conclude that current exposure affects thyroid function [epc-homburg2022]. A birth-weight meta-analysis found no clear overall effect, with stronger inverse links only in higher-exposure populations [epc-patti2021, epc-zhong2020].
factors.debate: Over 200 scientists' Florence Statement called triclosan and triclocarban persistent endocrine disruptors without benefit in most uses [epc-halden2017], and a systematic review found triclosan soaps no better than plain soap [epc-aiello2007]; the FDA agreed for consumer washes [epc-fda2016]. On the other side, a Cochrane review found triclosan/copolymer toothpaste reduced plaque, gingivitis and caries slightly, with no serious safety concerns over up to 3 years [epc-riley2013]. After the ban, triclosan fell in wastewater by 89% but parabens rose 72% [epc-adhikari2022] and other antibacterials replaced it in soaps [epc-rundle2019].

factors.name: Organic UV filters in sunscreen (oxybenzone and others)
factors.headline: Organic sunscreen filters are absorbed: in FDA trials all six tested passed the 0.5 ng/mL safety-testing threshold after one application and oxybenzone reached 170-260 ng/mL, so FDA asked for more data and the EU capped oxybenzone at 2.2% for body products; no human harm has been shown, and the proven skin-cancer benefit of daily sunscreen ([sunscreen]) outweighs the uncertainty.

dose.effective: Keep using sunscreen daily. To cut filter absorption, pick mineral sunscreens (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide), the only filters FDA proposed as safe and effective; zinc oxide nanoparticles stayed on the skin surface in volunteers. Use clothing, hats and shade to shrink the area that needs sunscreen. If pregnant or trying to conceive, a mineral product is a reasonable precaution.
dose.studied_range: 2 mg/cm2 applied to 75% of body surface, 1-4 times a day for up to 4 days (FDA trials); 10% filter creams over 1-2 weeks (Danish trials).
dose.too_much: No human harm level is known. FDA's 0.5 ng/mL is a trigger for toxicology testing, not a harm threshold. EU limits: oxybenzone (BP-3) 6% face/hand/lip, 2.2% body, 0.5% as a formula protector; octocrylene 10% (9% sprays); 4-MBC banned from 2025.
dose.timeframe: In plasma 1-2 h after application; oxybenzone still excreted in urine 5 days after the last application.
dose.notes: Oxybenzone is also used to stabilise other cosmetics. US urinary BP-3 is 10-20 times European and Asian levels. Octocrylene can degrade to benzophenone in stored products.

factors.mechanism: BP-3 and its metabolite BP-1 are weakly estrogenic and anti-androgenic at human-relevant concentrations [epc-mustieles2023, epc-krause2012]; several filters activate the sperm CatSper calcium channel in vitro [epc-rehfeld2016]. BP-3 tracked 17% higher urinary isoprostane in pregnant women [epc-watkins2015], though not independently of phthalates in a larger study [epc-ferguson2019]. On the skin the net redox effect is protective: filters absorb UV before it generates ROS ([sunscreen], [uv-sun-exposure]).
factors.interactions: Weigh against [sunscreen] (strong benefit) and [uv-sun-exposure]. Sunscreens are also a major source of parabens [epc-nassan2017] ([parabens]). See [uv-filters-sperm].
factors.caveats: Urinary BP-3 is a marker of sun exposure and outdoor life, so outcome associations are badly confounded: in IVF patients, higher BP-3 went with better pregnancy rates among outdoor workers [epc-minguez2019b]. Short-term whole-body trials found no hormone changes [epc-janjua2004, epc-janjua2007]. A meta-analysis found no clear link between prenatal BP-3 and birth size [epc-zhong2020].
factors.debate: FDA's absorption trials [epc-matta2019, epc-matta2020] and its 2019 proposed rule [epc-fda2019] ask for more safety data, and a comprehensive review supports Europe's limits [epc-mustieles2023, epc-eu2022]; both FDA authors and that review say people should not stop using sunscreen. A study found octocrylene sunscreens generate benzophenone during storage [epc-downs2021]; a published letter disputed it [epc-surber2021]. A 2025 review links benzophenones to poorer sperm quality in some studies but stresses photoprotection [epc-jaskulak2025].

factors.name: Fragrance chemicals and synthetic musks
factors.headline: Perfume use roughly triples urinary monoethyl phthalate (from the fragrance fixative diethyl phthalate) and synthetic musks like galaxolide build up in blood and breast milk of users; the clearly proven harm is contact allergy (about 2% of Europeans), while endocrine effects of musks are weak and mostly in vitro.

dose.effective: Choose 'fragrance-free' leave-on products ('unscented' can still contain masking fragrance); if you wear perfume, spray clothes rather than large skin areas; avoid air fresheners and ventilate after cleaning with scented products, especially on high-ozone afternoons. Labelled-free products cut urinary MEP by 27% in 3 days.
dose.studied_range: Perfume, deodorant and lotion use within 6-24 h before urine collection; blood musk levels up to 4,100 ng/L (galaxolide).
dose.too_much: No systemic harm threshold known. For allergy, the EU requires about 80 fragrance allergens to be named above 0.001% in leave-on and 0.01% in rinse-off products (transition to 2026-2028); the US fragrance-allergen labelling rule required by MoCRA has not been issued.
dose.timeframe: MEP rises within hours of use and falls within days; lipophilic musks persist longer (half-life not well measured).
dose.notes: 'Fragrance' on a label can hide dozens of undisclosed chemicals; many detected chemicals were not on labels in product testing.

factors.mechanism: Diethyl phthalate, used to fix fragrance, is metabolised to MEP, which tracked higher urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane in pregnancy alongside other phthalates [epc-ferguson2015]. Polycyclic musks are very weakly estrogenic but anti-estrogenic, anti-androgenic and anti-progestagenic in cell assays [epc-vanderburg2008]. Terpene fragrances react with indoor ozone to form formaldehyde and fine particles for hours [epc-carslaw2022].
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [plastics-chemicals] (diethyl phthalate) and [indoor-combustion-smoke]-type indoor air quality; see [clean-beauty-labels] and [parabens].
factors.caveats: Survey reports that a third of adults get symptoms from fragranced products are self-reported online data [epc-steinemann2016]. Nitro musks have been largely replaced and blood levels fell versus the 1990s [epc-hutter2009]. Breast-milk musk intake by infants is lower than for legacy pollutants such as PCBs [epc-reiner2007].
factors.debate: Some researchers call fragranced products a primary indoor pollutant with broad health effects [epc-steinemann2016]; general-population patch testing finds clinically relevant fragrance allergy in about 0.8-1.9% [epc-diepgen2015]. Reviews of musks range from 'no evidence for substantial human risk' [epc-kafferlein1998] to calls for epidemiology given animal and cell signals [epc-taylor2014]. Older women carry higher musk levels, possibly from more skin-cream use [epc-hutter2010].

factors.name: Hair dyes, relaxers and straightening treatments
factors.headline: Frequent chemical straightener use went with 1.8-2.6 times higher uterine cancer in the Sister Study (not replicated overall in the Black Women's Health Study) and slightly lower fecundability (FR 0.89 in former users); permanent hair dye showed no overall cancer increase in 117,200 nurses; formaldehyde- and glyoxylic-acid smoothing treatments carry acute risks.

dose.effective: If you use relaxers or straighteners, use them less often (risk was highest above 4 uses a year), avoid scalp burns and broken skin, and avoid keratin/'Brazilian' smoothing treatments that release formaldehyde, even when labelled formaldehyde-free, and glyoxylic-acid straighteners. Salons need local exhaust ventilation. For permanent dyes, current evidence does not call for avoiding them for cancer reasons; patch-test for dye (PPD) allergy.
dose.studied_range: Self-reported use in the prior 12 months or over years (Sister Study, Black Women's Health Study, Nurses' Health Study, PRESTO).
dose.too_much: Uterine cancer HR 2.55 with straighteners more than 4 times in the prior year (Sister Study); formaldehyde up to 1.19 ppm in salon air during smoothing treatments, at or above occupational limits. FDA's proposed formaldehyde ban has been under White House review since August 2026 and is not in effect.
dose.timeframe: Acute kidney injury after glyoxylic-acid straightening appeared at a median of 2 days; cancer associations reflect years of use.
dose.notes: Products marketed to Black women often contain unlabelled parabens, diethyl phthalate and other endocrine disruptors, and relaxer use is concentrated in Black women, so exposure and disease disparities overlap.

factors.mechanism: Formaldehyde (released from methylene glycol in smoothing products) is genotoxic and forms DNA-protein crosslinks; relaxers contain endocrine-active chemicals (parabens, phthalates, cyclosiloxanes) [epc-helm2018], and scalp burns may raise absorption [epc-wise2012]. Glyoxylic acid is absorbed and converted to oxalate, causing crystal nephropathy [epc-robert2024]. Oxidative-stress evidence is mechanistic only.
factors.interactions: Shares ingredients with [parabens] and [fragrance-musks]; occupational exposure overlaps with [nail-products-solvents].
factors.caveats: Product use is self-reported and product contents unknown; Sister Study participants have a sister with breast cancer; follow-up analyses tested many cancer sites with little dose-response [epc-bailey2026]; fibroid analyses may be biased by misclassification [epc-ogunsina2025]. Absolute uterine cancer risk is low, so even a doubled relative risk is a small absolute change. Litigation surrounds this topic on both sides.
factors.debate: Positive: uterine cancer HR 1.80 [epc-chang2022], breast cancer with permanent dye in Black women HR 1.45 [epc-eberle2020], fibroids IRR 1.17 [epc-wise2012], lower fecundability [epc-wise2023]. Null or mixed: no overall uterine cancer link in 44,798 Black women, only in postmenopausal heavy users [epc-bertrand2023]; permanent dye unrelated to most cancers in nurses [epc-zhang2020] and to bladder cancer in a meta-analysis [epc-turati2014]; hairdressers had no excess of breast or uterine cancer [epc-ogunsina2026]. An independent systematic review called evidence insufficient [epc-farooq2024]; a review by a private risk-consulting firm concluded relaxers are not a cancer risk factor [epc-hernandez2025]. Regulation: FDA's formaldehyde ban is still a pending proposal [epc-fda2026hair].

key_numbers.label: Uterine cancer, straighteners more than 4x/year (Sister Study)
Uterine cancer, heavy relaxer use, all ages (BWHS)
Fecundability, former relaxer users
Solid cancers, permanent dye ever-users (NHS)

factors.name: Nail polish, gel lamps and salon solvents
factors.headline: For customers the measured exposures are brief: painting nails with a triphenyl-phosphate polish raised its urinary metabolite about 7-fold for 10-14 h, and UV gel-lamp light caused ROS-type DNA damage in cultured cells (no human data); the bigger concern is nail technicians, who breathe formaldehyde, toluene and benzene daily.

dose.effective: Customers: apply and dry polish in a ventilated space, choose polishes without triphenyl phosphate, toluene or formaldehyde if you paint often, and for UV/LED gel manicures put broad-spectrum sunscreen on the backs of the hands or use fingertip-free UV gloves. Technicians: local exhaust ventilation at the table, nitrile gloves (gloves blocked most triphenyl phosphate uptake), and respirators for acrylic work.
dose.studied_range: Single nail-painting sessions; 2-day measurements in nail technicians; air measurements in 6 salons.
dose.too_much: Formaldehyde exceeded the NIOSH recommended exposure limit in 1 of 6 Colorado salons; modelled 20-year occupational cancer risks exceeded EPA benchmarks. Men with high occupational solvent exposure had about 3-4 times the odds of low motile sperm count.
dose.timeframe: Urinary triphenyl-phosphate metabolite peaks 10-14 h after painting; workplace exposure accumulates over each shift.
dose.notes: 'Free-of' claims (3-free, 5-free and so on) refer to a few named chemicals only.

factors.mechanism: Solvents (toluene, xylene, ethyl acetate) and formaldehyde are irritants and, at occupational doses, reproductive and carcinogenic hazards; triphenyl phosphate is an organophosphate flame retardant/plasticizer with endocrine activity in animals. UV-A from nail dryers generated ROS, 8-oxoguanine damage, mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS-signature mutations in mouse and human cells [epc-zhivagui2023].
factors.interactions: Occupational overlap with [hair-dyes-relaxers]; UV-lamp damage is the same chemistry as [uv-sun-exposure].
factors.caveats: The UV-lamp study used cells, not people, and no epidemiological link to skin cancer exists. Salon air studies are small. Occupational solvent and fertility evidence is mixed.
factors.debate: For men, a Canadian case-referent study found high solvent exposure linked to low motile sperm counts in two clinic series [epc-cherry2001]; a systematic review judged solvent evidence for time to pregnancy equivocal [epc-snijder2012]. Reviewers call for better data on cosmetologists' reproductive risks [epc-pak2013]. For customers, cell evidence of UV-lamp DNA damage [epc-zhivagui2023] has no human outcome data either way.

key_numbers.label: Urinary DPHP rise after painting nails
Low motile count, high solvent exposure (Montreal series)

factors.name: Tampons, pads, cups and intimate-care products
factors.headline: A 2024 study found lead (about 120 ng/g), arsenic and cadmium in all 30 tampons tested, but it measured content, not absorption; FDA's 2026 laboratory study judged releases far below harmful levels and the only biomarker study found no significant differences; douching, by contrast, tracked 81% higher blood 1,4-dichlorobenzene and has no health benefit.

dose.effective: Use the lowest-absorbency tampon you need and change it as directed (toxic shock prevention); menstrual cups were safe in a meta-analysis (watch for IUD dislodgement); skip douches, feminine sprays and powders; choose unscented products to avoid added fragrance chemicals.
dose.studied_range: Content testing of 30 tampons (14 brands) and 11 US products; NHANES questionnaires; 259 women in a biomarker cohort.
dose.too_much: No harm threshold from tampon metals is established. FDA's extraction study under exaggerated conditions found margins of safety indicating negligible concern for all 19 metals detected.
dose.timeframe: Not measured; no study has tracked body metal levels before and after changing products.
dose.notes: Organic tampons were not consistently lower in metals: lead was higher in non-organic tampons but arsenic higher in organic ones.

factors.mechanism: Vaginal tissue is permeable and bypasses first-pass liver metabolism [epc-upson2022], so absorption of contaminants is plausible. In the only biomarker study, tampon users had non-significantly higher blood mercury and urinary isoprostane [epc-singh2019]. Modelling suggests lead released into menstrual fluid binds red cells and is largely reabsorbed by the tampon [epc-ellison2026].
factors.interactions: Metals overlap with [heavy-metals]; scented products overlap with [fragrance-musks]; PFAS-treated period underwear overlaps with [pfas-personal-care].
factors.caveats: Content is not exposure: only 19 of 55 extractable chemicals leached under realistic simulated use [epc-marcelis2025]. Dioxin exposure from tampons is thousands of times lower than from diet [epc-devito2002]. The douching-VOC link is cross-sectional and douching itself marks other exposures.
factors.debate: The tampon-metal authors argue that, with no 'safe' lead level, content warrants concern until absorption is studied [epc-shearston2024, epc-shearston2024b]. FDA's laboratory risk assessment [epc-jin2026, epc-fdatampon] and a model by scientists from a major tampon manufacturer [epc-ellison2026] conclude releases are negligible; the latter is industry-authored. A systematic review lists many chemical classes in menstrual products but no exposure-per-cycle data [epc-marroquin2024].

key_numbers.label: Lead in tampons (geometric mean)
Blood 1,4-dichlorobenzene, douching 2+ times/month
Modelled lead available to vaginal tissue per tampon

factors.name: PFAS in cosmetics and dental floss
factors.headline: PFAS are added to some long-wear cosmetics and PTFE dental floss (FDA 2025: 51 PFAS in 1,744 cosmetic formulations, safety unestablished for most); one study linked Oral-B Glide flossing to higher serum PFHxS and short-chain PFAS cross skin models, but for most people water, food and dust dominate PFAS intake ([pfas]).

dose.effective: Check ingredient lists for 'PTFE', 'perfluoro-' or 'polyfluoro-' (common in waterproof or long-wear makeup and some floss); switch to nylon or silk floss and keep flossing. Deal first with bigger sources: contaminated water ([water-filtration]) and the steps in [pfas].
dose.studied_range: Product testing of tens of cosmetics; one cohort of 178 women with serum PFAS and product-use interviews.
dose.too_much: No cosmetic-specific threshold; serum guidance (NASEM 2 and 20 ng/mL for summed PFAS) is in [pfas].
dose.timeframe: Long-chain PFAS have serum half-lives of about 2.7-5.3 years, so body levels fall slowly after a source is removed.
dose.notes: Many cosmetic PFAS are polyfluoroalkyl phosphate esters that can break down to persistent acids.

factors.mechanism: PFAS act on PPAR nuclear receptors, lipid metabolism and immune function; oxidative-stress links in humans are inconsistent (see [pfas]). Short-chain PFAS permeate skin models while long chains lodge in skin tissue [epc-ragnarsdottir2024].
factors.interactions: Adds to the body burden described in [pfas], [pfas-sperm] and [pfas-egg]; flossing remains important for [periodontal-disease].
factors.caveats: The floss finding is from one study whose interviews came years after blood collection [epc-boronow2019]. Dermal-intake estimates come from skin models and assumed product concentrations [epc-wang2025].
factors.debate: Some modelling suggests cosmetics may rival diet for short-chain PFCA intake and add meaningfully to PFOA in regular users [epc-wang2025], while a European emissions study found cosmetics a smaller PFAS source than textiles [epc-putz2022]. FDA concluded it lacks data to judge safety of most cosmetic PFAS [epc-fda2025pfas]; products can contain very high levels of precursor PAPs [epc-harris2022].

key_numbers.label: PFAS used in US cosmetic formulations
PFHxS serum half-life

factors.name: 'Clean', 'natural' and 'free-of' product choices
factors.headline: Choosing products labelled free of specific chemicals works for those chemicals (within 3-5 days: parabens -30 to -45%, triclosan and BP-3 -36%, MEP -22 to -27%), but 'clean' and 'natural' are unregulated marketing terms: 94% of 1,470 'clean' products contained at least one contact allergen, and no study shows a health benefit from switching.

dose.effective: Read the ingredient list for specific chemicals rather than trusting 'clean' or 'natural'. Prioritise leave-on products used on large areas (body lotion, sunscreen, body spray, foundation) and perfume. Prefer 'fragrance-free'. If you have eczema or sensitive skin, patch-test new 'natural' products (essential oils such as ylang-ylang and lemongrass are common allergens). A 3-5 day switch measurably lowers urine levels; a 1-month web-based programme sustained 9-24% reductions for parabens.
dose.studied_range: Interventions of 2 days to 1 month in teenage girls, young women and mothers.
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels drop within 2-5 days of switching.
dose.notes: The switch did not work in Korean girls who used few cosmetics to begin with, and some chemicals rose when unlabelled substitutes were present.

factors.mechanism: Removing the dominant source of short-half-life chemicals (parabens, phthalates, triclosan, BP-3) lowers urinary levels within days; it does not change persistent chemicals much.
factors.interactions: The practical tool for [parabens], [triclosan-triclocarban], [uv-filters], [fragrance-musks] and the phthalate part of [plastics-chemicals]; keep [sunscreen] use when switching.
factors.caveats: Intervention studies are short, mostly uncontrolled pre-post designs, and measure urine chemicals, not health. Labels are incomplete: product testing found many unlisted chemicals, including in 'alternative' products [epc-dodson2012].
factors.debate: Dermatologists warn that 'natural does not mean safe' and that clean-labelled products are loaded with botanical allergens [epc-rubin2019, epc-tran2022, epc-geier2022]. Environmental-health researchers argue that targeted label reading lowers exposure [epc-harley2016, epc-kim2021] and that precaution is justified given endocrine activity [epc-dodson2012], while noting individual action is limited and regulation would be fairer [epc-jovanovic2026]. A 2-day restriction failed overall in low users [epc-kang2025]. US law (MoCRA) now requires safety substantiation but sets no definition of 'clean' [epc-fdamocra, epc-filley2023].

key_numbers.label: 'Clean' products with at least one potential allergen
Propylparaben after 3 days of labelled-free products
MEP after 5 days without usual products

factors.name: Phthalates (DEHP, DBP, BBzP, DiNP, DEP) and their replacements
factors.headline: Nearly everyone excretes phthalates, which clear within a day; the most consistent human signals are slightly more preterm births (12-16% higher odds per interquartile rise, 16 pooled US cohorts) and shorter anogenital distance in baby boys, while headline mortality estimates rest on NHANES analyses that disagree with each other, and a 2026 randomized trial cut urinary DBP and BBzP metabolites by 38-54% in 7 days with low-plastic food.

dose.effective: Food is the main lever for DEHP and DiNP: cook from fresh, minimally packaged ingredients and eat less fast food and ultra-processed food (people getting 35% or more of calories from fast food had 24% higher DEHP and 39% higher DiNP metabolites); store and reheat food in glass or steel. A 7-day randomized diet of food sourced to avoid plastic contact plus plastic-free kitchenware cut MnBP 37.5% and MBzP 53.5%. For DEP (fragrance carrier) and DBP: pick fragrance-free lotions, deodorants and aftershave (cologne or aftershave users had about double urinary MEP; a 3-day switch cut MEP 27%). If you take an enteric-coated drug long term (some mesalamine, omeprazole, didanosine or theophylline products), ask a pharmacist whether a phthalate-free formulation exists; never stop a medicine on your own. Replace soft PVC flooring when renovating, and wet-mop and vacuum dust (PVC bedroom flooring went with higher infant MBzP).
dose.studied_range: Interventions from 3 days to 2 months, in 20-100 people per study; outcomes are urinary metabolites. Typical intakes in Germany: median 2.7 ug/kg/day DEHP, 2.1 DnBP, 1.5 DiBP, 0.6 DiNP.
dose.too_much: EFSA (2019) group tolerable daily intake 50 ug/kg body weight/day as DEHP equivalents for DBP, BBP, DEHP and DINP (individual TDI for DBP 10 ug/kg); average European diets supply 0.9-7.2 ug/kg/day. HBM4EU urinary guidance values (e.g. 0.5 mg/L for 5-oxo- plus 5-OH-MEHP in adults) were exceeded in up to 5% of European children and teens, and a mixture risk could not be excluded for about 17%. Very high exposures come from medical PVC in neonatal intensive care and from DBP-coated medicines (urinary MBP up to 50-fold higher).
dose.timeframe: Metabolite half-lives are about 2-18 hours, so urine levels fall within 1-3 days of removing a source and rise again as soon as it returns. Pregnancy associations concern exposure during pregnancy itself (DEHP: first and second trimester in the largest pool).
dose.notes: One spot urine sample is a poor measure of usual DEHP exposure (intraclass correlation 0.08-0.3), which blurs associations. US and German exposure to DEHP, DBP, BBzP and DEP fell after 2001 while the replacements DINCH and DEHTP rose quickly (DEHTP from under 10% to 100% detection in German 24-hour urine, 2009-2017).

factors.mechanism: Several ortho-phthalates (DBP, DEHP, BBzP, DiNP; DEP only weakly) are anti-androgenic: during a fetal window their monoesters suppress Leydig-cell testosterone and INSL3, producing the rat 'phthalate syndrome' (hypospadias, undescended testes, malformed accessory glands, shorter anogenital distance); EFSA's group TDI rests on this fetal-testosterone effect. In people, oxidative stress is the best-documented intermediate: across repeated pregnancy samples, phthalate metabolites tracked urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane (an IQR rise in MBP or MiBP went with about 50% more 8-isoprostane in Puerto Rico), and in mediation analysis 8-isoprostane accounted for an estimated 47-60% of the DEHP-preterm-birth association. In 1,034 Chinese men every metabolite tracked 8-OHdG, 8-isoPGF2a and HNE-MA.
factors.interactions: Shares food and packaging sources with [bisphenols] and [microplastics]; fast food and ultra-processed diets raise several at once, so diet quality ([mediterranean-diet]) confounds most associations. Fragrance-free products also cut parabens and triclosan. Persistent chemicals are covered under [pfas]. Fertility evidence is in [phthalates-sperm] and [phthalates-egg].
factors.caveats: Most evidence is observational with single spot urines, so exposure is badly misclassified (DEHP ICC about 0.1-0.3), which usually biases toward the null but can also create chance findings when 11 or more metabolites are tested against many outcomes. Phthalates come with other exposures (processed food, low income, fragrance use, medical care), so residual confounding and reverse causation (sick people receive more medical PVC and coated drugs) are real threats in mortality studies. Exposure-reduction trials are short and small and none measured a health outcome. 'Phthalate-free' often means DINCH or DEHTP, which have far less human data.
factors.debate: Mortality: an NHANES analysis linked DEHP and high-molecular-weight metabolites to higher all-cause mortality and estimated 90,761-107,283 US deaths a year at ages 55-64 [ept-trasande2022], and burden models built on that hazard ratio attributed 356,238 global cardiovascular deaths and 1.97 million preterm births to DEHP [ept-hyman2025, ept-hyman2026] (the 2025 estimate was funded by Bloomberg Philanthropies and NIH, with the Beyond Petrochemicals campaign named in its disclosures). But other analyses of the same NHANES data found no link with cardiovascular death [ept-sturgeon2016], implicated different metabolites (MBzP and MnBP, not DEHP) [ept-beyer2022], or found the plasticizer-mixture link only in people with low vitamin D or folate [ept-zhang2025]; attributable-death figures assume the association is causal. Preterm birth: a 16-cohort pool [ept-welch2022], the ECHO cohort [ept-buckley2026] and an EPA systematic review [ept-radke2019] support a modest link, but the pool put the DEHP window in early pregnancy [ept-friedman2025] while a fertility cohort found it late [ept-yland2022]. Anogenital distance: shorter AGD with prenatal phthalates in US and Swedish cohorts [ept-swan2005, ept-swan2015, ept-bornehag2015] but no consistent association in a low-exposed Danish cohort [ept-jensen2016]. Sources: the PVC-flooring study [ept-carlstedt2013] drew a letter calling it 'anti-PVC advocacy' [ept-blakey2013]. Exposure reduction: food and personal-care swaps lowered metabolites in days [ept-rudel2011, ept-harley2016, ept-harray2026], but a catered low-exposure diet backfired on contaminated spices and milk [ept-sathyanarayana2013] and a plastic-free family saw mixed results [ept-hutter2016]; a scoping review concludes policy may matter more than individual action [ept-yang2023]. Replacements: DEHTP showed no developmental toxicity in older guideline rodent studies at hundreds of mg/kg [ept-faber2007] and intakes sit far below its TDI [ept-lessmann2019], yet a 2025 mouse study found ovarian effects from 10 ug/kg [ept-potts2025]; DINCH metabolites were unrelated to IVF outcomes in one cohort [ept-machtinger2018] but went with longer time to pregnancy, higher FSH and preterm birth in others [ept-blaauwendraad2025, ept-jiang2024, ept-yland2022], all single-study signals.

key_numbers.label: Preterm-birth odds per IQR rise in MiBP (16 pooled cohorts)
Fall in urinary MBzP after 7-day low-plastic diet (RCT)
Higher DiNP metabolites with high fast-food intake
Urinary MBP in mesalamine users vs non-users
EFSA group TDI (DBP, BBP, DEHP, DINP)
Within-person ICC of sum-DEHP in pregnancy

factors.name: Bisphenols (BPA, BPS, BPF, BPAF)
factors.headline: BPA and its replacements BPS and BPF clear with half-lives of about 6-7 hours, so urine tracks the last meal: a can of soup a day took urinary BPA from 1.1 to 20.8 ug/L and a 7-day low-plastic diet cut it 60%, but human disease links are observational and regulators disagree by up to 20,000-fold on the safe dose.

dose.effective: Avoid canned food and canned drinks (canned soup daily: urinary BPA 20.8 vs 1.1 ug/L; cans vs PET bottles: +22%); retire old hard polycarbonate bottles (+69% in a week); eat fresh food (3 days: BPA -66%; 7-day randomized low-plastic diet: -60%). Decline paper receipts or hold them briefly, and never right after hand sanitizer or lotion (2 hours of handling raised urinary BPA from 1.8 to 5.8 ug/L, prevented by gloves; sanitizer before handling plus finger food gave serum free BPA of about 7 ng/mL within 90 minutes). Treat 'BPA-free' as possibly BPS or BPF, not bisphenol-free.
dose.studied_range: Interventions from one meal to 3 weeks in 20-103 people; outcomes are urinary bisphenols. US medians 2013-14: BPA 1.24 ug/L, BPS 0.37, BPF 0.35.
dose.too_much: EFSA (2023) tolerable daily intake 0.2 ng/kg body weight/day, cut 20,000-fold from 4 ug/kg on immune (Th17) effects in mice; average and high diets exceed it 100-1,000-fold. Germany's BfR proposed a TDI 1,000-fold higher, and the US FDA kept its higher limits. The EU banned BPA in food contact materials by Regulation 2024/3190 (most uses from 20 July 2026, some to January 2028).
dose.timeframe: Urinary BPA peaks 2-4 hours after a canned meal and is back to baseline within about 24 hours; after skin contact with receipts it peaks later (8-12 hours) and is still raised at 24 hours.
dose.notes: A single spot urine is close to useless for ranking people's usual BPA exposure (ICC 0.12 in pregnancy; one sample attenuated a dose-response by 69%, and about 18 samples were needed to cut that bias to 10%).

factors.mechanism: Bisphenols act on nuclear and membrane estrogen signalling and have anti-androgenic activity in vitro and in animals. In 482 pregnant women with repeated samples, an IQR rise in urinary BPA went with 5-9% higher 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane and 9% higher IL-6. EFSA's critical effect is immune: expansion of pro-inflammatory Th17 cells in mice. BPS and BPF show hormonal potency of the same order as BPA in vitro and in animals.
factors.interactions: Comes from the same canned and packaged foods as [phthalates] and the plastic contact that sheds [microplastics]. Ultra-processed diets raise BPF along with several phthalates. Fertility evidence is in [bisphenols-sperm] and [bisphenols-egg]; soy intake modified BPA associations in one IVF cohort ([soy]).
factors.caveats: Human outcome studies rely on one or two spot urines for a chemical with an hours-long half-life, so exposure misclassification is severe. Mortality and cardiometabolic links come from NHANES-type cross-sections or cohorts with one sample, open to confounding by diet, income and obesity (BPS was higher in heavier men). Many endpoints and metabolites are tested. Industry-funded guideline studies and academic studies reach different conclusions, partly because they test different endpoints. Falling BPA has been offset by rising BPS (US: BPA -15%, BPS +20% after California's Prop 65 listing).
factors.debate: Safe dose: EFSA's 20,000-fold TDI cut [ept-efsa2023] is endorsed by academic endocrinologists [ept-vomsaal2024, ept-zoeller2023] but opposed by the European Medicines Agency and Germany's BfR, which proposed a TDI 1,000-fold higher based on sperm counts and rejected the Th17 endpoint [ept-zoeller2023, ept-kortenkamp2024]; the US FDA kept its higher limits [ept-vomsaal2024]. A consultant-written letter arguing EFSA's evidence did not support a lower TDI was withdrawn by the journal [ept-prueitt2023] and should not be relied on. The NTP CLARITY-BPA guideline study found no consistent effects except at the top dose [ept-camacho2019], while the linked academic studies on the same animals reported effects at the lowest dose, often non-monotonic [ept-heindel2020]. Half-life: dosing studies give about 6 hours [ept-thayer2015, ept-teeguarden2011], but NHANES BPA barely fell with fasting (apparent half-life 43 hours), implying non-food sources [ept-stahlhut2009], which receipt studies support [ept-ehrlich2014, ept-hormann2014]. Interventions: fresh food, a pilot RCT and the PERTH RCT lowered urinary BPA [ept-rudel2011, ept-hagobian2017, ept-harray2026], but a real-world teenager diet had no effect [ept-galloway2018] and a catered diet backfired [ept-sathyanarayana2013]. Substitutes: BPS and BPF show BPA-like hormonal activity and reproductive-toxicity signals [ept-rochester2015, ept-denbraversewradj2020, ept-mhaoutykodja2024]. Mortality: top-tertile BPA had HR 1.49 for all-cause death in NHANES [ept-bao2020], from 344 deaths and one urine sample.

Urinary BPA after daily canned soup (vs 1.1 fresh)
Fall in urinary BPA after 7-day low-plastic diet (RCT)
EFSA BPA tolerable daily intake (2023)
Within-person ICC of urinary BPA in pregnancy

factors.name: Glyphosate (Roundup) residues
factors.headline: Glyphosate is in the urine of most people (geometric means about 0.1-0.4 ug/L, mainly from grains and legumes); IARC calls it 'probably carcinogenic' while EFSA and ECHA found no carcinogenic hazard, the largest farmer cohort found no lymphoma excess, and urinary glyphosate tracked modestly higher 8-OHdG and MDA (about 15-20%) in farmers.

dose.effective: For the general public the main source is diet: an all-organic diet cut urinary glyphosate by about 70% within 3-6 days in an uncontrolled study, but only modestly in a randomized trial and not at all for people living within 0.5 km of sprayed fields. Glyphosate is systemic, so washing and peeling remove little. Home and garden users: wear gloves and long sleeves when mixing and spraying (farmers who did had about half the urinary levels).
dose.studied_range: General-population urine about 0.1-0.4 ug/L; farmers after spraying about 0.9 ug/L geometric mean, with peaks of about 20-30 ug/g creatinine.
dose.too_much: EU acceptable daily intake 0.5 mg/kg body weight per day; urinary data suggest typical exposure is under 3% of it [efw-vicini2021]. No human threshold for harm has been identified.
dose.timeframe: Urinary half-life roughly 7-18 hours; levels fall within days of changing diet or stopping spraying.
dose.notes: Commercial formulations contain surfactants (e.g. POEA) that are more toxic to cells than glyphosate alone; most human studies measure only glyphosate.

factors.mechanism: In cell and animal studies glyphosate and its formulations raise ROS, lipid peroxidation and DNA damage and disturb mitochondrial function; IARC judged the genotoxicity evidence strong. In humans, urinary glyphosate was associated with higher urinary 8-OHdG and MDA in farmers [efw-chang2023] and in rural Taiwanese adults [efw-ko2025], and with mosaic loss of chromosome Y in heavy users [efw-chang2023b].
factors.interactions: Exposure-reduction overlaps with [organic-food]; residues in grains are a reason some people avoid [whole-grains], but no evidence suggests that trade-off is worthwhile. Sperm data are in [glyphosate-sperm]. Other pesticide classes: [organophosphates], [pyrethroids], [neonicotinoids].
factors.caveats: Almost all human outcome data come from occupational exposure, which is 10-100 times higher than dietary exposure. Single spot urines misclassify exposure. Cross-sectional NHANES analyses linking glyphosate to sex hormones, cognition or grip strength [efw-wu2025] test many outcomes in one dataset and cannot establish direction. The pregnancy-length signal from small cohorts [efw-parvez2018, efw-lesseur2022] did not replicate in a cohort of about 1,800 [efw-ashleymartin2025]. The organic-diet study showing a 70% drop was small, uncontrolled and partly advocacy-funded [efw-fagan2020].
factors.debate: Hazard classification: IARC classed glyphosate as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A) on limited human evidence for non-Hodgkin lymphoma, sufficient animal evidence and strong genotoxicity evidence [efw-guyton2015], whereas EFSA's 2023 review found no critical areas of concern and accepted ECHA's conclusion that it is not carcinogenic [efw-efsa2023]. Epidemiology: the 54,251-person Agricultural Health Study found no NHL excess [efw-andreotti2018]; a meta-analysis using the highest-exposure groups found 41% higher NHL risk [efw-zhang2019], but a re-analysis showed this depends on exposure and lag choices, with RR 1.05 for ever-exposure [efw-kabat2021]. A 2025 lifetime rat study at the EU ADI reported multiple tumours [efw-panzacchi2025]. Integrity: an influential 2000 safety review concluding no human health concern was retracted in 2025 [efw-williams2000, efw-williams2025]. Oxidative stress: urinary glyphosate tracked 8-OHdG in farmers and rural adults [efw-chang2023, efw-ko2025] but only AMPA, not glyphosate, tracked 8-OHdG in children [efw-makris2022].

8-OHdG, top vs bottom urinary glyphosate quartile (farmers)
Drop in urinary glyphosate on organic diet (uncontrolled)
NHL meta-RR, highest exposure groups
NHL meta-RR, ever exposure, no lag

factors.name: Organophosphate insecticides (incl. chlorpyrifos)
factors.headline: Prenatal organophosphate exposure is consistently linked to lower child IQ (about 7 points between top and bottom quintiles of maternal urinary metabolites in one cohort), the EU withdrew chlorpyrifos in 2020 after EFSA said no safe level could be set, and an organic diet cuts urinary organophosphate metabolites by 60-95% within a week.

dose.effective: Diet is the main non-farm source: switching to organic produce lowered a malathion metabolite 95% and the chlorpyrifos metabolite 61% in 6 days. Peel or wash produce (peeling removes most surface residues). Avoid indoor organophosphate sprays; if you farm or garden, wear gloves and long sleeves. In pregnancy, these steps matter most.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary dialkyl phosphates and TCPy; cord-blood chlorpyrifos (SD 4.61 pg/g) in the Columbia cohort; occupational exposure in farmworkers.
dose.too_much: EFSA (2019) could not set any safe exposure level for chlorpyrifos because of possible genotoxicity and developmental neurotoxicity. Child IQ deficits were seen at maternal metabolite levels within the general US range.
dose.timeframe: Metabolites clear within 1-2 days (chlorpyrifos metabolite half-life ~27 h); neurodevelopmental effects relate to exposure during pregnancy and appear years later.
dose.notes: Organophosphates are the class most clearly linked to harm at everyday exposure. Chlorpyrifos is banned in the EU; in the US its food uses have been restricted but regulation has changed several times.

factors.mechanism: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase; at lower doses their oxon metabolites also deplete glutathione, raise lipid peroxidation and disrupt neural development by non-cholinergic routes. In pregnant women, urinary organophosphate metabolites tracked 8-OHdG and lipid-peroxidation markers across repeated samples [efw-wang2024].
factors.interactions: Sperm effects in occupational settings are summarized in [pesticides]. Co-exposure with [pyrethroids] and [neonicotinoids] is the norm. Organic diets ([organic-food]) and [washing-produce] lower intake; don't eat fewer fruit and vegetables ([high-fruit-vegetable-intake]).
factors.caveats: Spot urines vary greatly within a person (ICC <0.4) [efw-li2019], and urinary dialkyl phosphates also capture harmless preformed metabolites in food. Cohorts are few (New York, California, Mount Sinai) and the Columbia raw data have not been shared [efw-dourson2020]. Effect sizes per person are small but population-wide.
factors.debate: For harm: the Columbia (chlorpyrifos) and CHAMACOS (dialkyl phosphates) cohorts both found lower IQ at age 7 [efw-rauh2011, efw-bouchard2011]; a policy review recommended a class-wide phase-out [efw-hertzpicciotto2018]; EFSA found no safe level for chlorpyrifos [efw-efsa2019]. Regulatory integrity: an academic re-analysis found effects in raw industry neurotoxicity data that the summaries omitted [efw-mie2018], which a letter from authors including a Dow scientist disputed [efw-juberg2019]; neurotoxicity studies given to US EPA were not disclosed in the EU [efw-mie2023]. Against: a consultancy commentary could not reproduce the Columbia association from published figures and criticised the lack of data sharing [efw-dourson2020].

factors.name: Pyrethroid insecticides
factors.headline: Pyrethroids replaced many organophosphates and are found in most people's urine; one NHANES cohort linked the top tertile of urinary 3-PBA to 56% higher all-cause and 3-fold cardiovascular mortality, but it rests on a single urine sample of a metabolite with half-life about 6 hours and has not been replicated.

dose.effective: Peel, juice or cook produce where practical (peeling removes 60-100% of pyrethroid residues; tap-water washing 10-70%); choose organic for high-residue items; use indoor insect sprays, pet flea products and treated clothing sparingly and ventilate after use.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary 3-PBA (NHANES); residential and dietary exposure.
dose.too_much: No human threshold established. Mortality excess was in the top NHANES tertile of urinary 3-PBA.
dose.timeframe: 3-PBA half-life about 6 h; urine reflects the last day or so.
dose.notes: Pyrethroids are less acutely toxic to people than organophosphates; the concern is chronic, low-level exposure, which is poorly measured.

factors.mechanism: Pyrethroids prolong sodium-channel opening in nerves; in animals and cells they raise ROS, lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction and have anti-androgenic activity. In pregnant women and Cypriot children, urinary 3-PBA tracked 8-OHdG [efw-wang2024, efw-makris2022].
factors.interactions: Sperm data: [pyrethroids-sperm]. Co-exposure with [organophosphates] and [neonicotinoids]. Lower intake via [washing-produce] and [organic-food].
factors.caveats: Single spot urine has ICC <0.22 for 3-PBA [efw-morgan2016]; at least four samples months apart are needed [efw-lin2021], so cohort exposure groups are badly misclassified. 3-PBA is also formed from pyrethroid breakdown in food and the environment. Residual confounding by income, diet and health status is likely in NHANES.
factors.debate: For harm: the NHANES mortality cohort [efw-bao2020] and an invited commentary urging closer scrutiny [efw-stellman2020]; urinary pyrethroid metabolites track oxidative DNA damage markers [efw-wang2024, efw-makris2022]. Against: reliability studies show one urine sample cannot classify long-term pyrethroid exposure [efw-morgan2016, efw-lin2021], and no independent cohort has replicated the mortality finding.

factors.name: Neonicotinoid insecticides
factors.headline: About half of Americans have recent neonicotinoid exposure (higher in young children and in summer), but human health data are sparse: a systematic review found only suggestive, methodologically weak findings, and links to oxidative stress or sperm motility come from small cross-sectional studies.

dose.effective: Organic produce lowered urinary clothianidin by 83% in 6 days. Because neonicotinoids are systemic (taken up into the plant), washing removes little; peeling helps only for residues in the peel.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary neonicotinoids and metabolites (NHANES 2015-2016; Chinese cohorts).
dose.too_much: No human health threshold established.
dose.timeframe: Urinary half-lives 2.5-50 hours depending on compound.
dose.notes: Neonicotinoids are best known for harm to bees; their human health effects are largely unstudied.

factors.mechanism: Neonicotinoids bind nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (more weakly in mammals than insects); animal studies report oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and reproductive toxicity at high doses. In pregnant women a neonicotinoid metabolite contributed to associations with 8-OHdG [efw-wang2024].
factors.interactions: Co-exposure with [organophosphates] and [pyrethroids]. Organic diets ([organic-food]) lower intake; [washing-produce] does little for systemic pesticides.
factors.caveats: Single urines classify neonicotinoid exposure poorly (ICC 0.02-0.37; 16-172 samples needed per person) [efw-li2020]. One seminal-plasma study found lower motility with only one of several metabolites [efw-wang2022].
factors.debate: Exposure is common [efw-ospina2019, efw-zhang2022] and some cross-sectional studies link it to oxidative markers [efw-wang2024, efw-li2020] or motility [efw-wang2022], but the only systematic review judged the evidence too limited and weak to draw conclusions [efw-cimino2017]. No study has found a health outcome robust to repeated exposure measurement.

factors.name: Nitrate in drinking water
factors.headline: Large Danish and US cohorts link drinking-water nitrate well below legal limits (from about 4-9 mg/L nitrate, vs 50 mg/L EU / 44 mg/L US) to 16-50% more colorectal or colon cancer and slightly more preterm birth and neural tube defects, but meta-analyses disagree and the effects are small.

dose.effective: If you use a private well in a farming area, test it for nitrate yearly (and after floods). If nitrate is raised, use reverse osmosis or ion-exchange treatment or a different water source, especially for pregnancy and infant formula. Boiling concentrates nitrate; carbon filters do not remove it.
dose.studied_range: Tap-water nitrate from <1 to >50 mg/L nitrate (0-11 mg/L nitrate-N).
dose.too_much: Legal limits: 50 mg/L nitrate (EU, WHO) or 10 mg/L nitrate-N (US). Colorectal cancer risk rose from about 3.9 mg/L nitrate in Denmark; colon cancer HR 1.52 at >=9.25 mg/L.
dose.timeframe: Nitrate half-life in the body about 5 h; cancer associations reflect decades; birth outcomes relate to exposure during pregnancy.
dose.notes: Vegetable nitrate (beetroot, leafy greens) comes with vitamin C and polyphenols that block nitrosamine formation and was not linked to colorectal cancer; the concern is water and processed-meat nitrate/nitrite.

factors.mechanism: Ingested nitrate is reduced to nitrite by oral bacteria; in the stomach nitrite can form N-nitroso compounds that alkylate DNA. Vitamin C, vitamin E and polyphenols inhibit this nitrosation; red and processed meat promote it. Nitrite also oxidises haemoglobin (methaemoglobinaemia in infants) and nitrate competes with iodide uptake by the thyroid.
factors.interactions: Risk appeared stronger with smoking and high red-meat intake and weaker with high vitamin C, folate and flavonoid intake [efw-erichsen2025]; see [processed-meat], [vitamin-c-foods], [leafy-greens]. Agricultural well water often also carries [arsenic-drinking-water] or pesticides.
factors.caveats: Exposure is assigned from water-utility or well-zone data, not personal intake; rural residence, agricultural co-contaminants (atrazine, pesticides) and socioeconomic status confound. Many associations are near 1.0 (preterm OR 1.01-1.08), so residual confounding could explain them.
factors.debate: Harm below the limit: a Danish nationwide cohort found colorectal cancer risk rising from 3.87 mg/L [efw-schullehner2018], a Danish diet cohort found colon cancer HR 1.52 at >=9.25 mg/L [efw-erichsen2025], and reviews cite colorectal cancer, thyroid disease and neural tube defects [efw-ward2018]. Doubt: one meta-analysis found no colorectal link (OR 1.02) but a gastric-cancer link [efw-picetti2022], another judged the colorectal association weak, inconsistent and possibly confounded [efw-elwood2022], and a third found water nitrate unrelated to colorectal cancer [efw-hosseini2021]. Birth outcomes: a within-mother sibling design [efw-sherris2021] and national cohorts [efw-coffman2022, efw-chambers2026] found small preterm increases, and a meta-analysis found OR 1.05 for preterm and 1.51 for neural tube defects in case-control studies [efw-lin2023].

factors.name: Chlorination by-products (trihalomethanes) in tap water
factors.headline: Trihalomethanes from chlorinated water are linked to bladder cancer in men (pooled OR 1.24 above 1 ug/L, 1.44 above 50 ug/L; about 5% of EU bladder cancers if causal), but an early miscarriage signal (OR 1.8) was not confirmed in a larger study designed to test it, and links with birth weight and preterm birth are close to null.

dose.effective: If your utility reports high total trihalomethanes (above about 50-80 ug/L), drink water from a carbon-filter pitcher or under-sink carbon filter (a pitcher plus fridge storage removed about 92% of THMs and 66% of haloacetic acids) or let water stand in an open jug in the fridge. Showers and baths give more THM uptake than drinking: ventilate the bathroom and keep hot showers shorter.
dose.studied_range: Tap-water THM about 1-100+ ug/L; EU mean about 12 ug/L.
dose.too_much: Regulatory limits: 80 ug/L total THM (US), 100 ug/L (EU). Birth-defect associations appeared above about 60 ug/L THM in a dose-response meta-analysis.
dose.timeframe: THMs leave the blood within hours; bladder cancer associations reflect decades of exposure.
dose.notes: Disinfection prevents far more disease than by-products cause; never avoid treated water for untreated sources. Boiling removes volatile THMs but not most haloacetic acids.

factors.mechanism: Chlorine reacts with organic matter to form THMs and haloacetic acids. Brominated THMs are activated by GSTT1 to mutagens. In pregnant women, blood THMs and urinary haloacetic acids tracked 8-OHdG, 8-isoprostane and HNE-MA across repeated samples [efw-liu2020].
factors.interactions: Sperm data: [disinfection-byproducts-sperm]. Filtration for other contaminants: [water-filtration]. Swimming pools add exposure.
factors.caveats: Exposure is usually assigned from utility averages, missing showering, bathing and swimming (which raised bladder cancer risk independently [efw-villanueva2007]). The bladder cancer link appears in men but not women [efw-villanueva2004]. The EU burden estimate assumes causality [efw-evlampidou2020].
factors.debate: Miscarriage: a California cohort found OR 1.8 for heavy drinkers of high-THM water [efw-waller1998], but a three-site US study built to test this found no effect (OR 1.1) [efw-savitz2006] and no longer time to pregnancy [efw-maclehose2008]. Birth outcomes: a meta-analysis found little or no association with low birth weight or preterm birth [efw-grellier2010], while a newer dose-response meta-analysis reports defects above about 60 ug/L [efw-deiana2025]. Bladder cancer: pooled case-control studies support an association [efw-villanueva2004, efw-villanueva2007], but cohort data are scarce.

factors.name: Arsenic in well and tap water
factors.headline: About 2.1 million Americans drink well water above the 10 ug/L arsenic limit; arsenic is an established carcinogen at high levels, and at low-moderate levels each 20 ug/L is linked to about 9-16% more cardiovascular disease, while a randomized program of point-of-use filters cut urinary arsenic by 47-55%.

dose.effective: Test private well water for arsenic (and uranium) at least once, and again if the area is known for arsenic; if above 10 ug/L, install a certified point-of-use reverse-osmosis or arsenic-adsorption filter for drinking and cooking water and maintain it, or use another source. Cooking rice and pasta in high-arsenic water adds to intake.
dose.studied_range: Well water from <1 to several hundred ug/L; US cohorts mostly 1-50 ug/L.
dose.too_much: WHO/EU/US limit 10 ug/L. Fetal loss and infant death rose above 50 ug/L in Bangladesh. EFSA's reference point is 0.06 ug/kg body weight per day of inorganic arsenic (all sources).
dose.timeframe: Urinary arsenic falls over days to weeks after switching water; cardiovascular and cancer risks reflect years.
dose.notes: Arsenic in water is tasteless and odourless; only testing finds it. Boiling does not remove it.

factors.mechanism: Inorganic arsenic binds thiols, depletes glutathione, inhibits DNA repair and generates ROS during its methylation; arsenic-exposed populations show higher urinary 8-OHdG and comet-assay damage [efw-devizcaya2009, efw-fujino2005]. It also causes endothelial dysfunction and epigenetic changes.
factors.interactions: Rice is the other main source ([arsenic-rice]); arsenic and [uranium-drinking-water] often co-occur in wells; selenium and folate status affect arsenic methylation ([folic-acid]). See [heavy-metals] for other toxic metals.
factors.caveats: Low-level cardiovascular associations weaken after adjusting for diabetes, hypertension and kidney function, which may be mediators or confounders [efw-moon2013]. Cancer risk below about 100 ug/L is disputed. Semen data are mostly small cross-sectional studies; a meta-analysis's pooled concentration and motility differences were not significant [efw-akhigbe2024b].
factors.debate: Low-level harm: dose-response meta-analysis shows CVD risk without a threshold [efw-moon2017]; the Strong Heart Study links low-moderate arsenic to CVD [efw-moon2013]; EFSA judges current dietary exposure a health concern [efw-efsa2024]. Doubt: meta-analyses found no lung or bladder cancer increase up to 150 ug/L [efw-boffetta2019] or at low levels in never-smokers [efw-mink2008]; the 2019 analysis's lead author declared work as a litigation expert [efw-boffetta2019]. Pregnancy: fetal loss rose above 50 ug/L [efw-rahman2007], but a later Bangladesh cohort found a stage-dependent pattern suggesting survival bias [efw-ahmed2019].

factors.name: Lead from service lines and plumbing
factors.headline: Lead service lines raise children's blood lead even when utilities meet the 15 ppb action level; Flint's 2014 water switch doubled the share of young children with elevated blood lead (2.4% to 4.9%), and certified carbon-block filters brought filtered water below 0.5 ug/L lead in over 97% of Flint samples.

dose.effective: Find out from your utility whether your home has a lead service line. If so, or if a water test shows lead: use an NSF/ANSI-53 certified filter for lead (and NSF-42 for particles) for all drinking and cooking water and for infant formula, change cartridges on time, use only cold water for cooking, and run the tap until it turns cold after water has stood for hours. Full (not partial) line replacement is the long-term fix.
dose.studied_range: Water lead from <1 to >150 ug/L; children's blood lead 1-10 ug/dL.
dose.too_much: No safe level of lead is known. CDC's blood lead reference value for children is 3.5 ug/dL; the US action level for water has been 15 ug/L, but blood lead rose even when utilities met it. FDA's interim dietary reference is 8.8 ug/day for women of childbearing age.
dose.timeframe: Blood lead mean life about 35 days; bone stores last decades and are released in pregnancy and menopause.
dose.notes: Partial service-line replacement can disturb pipes and temporarily raise lead; changes in water chemistry (as in Flint and Washington DC) can release lead suddenly.

factors.mechanism: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and glutathione-related enzymes, displaces zinc and calcium, and generates oxidative stress; it impairs neurodevelopment without a known threshold and raises blood pressure and cardiovascular mortality in adults [efw-lanphear2018].
factors.interactions: Other lead sources: [lead-spices], lead-glazed pottery and some cookware ([metal-cookware]), old paint and dust. Iron and calcium deficiency increase lead absorption ([iron-deficiency]). Overall metal burden: [heavy-metals].
factors.caveats: Water is one of several lead sources and its share varies by house. Flint blood-lead data are ecological. Fertility and fetal-death effects of the Flint crisis are contested.
factors.debate: Flint blood lead: one analysis found the share of children with elevated levels doubled after the switch [efw-hannaattisha2016], whereas a 2006-2016 trend analysis called the 2014-2015 rise consistent with random variation within a long decline [efw-gomez2018]. Flint fertility: an economics analysis found a 12% fall in fertility and lower birth weight [efw-grossman2019]; a biokinetic and vital-records analysis found the drop within normal variation and no excess fetal deaths [efw-roy2022]. Service lines: lead lines raised blood lead even at compliant water levels, and partial replacement did not help [efw-brown2011, efw-levallois2018].

factors.name: Fluoride in drinking water
factors.headline: Fluoride above 1.5 mg/L (twice the 0.7 mg/L used in fluoridation) is consistently linked to lower child IQ (NTP 2024, moderate confidence), but whether fluoridation-level exposure lowers IQ is contested, and the dental benefit of fluoridation today is smaller than once thought (about a quarter of a decayed tooth per child).

dose.effective: If your well water exceeds 1.5 mg/L, use reverse osmosis or another source, especially in pregnancy and for infant formula. At fluoridation levels (0.7 mg/L), a cautious option during pregnancy and for formula-fed infants is to use low-fluoride water for formula; keep brushing with fluoride toothpaste (spit, don't swallow).
dose.studied_range: Drinking water 0.1 to >4 mg/L; maternal urinary fluoride 0.1-3 mg/L.
dose.too_much: WHO guideline 1.5 mg/L; fluorosis of aesthetic concern in about 12% of people at 0.7 mg/L. A pooled benchmark analysis put a possible threshold for prenatal neurotoxicity at about 0.3-0.45 mg/L in urine.
dose.timeframe: Plasma fluoride clears in hours; skeletal stores accumulate over years; neurodevelopmental sensitivity is in pregnancy and infancy.
dose.notes: Carbon pitcher filters do not remove fluoride; reverse osmosis, activated alumina or distillation do.

factors.mechanism: At high doses fluoride inhibits enzymes, induces oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in animal brain and testis; human mechanistic evidence was judged too limited by NTP [efw-ntp2024].
factors.interactions: Fluoride often co-occurs with arsenic in some groundwater ([arsenic-drinking-water]). Reverse osmosis that removes fluoride also removes nitrate, arsenic and PFAS ([water-filtration]).
factors.caveats: Most studies (64 of 74 in the main meta-analysis) are cross-sectional, mostly from endemic-fluorosis areas in China and India with co-exposures (arsenic, iodine deficiency) and poor adjustment; North American cohorts measure single urine samples in pregnancy and found sex-specific effects that differ between studies.
factors.debate: Harm at higher exposure is broadly accepted: NTP found moderate-confidence evidence above 1.5 mg/L [efw-ntp2024] and a meta-analysis found IQ 1.63 points lower per mg/L urinary fluoride [efw-taylor2025]. At fluoridation levels: Canadian and Los Angeles cohorts link maternal fluoride to lower IQ in boys and to behaviour problems [efw-green2019, efw-malin2024], and a three-cohort benchmark analysis suggests a low threshold [efw-grandjean2024]; the NTP authors defend these findings [efw-taylor2025b]. Against: an editorial urged caution because the evidence rests on high-exposure, high-risk-of-bias studies [efw-levy2025]; a meta-analysis at fluoridation levels found no IQ effect [efw-kumar2023]; the Dunedin cohort found none [efw-broadbent2015]; a Spanish cohort found better scores in boys [efw-ibarluzea2022]. Benefit: Cochrane finds only a small, uncertain contemporary caries benefit [efw-iheozorejiofor2024], while Calgary saw more decay after stopping fluoridation [efw-mclaren2022].

factors.name: Uranium in well and tap water
factors.headline: Natural uranium in groundwater is under-recognised in US public and private water, especially in the West, Great Plains and in Hispanic and American Indian communities; it mainly affects kidney tubules and blood pressure in observational studies, with no clear effect on diabetes at low levels.

dose.effective: Test private wells in uranium-bearing regions together with arsenic; reverse osmosis or anion exchange removes uranium.
dose.studied_range: Finnish drilled wells median 25 ug/L (up to 1,500); US public systems mostly <30 ug/L.
dose.too_much: Finnish data suggest tubular effects without a clear threshold and a safe level possibly within 2-30 ug/L; some Navajo Nation wells exceeded US standards.
dose.timeframe: Not measured in intervention studies; kidney and blood-pressure associations reflect long-term intake.
dose.notes: Toxicity from natural uranium in water is chemical (kidney) rather than radiological.

factors.mechanism: Uranyl ions accumulate in proximal tubules and bone and cause oxidative stress and tubular injury in animals.
factors.interactions: Co-occurs with [arsenic-drinking-water] in private wells; the same reverse-osmosis systems remove both.
factors.caveats: Few cohorts with individual exposure; findings mix weak tubular markers and blood pressure; region-specific results vary in direction.
factors.debate: Tubular effects without a threshold were reported in Finnish well users [efw-kurttio2002], but a later Finnish study at higher exposures found no kidney cytotoxicity, only higher blood pressure [efw-kurttio2006]. Hypertension was linked in Strong Heart [efw-patterson2025], while diabetes was not in two cohorts [efw-spaur2026]. Water is a major driver of urinary uranium [efw-spaur2024], with environmental-justice concerns [efw-ravalli2022, efw-corlin2016].
