factors.name: Non-stick (PTFE) and ceramic-coated cookware
factors.headline: Older non-stick pans released small amounts of residual PFOA when heated (7-337 ng per pan, falling with use), newer coatings mostly release no detectable PFAS, and scratched pans shed PTFE particles; overheating can cause polymer fume fever, but no study links non-stick cookware use to blood PFAS or disease.

dose.effective: Use non-stick pans at low-to-medium heat, never preheat empty, use the extractor fan, use wooden or silicone utensils, and replace pans once the coating is scratched or flaking. For high-heat searing use cast iron, carbon steel or stainless steel. Keep pet birds out of the kitchen when cooking with non-stick pans.
dose.studied_range: Laboratory heating of pans at 179-250 C surface temperature; simulated cooking with abrasion.
dose.too_much: Overheated fluoropolymer coatings release fumes that cause polymer fume fever, usually self-limited within 12-48 h but potentially serious with heart or lung disease.
dose.timeframe: Fume symptoms within hours; any chronic effect unknown.
dose.notes: PFOA has been replaced in coating manufacture by alternatives such as GenX, which may be similarly toxic. 'Ceramic' (sol-gel silica) coatings are PTFE-free but wear faster; their particle release is barely studied. Microwave popcorn bags and grease-proof packaging are a more established PFAS source than pans.

factors.mechanism: Residual PFOA or replacement PFAS can off-gas from coatings; PTFE particles are chemically inert but, like other microplastics, may cause inflammation and oxidative stress in cell and animal studies.
factors.interactions: Main PFAS routes and testing are in [pfas]; particle exposure in [microplastics]. Packaging matters more: daily microwave popcorn tracked higher serum PFAS [efw-susmann2019]. Switching to metal pans raises different questions ([metal-cookware]).
factors.caveats: All evidence is from laboratory release tests, some by the manufacturer; no human biomonitoring study isolates cookware. PFAS emissions vary by brand and decline with use.
factors.debate: PFOA release: independent tests detected PFOA in the gas phase from heated pans [efw-sinclair2007], whereas DuPont scientists found none extractable under simulated cooking [efw-powley2005]; a 2024 study found no PFAS in 12 of 18 coated items [efw-wolf2024]; a perspective warns replacements may be similarly toxic [efw-sajid2017]. Particles: Raman imaging suggests thousands to millions of PTFE particles from a scratched pan [efw-luo2022], while a food-simulant study counted only a few thousand plastic particles a year from plastic cookware and none from non-plastic cookware [efw-cole2024].

factors.name: Aluminium, cast iron, stainless steel and glazed pottery
factors.headline: Acidic food leaches metals from cookware: new stainless steel raised nickel and chromium in tomato sauce about 35-fold, artisanal scrap-aluminium pots can leach enough lead to raise children's blood lead, lead-glazed pottery leaches lead, and cast iron adds iron (helpful in deficiency, unhelpful in iron overload).

dose.effective: Avoid lead-glazed or decorative ceramics and artisanal scrap-aluminium pots for cooking; don't cook or store acidic or salty foods (tomato, citrus, vinegar) for long in uncoated aluminium; season new stainless steel pans (leaching falls after about six uses) and use them for acidic dishes rather than storing food in them; people with nickel allergy may prefer enamelled or glass for acidic stews; cast iron is fine for most people but avoid it if you have haemochromatosis.
dose.studied_range: Laboratory cooking with acidic simulants and tomato sauce; iron-pot trials in low- and middle-income countries.
dose.too_much: About 88 ug nickel and 86 ug chromium per serving of tomato sauce after ten uses of stainless steel. EFSA tolerable weekly intake for aluminium 1 mg/kg body weight; food alone supplies about half of it for average German adults. Lead leaching >250 ug/L from about 1 in 10 artisanal aluminium pots.
dose.timeframe: Leaching happens per meal; stainless-steel leaching falls over the first six cooking cycles.
dose.notes: Commercial anodised aluminium and enamelled pots leach little. Iron cookware raised haemoglobin in some trials in anaemic populations, but a fish-shaped iron ingot did not help Cambodian women where iron deficiency was uncommon.

factors.mechanism: Acids dissolve metal ions from cookware surfaces. Iron and nickel can catalyse Fenton chemistry; lead and aluminium impair antioxidant enzymes; nickel triggers allergic inflammation in sensitised people.
factors.interactions: Cast iron interacts with [iron-deficiency] (helps) and [iron-excess] (avoid). Lead from pots adds to [lead-drinking-water] and [lead-spices]. Non-stick alternatives: [nonstick-cookware].
factors.caveats: Mostly laboratory leaching with aggressive simulants; few human biomarker studies. The aluminium-Alzheimer hypothesis rests on weak and conflicting data.
factors.debate: Aluminium and dementia: aluminium in drinking water was associated with cognitive decline and dementia in the PAQUID cohort [efw-rondeau2009], but antacid users, who take in far more aluminium, had no excess Alzheimer's disease [efw-virk2015]; aggregated exposure can exceed EFSA's intake limit [efw-tietz2019]. Iron cookware: some trials raised haemoglobin [efw-alves2019], a well-run RCT of an iron ingot did not [efw-rappaport2017]. Lead from pots: lab studies find dangerous leaching from scrap-aluminium [efw-weidenhamer2023, efw-binkhorst2025] and glazed pottery [efw-castellanos2026], though the authors note test conditions may be harsher than real cooking [efw-binkhorst2025].

mechanisms.name: Hormesis (adaptive stress response)
mechanisms.description: A small, brief dose of a stressor (exercise ROS, heat, cold) triggers protective programs that leave the body more resistant than before; too much or too continuous a dose causes damage instead. This is why exercise transiently raises oxidative markers yet lowers resting oxidative stress over time, and why blocking the signal with megadose antioxidants can blunt adaptation.

mechanisms.name: Nrf2 / KEAP1 pathway
mechanisms.description: KEAP1 normally tags the transcription factor Nrf2 for destruction. Oxidants modify KEAP1 cysteines, freeing Nrf2 to switch on more than 200 protective genes (glutathione synthesis, SOD, catalase, HO-1, NQO1). Repeated exercise bouts up-regulate this system.

mechanisms.name: Mitochondrial electron leak
mechanisms.description: Electrons escaping the respiratory chain reduce oxygen to superoxide. Leak rises when fuel supply outstrips demand (obesity, hyperglycemia, overfeeding), during extreme exercise loads, and with toxic exposures. Hyperglycemia-driven mitochondrial superoxide is proposed as the common trigger of diabetic damage pathways.

mechanisms.name: NADPH oxidases (NOX)
mechanisms.description: Enzymes whose job is to make superoxide/H2O2: in immune cells (killing microbes), blood vessels and fat tissue. They are activated by smoke, particles, obesity, high glucose and inflammation, and also produce the signalling ROS of exercising muscle.

mechanisms.name: Inflammation / NF-kB
mechanisms.description: Inflammatory cells release oxidants, and oxidants activate the NF-kB inflammatory switch, creating a self-reinforcing loop. Smoking, visceral fat, air pollution, gum disease and chronic stress all feed this loop.

mechanisms.name: Transition metals and Fenton chemistry
mechanisms.description: Free iron and copper convert H2O2 into the highly reactive hydroxyl radical. Particulate air pollution and smoke carry redox-active metals; cadmium, lead and arsenic instead deplete glutathione by binding thiols.

mechanisms.name: Glycation and AGEs
mechanisms.description: High glucose glycates proteins to form advanced glycation end-products, which bind RAGE receptors and activate NADPH oxidase and NF-kB. Glucose swings may be especially damaging.

mechanisms.name: Hormonal regulation (melatonin, cortisol, catecholamines)
mechanisms.description: Melatonin, suppressed by light at night, supports repair of oxidative DNA lesions; cortisol and catecholamines from chronic stress or cold raise metabolic rate and inflammatory signalling.

mechanisms.name: Thermal stress
mechanisms.description: Heat induces heat-shock proteins and exercise-like vascular shear stress; the testes are highly heat-sensitive, so heat that may benefit blood vessels harms sperm production.

mechanisms.name: Oxidative DNA damage and repair
mechanisms.description: ROS oxidize guanine to 8-oxoguanine; repair enzymes excise it and it is excreted as urinary 8-OHdG. Urinary 8-OHdG therefore reflects both damage and repair, which complicates interpretation.

mechanisms.name: Direct radical scavenging
mechanisms.description: Small molecules (vitamin C, vitamin E, glutathione, hydrogen) react directly with radicals. In vivo, enzymes and regulated glutathione handle most of the load, so extra scavenger intake has limited effect and can blunt useful signals.

references.authors: Ristow M, Zarse K, Oberbach A, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants prevent health-promoting effects of physical exercise in humans.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Vitamin C 1000 mg/d plus vitamin E 400 IU/d during 4 weeks of training abolished the training-induced rise in insulin sensitivity (clamp) and in muscle expression of ROS-responsive genes, in both untrained and pretrained men.

references.authors: Gomez-Cabrera MC, Domenech E, Romagnoli M, et al.
references.title: Oral administration of vitamin C decreases muscle mitochondrial biogenesis and hampers training-induced adaptations in endurance performance.
references.finding: Vitamin C (1 g/d in humans, equivalent dose in rats) during endurance training hampered endurance-capacity gains in rats and reduced training-induced expression of mitochondrial-biogenesis transcription factors; the human arm was very small.

references.authors: Paulsen G, Cumming KT, Holden G, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation hampers cellular adaptation to endurance training in humans: a double-blind, randomised, controlled trial.
references.finding: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 235 mg vitamin E daily for 11 weeks of endurance training did not change VO2max gains (8% in both groups) but blunted training-induced increases in muscle mitochondrial markers.

references.authors: Yfanti C, Nielsen AR, Akerström T, et al.
references.title: Effect of antioxidant supplementation on insulin sensitivity in response to endurance exercise training.
references.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E during 12 weeks of intense endurance training (5x/week) did not change the ~17-19% training-induced gain in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake or VO2max.

references.authors: Bjørnsen T, Salvesen S, Berntsen S, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation blunts increases in total lean body mass in elderly men after strength training.
references.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 117.5 mg vitamin E around each of three weekly strength sessions for 12 weeks blunted lean-mass gain (1.4% vs 3.9% on placebo) but not strength gains.

references.authors: Clifford T, Jeffries O, Stevenson EJ, et al.
references.title: The effects of vitamin C and E on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: a systematic review and Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Across 9 aerobic and 9 resistance-training RCTs, vitamin C and/or E did not significantly attenuate gains in VO2max, endurance performance, lean mass or strength; trials were small.

references.authors: Mason SA, Trewin AJ, Parker L, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant supplements and endurance exercise: Current evidence and mechanistic insights.
references.finding: Review concluding that chronic intake of 1000 mg vitamin C plus vitamin E is not recommended during heavy training, and that most marketed antioxidant compounds lack supportive human evidence.

references.authors: Radak Z, Chung HY, Koltai E, et al.
references.title: Exercise, oxidative stress and hormesis.
references.finding: Review framing exercise as a hormetic stressor: repeated moderate ROS exposure up-regulates antioxidant and repair systems, with a bell-shaped dose-response curve.

references.authors: Powers SK, Radak Z, Ji LL
references.title: Exercise-induced oxidative stress: past, present and future.
references.finding: Review of sources of exercise-induced ROS (mitochondria, NADPH oxidases, xanthine oxidase) and evidence that these ROS act as signals required for training adaptation.

references.authors: Done AJ, Traustadóttir T
references.title: Nrf2 mediates redox adaptations to exercise.
references.finding: Review of evidence that acute exercise activates Nrf2 and that repeated bouts up-regulate Nrf2-controlled antioxidant defences, with emerging human data.

references.authors: Torres-Rojo FI, Enríquez-Del Castillo LA, González-Chávez SA, et al.
references.title: Effect of exercise intensity on redox biomarkers in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
references.finding: Chronic exercise training raised antioxidant capacity and lowered pro-oxidant markers in healthy adults; the effect was significant for vigorous protocols but not for non-vigorous ones.

references.authors: Zhou Z, Chen C, Teo EC, et al.
references.title: Intracellular Oxidative Stress Induced by Physical Exercise in Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Exercise-induced oxidative damage (8-OHdG, F2-isoprostanes, protein carbonyls) depends on intensity times volume; moderate continuous exercise and low-volume HIIT carried the lowest probability of large oxidative stress in unhealthy adults.

references.authors: Cordeiro LS, Linhares DG, Castro JBP, et al.
references.title: Impacts of Resistance Training on Endogenous Antioxidants in Older Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Resistance training in healthy older adults raised glutathione peroxidase (SMD 0.57) but did not significantly change catalase or total antioxidant activity.

references.authors: Campbell PT, Gross MD, Potter JD, et al.
references.title: Effect of exercise on oxidative stress: a 12-month randomized, controlled trial.
references.finding: 12 months of aerobic exercise (>=45 min/day, 5 days/week, 60-75% HRmax) lowered F2-isoprostanes 6% vs controls (not significant overall); women whose VO2max rose >15% had a 14% reduction.

references.authors: Flockhart M, Nilsson LC, Tais S, et al.
references.title: Excessive exercise training causes mitochondrial functional impairment and decreases glucose tolerance in healthy volunteers.
references.n: healthy volunteers (small progressive-load training study) plus elite athletes
references.finding: When training load was ramped up over 4 weeks, the highest-load week caused a sharp fall in intrinsic mitochondrial function and impaired glucose tolerance.

references.authors: Margonis K, Fatouros IG, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
references.title: Oxidative stress biomarkers responses to physical overtraining: implications for diagnosis.
references.finding: An overreaching resistance-training block raised urinary isoprostanes 7-fold, TBARS 56% and protein carbonyls 73% and lowered GSH 31%; markers tracked the performance decline.

references.authors: Mastaloudis A, Leonard SW, Traber MG
references.title: Oxidative stress in athletes during extreme endurance exercise.
references.finding: A 50 km ultramarathon (~6.5 h) raised plasma F2-isoprostanes from 75 to 131 pg/ml, with return to baseline by 24 h.

references.authors: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al.
references.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour.
references.finding: WHO 2020 guidelines: adults should do 150-300 min/week of moderate or 75-150 min/week of vigorous aerobic activity, muscle strengthening on >=2 days/week, and limit sedentary time.

references.authors: Dirks ML, Miotto PM, Goossens GH, et al.
references.title: Short-term bed rest-induced insulin resistance cannot be explained by increased mitochondrial H(2) O(2) emission.
references.finding: Short-term bed rest cut insulin sensitivity by 42% and lowered mitochondrial respiration, but did not raise resting mitochondrial H2O2 emission or oxidative stress markers.

references.authors: Vaccaro A, Kaplan Dor Y, Nambara K, et al.
references.title: Sleep Loss Can Cause Death through Accumulation of Reactive Oxygen Species in the Gut.
references.finding: In flies and mice, severe sleep deprivation caused ROS accumulation in the gut; oral antioxidants or gut-targeted antioxidant enzymes prevented early death.

references.authors: Shah R, Shah VK, Emin M, et al.
references.title: Mild sleep restriction increases endothelial oxidative stress in female persons.
references.finding: Six weeks of sleeping 1.5 h less than habitual (randomized crossover) increased endothelial-cell oxidative stress without a compensatory antioxidant response.

references.authors: Trivedi MS, Holger D, Bui AT, et al.
references.title: Short-term sleep deprivation leads to decreased systemic redox metabolites and altered epigenetic status.
references.finding: One night of total sleep deprivation significantly lowered plasma glutathione, cysteine, ATP and homocysteine.

references.authors: Nagata C, Tamura T, Wada K, et al.
references.title: Sleep duration, nightshift work, and the timing of meals and urinary levels of 8-isoprostane and 6-sulfatoxymelatonin in Japanese women.
references.finding: Women sleeping 6 h or less had about 12% higher urinary 8-isoprostane than women sleeping more than 8 h.

references.authors: Watson NF, Badr MS, Belenky G, et al.
references.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society.
references.finding: AASM/SRS consensus statement: adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis.

references.authors: Bhatti P, Mirick DK, Randolph TW, et al.
references.title: Oxidative DNA damage during night shift work.
references.finding: During night work (low melatonin) urinary 8-OH-dG excretion was only 20% of that during night sleep, interpreted as reduced repair of oxidative DNA lesions.

references.authors: Zanif U, Lai AS, Parks J, et al.
references.title: Melatonin supplementation and oxidative DNA damage repair capacity among night shift workers: a randomised placebo-controlled trial.
references.finding: Melatonin taken before day sleep for 4 weeks gave a borderline-significant 1.8-fold increase in urinary 8-OH-dG during day sleep, suggesting improved oxidative DNA repair.

references.authors: Hosseini H, Homayouni-Tabrizi M, Amiri H, et al.
references.title: The effect of continuous positive airway pressure on total antioxidant capacity in obstructive sleep apnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: CPAP treatment of obstructive sleep apnea increased total antioxidant capacity (SMD 0.50).

references.authors: Morrow JD, Frei B, Longmire AW, et al.
references.title: Increase in circulating products of lipid peroxidation (F2-isoprostanes) in smokers. Smoking as a cause of oxidative damage.
references.finding: Smokers had roughly double the plasma free F2-isoprostanes of nonsmokers; levels fell significantly after 2 weeks of abstinence.

references.authors: Reilly M, Delanty N, Lawson JA, et al.
references.title: Modulation of oxidant stress in vivo in chronic cigarette smokers.
references.finding: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a rose with smoking dose (heavy 177, moderate 93, nonsmokers 54 pmol/mmol) and fell within 2-3 weeks of quitting; high-dose vitamin C lowered it, vitamin E alone did not.

references.authors: Pilz H, Oguogho A, Chehne F, et al.
references.title: Quitting cigarette smoking results in a fast improvement of in vivo oxidation injury (determined via plasma, serum and urinary isoprostane).
references.finding: Isoprostanes in plasma, serum and urine dropped within days of quitting and reached a new steady state about 4 weeks after cessation.

references.authors: King CC, Piper ME, Gepner AD, et al.
references.title: Longitudinal Impact of Smoking and Smoking Cessation on Inflammatory Markers of Cardiovascular Disease Risk.
references.finding: Smoking heaviness was independently tied to urinary F2-isoprostanes; after one year, successful quitters had lower F2-isoprostanes and white-cell counts despite gaining weight.

references.authors: Joseph AM, Hecht SS, Murphy SE, et al.
references.title: Smoking reduction fails to improve clinical and biological markers of cardiac disease: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: Cutting cigarettes from ~27 to ~18/day over 6 months did not change F2-isoprostanes, inflammatory markers or symptoms; only carbon monoxide fell.

references.authors: Otsuka R, Watanabe H, Hirata K, et al.
references.title: Acute effects of passive smoking on the coronary circulation in healthy young adults.
references.finding: A 30-minute exposure to environmental tobacco smoke reduced coronary flow velocity reserve in healthy nonsmokers (4.4 to 3.4), indicating acute coronary endothelial dysfunction.

references.authors: Duncan MS, Freiberg MS, Greevy RA Jr, et al.
references.title: Association of Smoking Cessation With Subsequent Risk of Cardiovascular Disease.
references.finding: Quitting was linked to 39% lower CVD risk within 5 years versus continued smoking, but heavy smokers' risk stayed above never-smokers for well over 5 years (10-15+ years).

references.authors: Bermúdez E, Stone K, Carter KM, et al.
references.title: Environmental tobacco smoke is just as damaging to DNA as mainstream smoke.
references.finding: Tar from environmental (secondhand) tobacco smoke generated hydrogen peroxide and nicked DNA in cells much like mainstream-smoke tar; catalase was protective.

references.authors: Barnoya J, Glantz SA
references.title: Cardiovascular effects of secondhand smoke: nearly as large as smoking.
references.finding: Secondhand smoke raises coronary heart disease risk ~30%; even brief exposure produces effects on platelets, endothelium and oxidative stress averaging 80-90% of those of chronic active smoking.

references.authors: Siti Hajar MH, Zulkefli S, Juwita S, et al.
references.title: Metabolic, inflammatory, and oxidative stress markers in women exposed to secondhand smoke.
references.finding: Women with modest secondhand-smoke exposure (>=15 min on >=2 days/week) did not differ from unexposed women in 8-isoprostane, oxidized LDL or inflammatory markers.

references.authors: Carnevale R, Sciarretta S, Violi F, et al.
references.title: Acute Impact of Tobacco vs Electronic Cigarette Smoking on Oxidative Stress and Vascular Function.
references.finding: A single e-cigarette and a single tobacco cigarette both acutely raised 8-iso-PGF2a and NOX2 activation and lowered flow-mediated dilation; the e-cigarette's oxidative effects were smaller.

references.authors: Christensen CH, Chang JT, Rostron BL, et al.
references.title: Biomarkers of Inflammation and Oxidative Stress among Adult Former Smoker, Current E-Cigarette Users-Results from Wave 1 PATH Study.
references.finding: Former smokers who now only vape had F2-isoprostane levels similar to former smokers using nothing; dual users had 9% higher levels than cigarette-only smokers.

references.authors: Sharma R, Harlev A, Agarwal A, et al.
references.title: Cigarette Smoking and Semen Quality: A New Meta-analysis Examining the Effect of the 2010 World Health Organization Laboratory Methods for the Examination of Human Semen.
references.finding: Smoking was associated with lower sperm count, motility and morphology, with larger effects in moderate/heavy smokers.

references.authors: Lu Y, Cederbaum AI
references.title: CYP2E1 and oxidative liver injury by alcohol.
references.finding: Review: chronic ethanol induces CYP2E1, which leaks superoxide and hydrogen peroxide and drives lipid peroxidation in alcoholic liver injury.

references.authors: Meagher EA, Barry OP, Burke A, et al.
references.title: Alcohol-induced generation of lipid peroxidation products in humans.
references.n: healthy volunteers and patients with alcoholic liver disease
references.finding: Alcohol given to healthy volunteers raised urinary isoprostanes; levels were highest in alcoholic cirrhosis, and vitamin C (not aspirin) lowered them.

references.authors: Schrieks IC, van den Berg R, Sierksma A, et al.
references.title: Effect of red wine consumption on biomarkers of oxidative stress.
references.finding: Four weeks of 450 ml/day red wine (4 drinks, 41 g alcohol) raised urinary 8-iso-PGF2a versus the same wine dealcoholized (157 vs 141 pg/mg creatinine).

references.authors: Wood AM, Kaptoge S, Butterworth AS, et al.
references.title: Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies.
references.finding: All-cause mortality was lowest at or below ~100 g alcohol per week and rose with higher intake; stroke, heart failure and fatal hypertensive disease rose roughly linearly.

references.authors: Keaney JF Jr, Larson MG, Vasan RS, et al.
references.title: Obesity and systemic oxidative stress: clinical correlates of oxidative stress in the Framingham Study.
references.finding: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a was independently associated with BMI, smoking, diabetes and blood glucose in a community cohort.

references.authors: Pou KM, Massaro JM, Hoffmann U, et al.
references.title: Visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue volumes are cross-sectionally related to markers of inflammation and oxidative stress: the Framingham Heart Study.
references.finding: Visceral fat was more strongly associated with urinary isoprostanes than subcutaneous abdominal fat.

references.authors: Furukawa S, Fujita T, Shimabukuro M, et al.
references.title: Increased oxidative stress in obesity and its impact on metabolic syndrome.
references.finding: Fat accumulation correlated with systemic oxidative stress in humans and mice; adipose NADPH oxidase produced ROS that dysregulated adipokines, and blocking it improved metabolic disease in mice.

references.authors: Duggan C, Tapsoba JD, Wang CY, et al.
references.title: Dietary Weight Loss, Exercise, and Oxidative Stress in Postmenopausal Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
references.finding: 12 months of calorie-restricted weight-loss diet lowered F2-isoprostanes by ~23% (diet) and ~24% (diet plus exercise) vs 3% in controls; greater weight loss gave greater reductions.

references.authors: Il'yasova D, Fontana L, Bhapkar M, et al.
references.title: Effects of 2 years of caloric restriction on oxidative status assessed by urinary F2-isoprostanes: The CALERIE 2 randomized clinical trial.
references.finding: Two years of prescribed 25% calorie restriction (CALERIE 2) lowered the main urinary F2-isoprostane metabolite by 13-17% versus ad libitum controls.

references.authors: Monzo-Beltran L, Vazquez-Tarragón A, Cerdà C, et al.
references.title: One-year follow-up of clinical, metabolic and oxidative stress profile of morbid obese patients after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. 8-oxo-dG as a clinical marker.
references.n: morbidly obese patients vs normal-weight controls
references.finding: Morbidly obese patients had raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and 8-oxo-dG; after sleeve gastrectomy these declined progressively and antioxidant enzymes recovered over one year.

references.authors: Il'yasova D, Wang F, Spasojevic I, et al.
references.title: Urinary F2-isoprostanes, obesity, and weight gain in the IRAS cohort.
references.finding: Urinary F2-isoprostanes were higher with obesity cross-sectionally, yet some isoprostanes predicted less weight gain over 5 years, cautioning against naive reading of the marker.

references.authors: Sermondade N, Faure C, Fezeu L, et al.
references.title: BMI in relation to sperm count: an updated systematic review and collaborative meta-analysis.
references.finding: Obesity was associated with higher odds of oligozoospermia or azoospermia (OR 1.28; morbid obesity OR 2.04).

references.authors: Li Z, Liu Q, Xu Z, et al.
references.title: Association between short-term exposure to ambient particulate air pollution and biomarkers of oxidative stress: A meta-analysis.
references.finding: Each 10 ug/m3 rise in short-term PM2.5 was associated with 1.6% higher malondialdehyde and a borderline 2.1% higher 8-OHdG.

references.authors: Kelly FJ, Fussell JC
references.title: Role of oxidative stress in cardiovascular disease outcomes following exposure to ambient air pollution.
references.finding: Review of epidemiological, controlled-exposure and experimental data concluding that oxidative stress is central to the cardiovascular effects of ambient air pollution.

references.authors: Chen R, Zhao A, Chen H, et al.
references.title: Cardiopulmonary benefits of reducing indoor particles of outdoor origin: a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of air purifiers.
references.finding: 48 h of real vs sham air purification cut indoor PM2.5 by 57% (96 to 41 ug/m3) and lowered inflammatory and thrombotic markers (e.g., myeloperoxidase -33%) and blood pressure.

references.authors: Wang Y, Zhao Y, Xue L, et al.
references.title: Effects of air purification of indoor PM(2.5) on the cardiorespiratory biomarkers in young healthy adults.
references.finding: One week of real vs sham HEPA purification lowered diastolic blood pressure, exhaled NO and 8-isoprostane and improved lung function.

references.authors: Hoffmann B, Boogaard H, de Nazelle A, et al.
references.title: WHO Air Quality Guidelines 2021-Aiming for Healthier Air for all: A Joint Statement by Medical, Public Health, Scientific Societies and Patient Representative Organisations.
references.finding: Joint statement endorsing the WHO 2021 Air Quality Guidelines, including annual mean PM2.5 not exceeding 5 ug/m3 and peak-season 8-h ozone not exceeding 60 ug/m3.

references.authors: Forchhammer L, Møller P, Riddervold IS, et al.
references.title: Controlled human wood smoke exposure: oxidative stress, inflammation and microvascular function.
references.finding: Three-hour controlled exposures to 220-354 ug/m3 particles from a modern wood stove had no effect on oxidatively damaged DNA, inflammatory markers or microvascular function.

references.authors: Barregard L, Sällsten G, Andersson L, et al.
references.title: Experimental exposure to wood smoke: effects on airway inflammation and oxidative stress.
references.finding: Four-hour exposure to 240-280 ug/m3 wood smoke raised malondialdehyde in exhaled breath condensate and alveolar NO, indicating airway oxidative stress.

references.authors: Lin W, Brunekreef B, Gehring U
references.title: Meta-analysis of the effects of indoor nitrogen dioxide and gas cooking on asthma and wheeze in children.
references.finding: Gas cooking was associated with higher odds of childhood asthma (OR 1.32) and indoor NO2 with current wheeze (OR 1.15 per 15 ppb).

references.authors: Li W, Long C, Fan T, et al.
references.title: Gas cooking and respiratory outcomes in children: A systematic review.
references.finding: Systematic review concluding the gas-cooking and childhood asthma literature is heterogeneous, mostly cross-sectional and low quality, and insufficient to establish causation.

references.authors: Kammeyer A, Luiten RM
references.title: Oxidation events and skin aging.
references.finding: Review: UV drives skin photoaging through direct DNA damage and indirect ROS/RNS-mediated oxidation of lipids, proteins and DNA.

references.authors: Hughes MC, Williams GM, Baker P, et al.
references.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial.
references.finding: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years gave 24% less skin aging than discretionary use; 30 mg/day beta-carotene had no overall effect.

references.authors: Hanson KM, Gratton E, Bardeen CJ
references.title: Sunscreen enhancement of UV-induced reactive oxygen species in the skin.
references.finding: Organic UV filters that penetrate into the epidermis increased UV-induced ROS above unprotected skin after about 60 minutes, arguing for reapplication.

references.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
references.title: Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease.
references.finding: Vitamin D3 2000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years did not lower invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events (VITAL).

references.authors: Epel ES, Blackburn EH, Lin J, et al.
references.title: Accelerated telomere shortening in response to life stress.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Higher perceived and chronic stress was associated with higher oxidative stress, lower telomerase and telomeres shorter by the equivalent of about a decade of aging.

references.authors: Black CN, Bot M, Scheffer PG, et al.
references.title: Is depression associated with increased oxidative stress? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Depression was associated with higher 8-OHdG (g = 0.31) and F2-isoprostanes (g = 0.48).

references.authors: Pascoe MC, Thompson DR, Ski CF
references.title: Yoga, mindfulness-based stress reduction and stress-related physiological measures: A meta-analysis.
references.finding: Yoga-based practices, versus active controls, lowered cortisol, ambulatory blood pressure and resting heart rate; trials were heterogeneous.

references.authors: Buric I, Farias M, Jong J, et al.
references.title: What Is the Molecular Signature of Mind-Body Interventions? A Systematic Review of Gene Expression Changes Induced by Meditation and Related Practices.
references.finding: Meditation, yoga, tai chi and related practices were associated with down-regulation of NF-kB pathway gene expression; studies were small and heterogeneous.

references.authors: Hegde SV, Adhikari P, Shetty S, et al.
references.title: Effect of community-based yoga intervention on oxidative stress and glycemic parameters in prediabetes: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: Three months of community yoga lowered malondialdehyde versus wait-list control but did not change antioxidant levels; no active control.

references.authors: Laukkanen T, Khan H, Zaccardi F, et al.
references.title: Association between sauna bathing and fatal cardiovascular and all-cause mortality events.
references.finding: Compared with one session/week, 4-7 sauna sessions/week was associated with 63% lower sudden cardiac death and lower CVD and all-cause mortality; sessions >19 min were also associated with lower risk.

references.authors: Kunutsor SK, Laukkanen T, Laukkanen JA
references.title: Longitudinal associations of sauna bathing with inflammation and oxidative stress: the KIHD prospective cohort study.
references.finding: 4-7 sauna sessions/week was associated with lower CRP and leukocyte counts over 11 years, but not with gamma-glutamyltransferase, the oxidative-stress proxy studied.

references.authors: Laukkanen JA, Laukkanen T, Kunutsor SK
references.title: Cardiovascular and Other Health Benefits of Sauna Bathing: A Review of the Evidence.
references.finding: Review of observational and interventional evidence linking Finnish sauna bathing to lower blood pressure, cardiovascular disease and mortality, with proposed vascular and autonomic mechanisms.

references.authors: Brunt VE, Howard MJ, Francisco MA, et al.
references.title: Passive heat therapy improves endothelial function, arterial stiffness and blood pressure in sedentary humans.
references.finding: Eight weeks of 40.5 C hot-water immersion 4-5 times/week (rectal temperature >=38.5 C for 60 min) doubled flow-mediated dilation (5.6 to 10.9%) and lowered blood pressure versus thermoneutral sham.

references.authors: Garolla A, Torino M, Sartini B, et al.
references.title: Seminal and molecular evidence that sauna exposure affects human spermatogenesis.
references.finding: Two sauna sessions/week at 80-90 C, 15 min each, for 3 months impaired sperm count, motility, chromatin condensation and mitochondrial function; fully reversed 6 months after stopping.

references.authors: Siems WG, Brenke R, Sommerburg O, et al.
references.title: Improved antioxidative protection in winter swimmers.
references.finding: Winter swimmers had higher baseline erythrocyte glutathione and higher SOD and catalase activity, interpreted as adaptation to repeated cold-induced oxidative stress.

references.authors: Esperland D, de Weerd L, Mercer JB
references.title: Health effects of voluntary exposure to cold water - a continuing subject of debate.
references.finding: Review of voluntary cold-water immersion: studies are small and heterogeneous; possible benefits on insulin sensitivity and adipose tissue, but no firm conclusions.

references.authors: Tipton MJ, Collier N, Massey H, et al.
references.title: Cold water immersion: kill or cure?
references.finding: Review of cold-water immersion as hazard (cold shock, drowning, cardiac arrest, hypothermia) and treatment; evidence for many claimed benefits ranges from credible to anecdotal.

references.authors: Roberts LA, Raastad T, Markworth JF, et al.
references.title: Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training.
references.finding: Ten minutes of cold-water immersion after each strength session for 12 weeks blunted gains in strength and muscle mass versus active recovery.

references.authors: Jomova K, Valko M
references.title: Advances in metal-induced oxidative stress and human disease.
references.finding: Review: redox-active metals (iron, copper, chromium) generate radicals via Fenton chemistry, while cadmium, arsenic and lead act mainly by binding thiols and depleting glutathione.

references.authors: Urbano T, Filippini T, Wise LA, et al.
references.title: Associations of urinary and dietary cadmium with urinary 8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2'-deoxyguanosine and blood biochemical parameters.
references.finding: Urinary and dietary cadmium were positively and linearly correlated with urinary 8-oxodG in non-smoking blood donors.

references.authors: Kim SS, Meeker JD, Keil AP, et al.
references.title: Exposure to 17 trace metals in pregnancy and associations with urinary oxidative stress biomarkers.
references.finding: Among 17 urinary metals, the strongest associations with 8-isoprostane and 8-OHdG were for essential selenium and copper, illustrating confounding in spot-urine biomarker studies.

references.authors: Ferguson KK, McElrath TF, Chen YH, et al.
references.title: Urinary phthalate metabolites and biomarkers of oxidative stress in pregnant women: a repeated measures analysis.
references.finding: Urinary phthalate metabolites were associated with higher urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane across repeated measures in pregnancy.

references.authors: Chen JC, Baumert BO, Li Y, et al.
references.title: Associations of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, polychlorinated biphenyls, organochlorine pesticides, and polybrominated diphenyl ethers with oxidative stress markers: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Associations of PFAS, PCBs, organochlorine pesticides and PBDEs with oxidative stress markers were mostly inconsistent; only a few pooled associations (e.g., DDE with malondialdehyde) were significant.

references.authors: Monnier L, Mas E, Ginet C, et al.
references.title: Activation of oxidative stress by acute glucose fluctuations compared with sustained chronic hyperglycemia in patients with type 2 diabetes.
references.finding: Urinary 8-iso-PGF2a was ~75% higher in type 2 diabetes (482 vs 275 pg/mg creatinine) and correlated strongly with glucose swings (r = 0.86) rather than HbA1c.

references.authors: Brownlee M
references.title: Biochemistry and molecular cell biology of diabetic complications.
references.finding: Review proposing that hyperglycemia-driven mitochondrial superoxide overproduction is the unifying trigger of the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine damage pathways.

references.authors: Liu Z, Liu Y, Song Y, et al.
references.title: Systemic oxidative stress biomarkers in chronic periodontitis: a meta-analysis.
references.finding: Chronic periodontitis was associated with lower serum total antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde and nitric oxide.

references.authors: da Silva JC, Muniz FWMG, Oballe HJR, et al.
references.title: The effect of periodontal therapy on oxidative stress biomarkers: A systematic review.
references.finding: Mechanical periodontal treatment generally reduced oxidative markers (8-OHdG, total oxidant status) in saliva and gingival fluid, and in serum in most studies.

references.authors: Ohsawa I, Ishikawa M, Takahashi K, et al.
references.title: Hydrogen acts as a therapeutic antioxidant by selectively reducing cytotoxic oxygen radicals.
references.finding: Molecular hydrogen selectively reduced hydroxyl radical and peroxynitrite in cells and, inhaled, limited brain ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats.

references.authors: Zanini D, Todorovic N, Korovljev D, et al.
references.title: The effects of 6-month hydrogen-rich water intake on molecular and phenotypic biomarkers of aging in older adults aged 70 years and over: A randomized controlled pilot trial.
references.finding: Pilot trial of 0.5 L/day hydrogen-rich water for 6 months reported small differences in telomere length and some molecular markers; exploratory, many outcomes.

references.authors: Todorovic N, Fernández-Landa J, Santibañez A, et al.
references.title: The Effects of Hydrogen-Rich Water on Blood Lipid Profiles in Clinical Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Hydrogen-rich water modestly lowered total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides in small clinical trials (pooled SMD about -0.2 to -0.4).

references.authors: Chevalier G, Sinatra ST, Oschman JL, et al.
references.title: Earthing: health implications of reconnecting the human body to the Earth's surface electrons.
references.finding: Narrative review by proponents of earthing summarizing small studies claiming better sleep, less pain and other effects from conductive contact with the ground.

references.authors: Liu J, Zhang P, Tian J, et al.
references.title: Ozone therapy for treating foot ulcers in people with diabetes.
references.finding: Cochrane review: three small, high or unclear risk-of-bias trials; no firm conclusions possible on ozone therapy for diabetic foot ulcers.

references.authors: Aebi S, Assereto R, Lauterburg BH
references.title: High-dose intravenous glutathione in man. Pharmacokinetics and effects on cyst(e)ine in plasma and urine.
references.finding: Intravenous glutathione (2 g/m2) had a plasma half-life of about 14 minutes and was rapidly broken down or excreted in urine.

references.authors: Richie JP Jr, Nichenametla S, Neidig W, et al.
references.title: Randomized controlled trial of oral glutathione supplementation on body stores of glutathione.
references.finding: Oral glutathione 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months raised blood glutathione stores by 17-35%, which returned to baseline after a 1-month washout.

references.authors: Luk HY, Jiwan NC, Appell CR, et al.
references.title: Passive dehydration increases oxidative stress and mTOR signalling pathway activation in young men following resistance exercise.
references.finding: Fluid restriction from 24 h before resistance exercise raised muscle H2O2 compared with euhydration.

references.authors: Aengevaeren VL, Mosterd A, Braber TL, et al.
references.title: Relationship Between Lifelong Exercise Volume and Coronary Atherosclerosis in Athletes.
references.finding: Men with lifelong exercise volume above 2000 MET-min/week had more coronary calcification (OR 3.2) and plaque, but more benign plaque composition (fewer mixed, more calcified-only plaques).

references.authors: Ahmadi MN, Hamer M, Gill JMR, et al.
references.title: Brief bouts of device-measured intermittent lifestyle physical activity and its association with major adverse cardiovascular events and mortality in people who do not exercise: a prospective cohort study.
references.finding: Intermittent lifestyle activity bouts of 1-3 minutes were associated with lower mortality than bouts under 1 minute, with benefit increasing with the vigorous share of each bout.

references.authors: Andersen K, Farahmand B, Ahlbom A, et al.
references.title: Risk of arrhythmias in 52 755 long-distance cross-country skiers: a cohort study.
references.finding: Men completing 5+ Vasaloppet 90 km races had higher AF risk (HR 1.29) and more bradyarrhythmias than those completing one.

references.authors: Arem H, Moore SC, Patel A, et al.
references.title: Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship.
references.finding: Versus no leisure activity, mortality HR was 0.80 below the guideline minimum, 0.69 at 1-2x, 0.63 at 2-3x, 0.61 at 3-5x (plateau) and 0.69 at 10x or more: no evidence of harm at very high volumes.

references.authors: Ballin M, Nordström P
references.title: Does exercise prevent major non-communicable diseases and premature mortality? A critical review based on results from randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Critical review of RCTs (~50,000 participants): exercise has not been shown to reduce all-cause mortality or CVD in older or chronically ill adults; it prevents type 2 diabetes when combined with diet.

references.authors: Banach M, Lewek J, Surma S, et al.
references.title: The association between daily step count and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: a meta-analysis.
references.finding: Each 1,000 extra steps/day was associated with 15% lower all-cause mortality, with benefit starting at about 3,900 steps/day.

references.authors: Berry JD, Zabad N, Kyrouac D, et al.
references.title: High-Volume Physical Activity and Clinical Coronary Artery Disease Outcomes: Findings From the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study.
references.finding: High-volume activity (3000+ MET-min/week) was linked to similar coronary event risk (MI HR 0.95) but the lowest mortality (HR 0.71); CAC predicted CAD at every activity level.

references.authors: Bishop DJ, Botella J, Granata C
references.title: CrossTalk opposing view: Exercise training volume is more important than training intensity to promote increases in mitochondrial content.
references.finding: CrossTalk 'opposing view' arguing training volume matters more than intensity for mitochondrial content.

references.authors: Bjørnsen T, Salvesen S, Berntsen S, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation blunts increases in total lean body mass in elderly men after strength training.
references.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 117.5 mg vitamin E around strength training cut lean-mass gains to 1.4% from 3.9%.

references.authors: Buffey AJ, Herring MP, Langley CK, et al.
references.title: The Acute Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting Time in Adults with Standing and Light-Intensity Walking on Biomarkers of Cardiometabolic Health in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
references.finding: Light walking breaks lowered postprandial glucose (d -0.72) and insulin (d -0.83) versus sitting and beat standing breaks; neither changed blood pressure.

references.authors: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al.
references.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour.
references.finding: WHO 2020: 150-300 min/week moderate or 75-150 min/week vigorous aerobic activity plus muscle strengthening 2+ days/week; limit and replace sedentary time; some is better than none.

references.authors: Campbell PT, Gross MD, Potter JD, et al.
references.title: Effect of exercise on oxidative stress: a 12-month randomized, controlled trial.
references.finding: A 12-month aerobic program lowered F2-isoprostanes 6% overall (NS) and 14% in women whose VO2max rose more than 15%.

references.authors: Chenhuichen C, Ezzatvar Y, Zambom-Ferraresi F, et al.
references.title: Impact of supervised physical exercise on inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Supervised exercise modestly lowered CRP and raised IL-10 in adults 65+; only 6 trials addressed redox balance, suggesting improvement, with moderate-to-high bias.

references.authors: Clifford T, Jeffries O, Stevenson EJ, et al.
references.title: The effects of vitamin C and E on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: a systematic review and Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Vitamin C and/or E did not significantly blunt VO2max (SMD -0.14), endurance performance, lean mass or strength gains; trials were small.

references.authors: Cordeiro LS, Linhares DG, Castro JBP, et al.
references.title: Impacts of Resistance Training on Endogenous Antioxidants in Older Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Resistance training raised glutathione peroxidase in older people but did not change catalase or total antioxidant activity and slightly lowered SOD.

references.authors: De Bosscher R, Dausin C, Claus P, et al.
references.title: Lifelong endurance exercise and its relation with coronary atherosclerosis.
references.finding: Lifelong endurance athletes had more coronary plaques (OR 1.86), including non-calcified proximal plaques, than healthy non-athletes; plaque composition was not more benign.

references.authors: DeFina LF, Radford NB, Barlow CE, et al.
references.title: Association of All-Cause and Cardiovascular Mortality With High Levels of Physical Activity and Concurrent Coronary Artery Calcification.
references.finding: Men doing 3000+ MET-min/week had slightly more CAC of 100 or above (RR 1.11) but no higher mortality even with high CAC (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.52-1.15).

references.authors: De Souza MJ, Arce JC, Pescatello LS, et al.
references.title: Gonadal hormones and semen quality in male runners. A volume threshold effect of endurance training.
references.finding: High-mileage runners (~108 km/week) had lower testosterone, sperm motility and density than moderate-mileage runners or sedentary men.

references.authors: Ding D, Nguyen B, Nau T, et al.
references.title: Daily steps and health outcomes in adults: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis.
references.finding: Versus 2,000 steps/day, 7,000 steps/day was associated with 47% lower all-cause mortality and lower CVD, dementia, depression and falls; curves flattened around 5,000-7,000 steps for several outcomes.

references.authors: DiPietro L, Gribok A, Stevens MS, et al.
references.title: Three 15-min bouts of moderate postmeal walking significantly improves 24-h glycemic control in older people at risk for impaired glucose tolerance.
references.finding: Three 15-minute post-meal walks improved 24-h glucose as well as one 45-minute morning walk and were better for evening glucose.

references.authors: Dirks ML, Miotto PM, Goossens GH, et al.
references.title: Short-term bed rest-induced insulin resistance cannot be explained by increased mitochondrial H(2) O(2) emission.
references.finding: Days of bed rest cut insulin sensitivity 42% without raising muscle mitochondrial H2O2 emission or oxidative markers.

references.authors: Done AJ, Traustadóttir T
references.title: Nrf2 mediates redox adaptations to exercise.
references.finding: Nrf2 is activated by exercise ROS and mediates training-induced antioxidant enzyme up-regulation.

references.authors: Dos Santos M, Ferrari G, Lee DH, et al.
references.title: Association of the "Weekend Warrior" and Other Leisure-time Physical Activity Patterns With All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
references.finding: For the same total MVPA, weekend warriors had similar mortality to regularly active people (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.97-1.20).

references.authors: Duggan C, Tapsoba JD, Wang CY, et al.
references.title: Dietary Weight Loss, Exercise, and Oxidative Stress in Postmenopausal Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
references.finding: Exercise alone lowered F2-isoprostanes 14.5% (not significant after correction) while diet-induced weight loss lowered them about 23%.

references.authors: Dunstan DW, Kingwell BA, Larsen R, et al.
references.title: Breaking up prolonged sitting reduces postprandial glucose and insulin responses.
references.finding: 2-minute walking breaks every 20 minutes cut post-drink glucose area by about 24-30% and insulin by about 23% versus uninterrupted sitting.

references.authors: Dutra MT, Martins WR, Ribeiro ALA, et al.
references.title: The Effects of Strength Training Combined with Vitamin C and E Supplementation on Skeletal Muscle Mass and Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Vitamin C/E had no effect on strength gains and possibly attenuates hypertrophy over time.

references.authors: Edwards SJ, Shad BJ, Marshall RN, et al.
references.title: Short-term step reduction reduces citrate synthase activity without altering skeletal muscle markers of oxidative metabolism or insulin-mediated signaling in young males.
references.finding: Cutting steps from ~13,000 to ~1,200/day for 7 days lowered citrate synthase activity without changing insulin-signalling proteins.

references.authors: Ekelund U, Steene-Johannessen J, Brown WJ, et al.
references.title: Does physical activity attenuate, or even eliminate, the detrimental association of sitting time with mortality? A harmonised meta-analysis of data from more than 1 million men and women.
references.finding: About 60-75 min/day of moderate activity eliminated the extra mortality of sitting more than 8 h/day, but only attenuated the risk tied to high TV time.

references.authors: Ekelund U, Tarp J, Steene-Johannessen J, et al.
references.title: Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis.
references.finding: Mortality HRs for the 2nd-4th quarters of total activity were 0.48, 0.34 and 0.27; for light activity 0.60-0.38; most-sedentary quarter HR 2.63 versus least sedentary.

references.authors: Elliott AD, Linz D, Mishima R, et al.
references.title: Association between physical activity and risk of incident arrhythmias in 402 406 individuals: evidence from the UK Biobank cohort.
references.finding: Physical activity was associated with lower AF risk, more clearly in women (HR 0.85 at 1500 MET-min/week), and lower ventricular arrhythmia risk.

references.authors: Flockhart M, Nilsson LC, Tais S, et al.
references.title: Excessive exercise training causes mitochondrial functional impairment and decreases glucose tolerance in healthy volunteers.
references.finding: Ramping HIIT load over 4 weeks: the hardest week sharply reduced mitochondrial respiration and worsened glucose tolerance.

references.authors: Fragala MS, Cadore EL, Dorgo S, et al.
references.title: Resistance Training for Older Adults: Position Statement From the National Strength and Conditioning Association.
references.finding: NSCA position statement: resistance training 2-3 times/week counters age-related loss of strength, muscle and function, including in frail and sarcopenic adults.

references.authors: Francois ME, Baldi JC, Manning PJ, et al.
references.title: 'Exercise snacks' before meals: a novel strategy to improve glycaemic control in individuals with insulin resistance.
references.finding: Six 1-minute intense incline-walking intervals before meals lowered 24-h mean glucose by 0.7 mmol/L, better than 30 minutes of continuous walking before dinner.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Mendiola J, Afeiche M, et al.
references.title: Physical activity and television watching in relation to semen quality in young men.
references.finding: Men doing 15+ h/week of moderate-to-vigorous activity had 73% higher sperm concentration than those under 5 h/week; 20+ h/week TV was linked to 44% lower concentration.

references.authors: Gliemann L, Schmidt JF, Olesen J, et al.
references.title: Resveratrol blunts the positive effects of exercise training on cardiovascular health in aged men.
references.finding: 250 mg/day resveratrol with 8 weeks of HIIT cut the VO2max gain by 45% and abolished the blood-pressure and lipid improvements versus placebo.

references.authors: Gomez-Cabrera MC, Domenech E, Romagnoli M, et al.
references.title: Oral administration of vitamin C decreases muscle mitochondrial biogenesis and hampers training-induced adaptations in endurance performance.
references.n: 14 men (5 on vitamin C) plus rats
references.finding: Vitamin C (1 g/day) hampered endurance gains and mitochondrial-biogenesis signalling in rats; the small human arm showed blunted VO2max gain trends.

references.authors: Gomez-Cabrera MC, Salvador-Pascual A, Cabo H, et al.
references.title: Redox modulation of mitochondriogenesis in exercise. Does antioxidant supplementation blunt the benefits of exercise training?
references.finding: Argues exercise ROS come mainly from extramitochondrial sources (NADPH oxidase, xanthine oxidase) and that 'exercise is itself an antioxidant'; antioxidant supplements may blunt mitochondriogenesis.

references.authors: Gorzelitz J, Trabert B, Katki HA, et al.
references.title: Independent and joint associations of weightlifting and aerobic activity with all-cause, cardiovascular disease and cancer mortality in the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial.
references.finding: Meeting aerobic guidelines plus weightlifting 1-2 times/week was associated with 41% lower mortality versus neither, compared with 32% for aerobic alone.

references.authors: Granata C, Jamnick NA, Bishop DJ
references.title: Training-Induced Changes in Mitochondrial Content and Respiratory Function in Human Skeletal Muscle.
references.finding: Training volume appears critical for mitochondrial content, while relative intensity matters more for mitochondrial respiratory function.

references.authors: Hajizadeh Maleki B, Tartibian B, Chehrazi M
references.title: The effects of three different exercise modalities on markers of male reproduction in healthy subjects: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: 24 weeks of moderate continuous, high-intensity continuous or interval training lowered seminal oxidative and inflammatory markers and improved semen and sperm DNA integrity, moderate training most; the group has other retracted papers.

references.authors: Han M, Qie R, Shi X, et al.
references.title: Cardiorespiratory fitness and mortality from all causes, cardiovascular disease and cancer: dose-response meta-analysis of cohort studies.
references.finding: Per 1-MET higher fitness, RR 0.88 for all-cause, 0.87 for CVD and 0.93 for cancer mortality; highest versus lowest fitness RR 0.47.

references.authors: Henríquez-Olguin C, Knudsen JR, Raun SH, et al.
references.title: Cytosolic ROS production by NADPH oxidase 2 regulates muscle glucose uptake during exercise.
references.finding: NOX2, not mitochondria, was the main source of cytosolic ROS during moderate exercise in muscle; NOX2-deficient mice had much lower exercise-stimulated glucose uptake.

references.authors: Henríquez-Olguín C, Renani LB, Arab-Ceschia L, et al.
references.title: Adaptations to high-intensity interval training in skeletal muscle require NADPH oxidase 2.
references.finding: In mice lacking functional NOX2, 6 weeks of HIIT produced smaller gains in running capacity, SOD2, catalase and mitochondrial proteins.

references.authors: Higgins MR, Izadi A, Kaviani M
references.title: Antioxidants and Exercise Performance: With a Focus on Vitamin E and C Supplementation.
references.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health
references.finding: Vitamin C and E supplements are not recommended for athletes beyond specific situations; they may block anabolic signalling; a fruit- and vegetable-rich diet is advised.

references.authors: Ibañez-Perez J, Santos-Zorrozua B, Lopez-Lopez E, et al.
references.title: An update on the implication of physical activity on semen quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Most data show no major effect of activity on semen; recreational activity may help concentration or motility, while elite activity may harm motility, and cycling may lower concentration.

references.authors: Imboden MT, Harber MP, Whaley MH, et al.
references.title: The Association between the Change in Directly Measured Cardiorespiratory Fitness across Time and Mortality Risk.
references.finding: Change in directly measured VO2peak over time was inversely related to mortality (about 11% lower per 1 mL/kg/min gained), and the later test predicted death better than the first.

references.authors: Islam H, Bonafiglia JT, Turnbull PC, et al.
references.title: The impact of acute and chronic exercise on Nrf2 expression in relation to markers of mitochondrial biogenesis in human skeletal muscle.
references.finding: Acute and 4-week interval exercise raised Nrf2 and downstream targets in human muscle in step with mitochondrial biogenesis markers.

references.authors: Islam H, Gibala MJ, Little JP
references.title: Exercise Snacks: A Novel Strategy to Improve Cardiometabolic Health.
references.finding: Defines exercise snacks as 1 minute or less of vigorous exercise several times a day and summarises small proof-of-concept trials.

references.authors: Jackson MJ
references.title: Exercise-induced adaptations to homeostasis of reactive oxygen species in skeletal muscle.
references.finding: Reviews sources of superoxide and H2O2 in contracting muscle and proposes peroxiredoxins as the effectors that turn low H2O2 levels into adaptive signals.

references.authors: Jenkins EM, Nairn LN, Skelly LE, et al.
references.title: Do stair climbing exercise "snacks" improve cardiorespiratory fitness?
references.finding: Vigorously climbing 60 stairs 3 times a day, 3 days/week for 6 weeks modestly raised VO2peak.

references.authors: Kamada M, Shiroma EJ, Buring JE, et al.
references.title: Strength Training and All-Cause, Cardiovascular Disease, and Cancer Mortality in Older Women: A Cohort Study.
references.finding: Strength training showed a J-shaped association with mortality; benefit at moderate amounts, with point estimates returning to 1.0 at 146+ min/week (wide CIs).

references.authors: Kang J, Fardman BM, Ratamess NA, et al.
references.title: Efficacy of Postprandial Exercise in Mitigating Glycemic Responses in Overweight Individuals and Individuals with Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Post-meal exercise reduced glucose AUC (g -0.32) and 24-h mean glucose; bouts longer than 30 minutes worked better.

references.authors: Kankaanpää A, Tolvanen A, Joensuu L, et al.
references.title: The associations of long-term physical activity in adulthood with later biological ageing and all-cause mortality - a prospective twin study.
references.finding: Active classes had at most 7% lower mortality, mainly short-term; after accounting for familial factors and prevalent CVD, associations weakened, suggesting genetic confounding and reverse causation.

references.authors: Khurshid S, Al-Alusi MA, Churchill TW, et al.
references.title: Accelerometer-Derived "Weekend Warrior" Physical Activity and Incident Cardiovascular Disease.
references.finding: Accelerometer-defined weekend warriors and regularly active people had similarly lower risks of AF, MI, heart failure and stroke versus inactive people.

references.authors: Kim YS, Shin YH, Oh M, et al.
references.title: Association of weekend warrior physical activity pattern with health outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Weekend-warrior and regular patterns had similar associations with all-cause (RR 0.76 vs 0.71), CVD and cancer mortality compared with inactivity.

references.authors: Kjaergaard AD, Ellervik C, Jessen N, et al.
references.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness, Body Composition, Diabetes, and Longevity: A 2-Sample Mendelian Randomization Study.
references.finding: Two-sample Mendelian randomization: physical activity, lean mass and lower body fat raised genetically predicted VO2max, but genetically predicted VO2max was not causally associated with longevity or diabetes.

references.authors: Kodama S, Saito K, Tanaka S, et al.
references.title: Cardiorespiratory fitness as a quantitative predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy men and women: a meta-analysis.
references.finding: Each 1-MET higher fitness was associated with 13% lower all-cause mortality and 15% fewer CHD/CVD events; below 7.9 METs risk rose sharply.

references.authors: Koemel NA, Ahmadi MN, Biswas RK, et al.
references.title: Vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity (VILPA) and mortality risk among US adults: a wearables-based national cohort study.
references.journal: Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act
references.finding: About 5 VILPA bouts/day was associated with 44% lower mortality (HR 0.56), but after excluding people with prevalent CVD or cancer the confidence intervals mostly crossed 1.

references.authors: Kokkinos P, Faselis C, Samuel IBH, et al.
references.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Mortality Risk Across the Spectra of Age, Race, and Sex.
references.finding: Lowest mortality at about 14 METs (HR 0.24); the least fit had 4-fold higher risk than the extremely fit; no increase in risk at extreme fitness across age, sex and race.

references.authors: Kressler J, Millard-Stafford M, Warren GL
references.title: Quercetin and endurance exercise capacity: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Quercetin (median 1000 mg/day) gave a trivial-to-small improvement in endurance (ES 0.15, about 2%).

references.authors: Kujala UM, Kaprio J, Sarna S, et al.
references.title: Relationship of leisure-time physical activity and mortality: the Finnish twin cohort.
references.finding: Conditioning exercisers had 43% lower mortality than sedentary people, and the association persisted within twin pairs, i.e. beyond shared genes and family background.

references.authors: Kunutsor SK, Seidu S, Mäkikallio TH, et al.
references.title: Physical activity and risk of atrial fibrillation in the general population: meta-analysis of 23 cohort studies involving about 2 million participants.
references.finding: Most versus least active had no overall difference in AF (RR 0.99), but risk was higher in men (RR 1.20) and lower in women (RR 0.91).

references.authors: Lane AR, Magallanes CA, Hackney AC
references.title: Reproductive Dysfunction from Exercise Training: The "Exercise-Hypogonadal Male Condition".
references.finding: Men chronically doing endurance training can show persistently low free and total testosterone without raised LH ('exercise-hypogonadal male condition'); spermatogenesis problems may occur in some.

references.authors: Lang JJ, Prince SA, Merucci K, et al.
references.title: Cardiorespiratory fitness is a strong and consistent predictor of morbidity and mortality among adults: an overview of meta-analyses representing over 20.9 million observations from 199 unique cohort studies.
references.finding: High versus low fitness was associated with HR 0.47 for all-cause mortality; each 1 MET was linked to 11-17% lower mortality; certainty very low to moderate.

references.authors: Lee DC, Pate RR, Lavie CJ, et al.
references.title: Leisure-time running reduces all-cause and cardiovascular mortality risk.
references.finding: Runners had 30% lower all-cause and 45% lower CVD mortality than non-runners, with similar benefit across running doses down to 5-10 min/day at slow speeds.

references.authors: Lee IM, Shiroma EJ, Kamada M, et al.
references.title: Association of Step Volume and Intensity With All-Cause Mortality in Older Women.
references.finding: In women averaging 72 years, about 4,400 steps/day lowered mortality versus 2,700 (HR 0.59), levelling off around 7,500 steps/day; intensity did not add after volume.

references.authors: Lee DH, Rezende LFM, Ferrari G, et al.
references.title: Physical activity and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: assessing the impact of reverse causation and measurement error in two large prospective cohorts.
references.finding: Single or recent activity measures overstated benefit through reverse causation (J/U-shapes appeared); cumulative-average activity with lag time showed a robust inverse dose-response up to 150 MET-h/week.

references.authors: Leong DP, Teo KK, Rangarajan S, et al.
references.title: Prognostic value of grip strength: findings from the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study.
references.finding: Each 5 kg lower grip strength was associated with 16% higher all-cause mortality.

references.authors: Li GQ, Tang SY, Luo J, et al.
references.title: The intervention effects of resistance exercise on sarcopenia in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: In sarcopenia, resistance training raised grip strength by 2.95 kg, gait speed by 0.15 m/s and appendicular muscle index by 0.25 kg/m2.

references.authors: Little JP, Langley J, Lee M, et al.
references.title: Sprint exercise snacks: a novel approach to increase aerobic fitness.
references.finding: 3 x 20-second sprints spread through the day raised VO2peak about 4%, similar to the same sprints done in one session (~6%).

references.authors: Loh R, Stamatakis E, Folkerts D, et al.
references.title: Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting with Physical Activity Breaks on Blood Glucose, Insulin and Triacylglycerol Measures: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
references.finding: Activity breaks in sitting moderately lowered glucose (SMD -0.54), insulin (-0.56) and triglycerides (-0.26), with larger effects at higher BMI.

references.authors: MacInnis MJ, Zacharewicz E, Martin BJ, et al.
references.title: Superior mitochondrial adaptations in human skeletal muscle after interval compared to continuous single-leg cycling matched for total work.
references.finding: Single-leg HIIT increased citrate synthase and mitochondrial respiration more than work-matched moderate continuous training in the other leg.

references.authors: MacInnis MJ, Gibala MJ
references.title: Physiological adaptations to interval training and the role of exercise intensity.
references.finding: Interval training increases VO2max more than moderate training for a given volume; sprint training matches moderate training despite less volume.

references.authors: MacInnis MJ, Skelly LE, Gibala MJ
references.title: CrossTalk proposal: Exercise training intensity is more important than volume to promote increases in human skeletal muscle mitochondrial content.
references.finding: CrossTalk 'proposal' arguing training intensity matters more than volume for increasing human muscle mitochondrial content.

references.authors: Mandsager K, Harb S, Cremer P, et al.
references.title: Association of Cardiorespiratory Fitness With Long-term Mortality Among Adults Undergoing Exercise Treadmill Testing.
references.finding: Treadmill-measured fitness was inversely related to mortality with no upper limit: elite versus low performers HR 0.20.

references.authors: Margaritelis NV, Theodorou AA, Paschalis V, et al.
references.title: Adaptations to endurance training depend on exercise-induced oxidative stress: exploiting redox interindividual variability.
references.finding: Men with the smallest exercise-induced oxidative stress gained least in VO2max, time trial and Wingate after 6 weeks of training, supporting a role for ROS in adaptation without any supplement.

references.authors: Margaritelis NV, Paschalis V, Theodorou AA, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants in Personalized Nutrition and Exercise.
references.finding: Proposes that antioxidants help only people with a measured deficiency, arguing for personalised rather than blanket supplementation.

references.authors: Margonis K, Fatouros IG, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
references.title: Oxidative stress biomarkers responses to physical overtraining: implications for diagnosis.
references.finding: An overreaching resistance block raised urinary isoprostanes up to 7-fold and cut glutathione 31%, tracking the performance drop.

references.authors: Marijon E, Tafflet M, Antero-Jacquemin J, et al.
references.title: Mortality of French participants in the Tour de France (1947-2012).
references.finding: French Tour de France riders had 41% lower mortality than the general male population (SMR 0.59), though healthy-athlete selection cannot be excluded.

references.authors: Martinez-Negrin G, Acton JP, Cocksedge SP, et al.
references.title: The effect of dietary (poly)phenols on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: A systematic review and meta-analysis of human intervention trials.
references.finding: (Poly)phenols did not change training gains in strength, power or VO2max; isoflavones may add lean mass while resveratrol tended to impair adaptations (SMD -0.54, NS).

references.authors: Mason SA, Trewin AJ, Parker L, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant supplements and endurance exercise: Current evidence and mechanistic insights.
references.finding: No compelling support for most antioxidant supplements in endurance athletes; chronic 1000 mg vitamin C plus vitamin E is not recommended during heavy training, while acute NAC before an event may help.

references.authors: Mastaloudis A, Leonard SW, Traber MG
references.title: Oxidative stress in athletes during extreme endurance exercise.
references.finding: A 50 km ultramarathon raised plasma F2-isoprostanes from about 75 to 131 pg/mL, returning to baseline within 24 h.

references.authors: Merghani A, Maestrini V, Rosmini S, et al.
references.title: Prevalence of Subclinical Coronary Artery Disease in Masters Endurance Athletes With a Low Atherosclerotic Risk Profile.
references.finding: Most lifelong endurance athletes had normal CAC, but male athletes more often had CAC above 300 or plaques; plaques were mostly calcified.

references.authors: Merry TL, Ristow M
references.title: Do antioxidant supplements interfere with skeletal muscle adaptation to exercise training?
references.finding: Antioxidant supplements can blunt training-induced gains in antioxidant capacity, mitochondrial biogenesis and insulin sensitivity, but not universally, suggesting redundant signalling; harm is more consistent for resistance and high-intensity training.

references.authors: Milanović Z, Sporiš G, Weston M
references.title: Effectiveness of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) and Continuous Endurance Training for VO2max Improvements: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Endurance training raised VO2max by 4.9 and HIIT by 5.5 mL/kg/min versus controls; HIIT beat continuous training by a small 1.2 mL/kg/min.

references.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Chavarro JE, Mendiola J, et al.
references.title: Physical activity is not related to semen quality in young healthy men.
references.finding: Physical activity (top quartile 9.5+ h/week) was not related to semen quality.

references.authors: Mishima RS, Verdicchio CV, Noubiap JJ, et al.
references.title: Self-reported physical activity and atrial fibrillation risk: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Meeting activity guidelines was associated with lower AF risk (HR 0.94); the benefit was uncertain above about 2000 MET-min/week.

references.authors: Möhlenkamp S, Lehmann N, Breuckmann F, et al.
references.title: Running: the risk of coronary events : Prevalence and prognostic relevance of coronary atherosclerosis in marathon runners.
references.finding: Conventional risk scores underestimated coronary calcification in older marathon runners; higher CAC predicted events.

references.authors: Mølmen KS, Almquist NW, Skattebo Ø
references.title: Effects of Exercise Training on Mitochondrial and Capillary Growth in Human Skeletal Muscle: A Systematic Review and Meta-Regression.
references.finding: After adjustment, mitochondrial content rose similarly with continuous endurance (23%), HIIT (27%) and sprint training (27%); per hour, sprint and HIIT were 2.3-3.9x more time-efficient; higher frequency gave more gain.

references.authors: Momma H, Kawakami R, Honda T, et al.
references.title: Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies.
references.finding: Muscle-strengthening was associated with 10-17% lower all-cause, CVD and cancer mortality, with J-shaped curves peaking at about 30-60 min/week.

references.authors: Montero D, Lundby C
references.title: Refuting the myth of non-response to exercise training: 'non-responders' do respond to higher dose of training.
references.finding: Fitness 'non-response' fell as weekly training rose from 60 to 300 min and disappeared in all non-responders after adding two more sessions a week.

references.authors: Morrison D, Hughes J, Della Gatta PA, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation prevents some of the cellular adaptations to endurance-training in humans.
references.finding: Vitamin C plus E did not stop gains in VO2peak or mitochondrial markers but prevented some cellular adaptations (e.g. SOD2) after 4 weeks of HIIT.

references.authors: Morseth B, Graff-Iversen S, Jacobsen BK, et al.
references.title: Physical activity, resting heart rate, and atrial fibrillation: the Tromsø Study.
references.finding: Moderate activity was associated with 19% lower AF, while high and vigorous activity was not protective (vigorous HR 1.37, NS): a J-shaped pattern.

references.authors: Morseth B, Løchen ML, Ariansen I, et al.
references.title: The ambiguity of physical activity, exercise and atrial fibrillation.
references.finding: Describes a J-shaped activity-AF association and proposes different mechanisms (atrial remodelling, vagal tone) at very high training volumes.

references.authors: Mozaffarian D, Furberg CD, Psaty BM, et al.
references.title: Physical activity and incidence of atrial fibrillation in older adults: the cardiovascular health study.
references.finding: Leisure activity and walking were associated with up to 36% lower AF incidence in older adults.

references.authors: Newman W, Parry-Williams G, Wiles J, et al.
references.title: Risk of atrial fibrillation in athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Athletes had about 2.5 times the odds of atrial fibrillation of non-athlete controls (OR 2.46), with mixed-sport and younger athletes at highest risk.

references.authors: Nikolaidis MG, Kerksick CM, Lamprecht M, et al.
references.title: Does vitamin C and E supplementation impair the favorable adaptations of regular exercise?
references.finding: Concludes evidence on vitamin C/E blunting adaptation is contradictory, largely because of methodological differences, but that chronic non-physiological doses cannot be recommended.

references.authors: Norris T, Cooper R, Garfield V, et al.
references.title: Unpicking Causal Relationships Between Grip Strength and Cardiorespiratory Fitness: A Bidirectional Mendelian Randomization Study.
references.finding: Bidirectional Mendelian randomization: greater grip strength raised cardiorespiratory fitness, but fitness did not raise grip strength.
